Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 1–2 (part 1 of 3):

The basmalah has already been discussed, and much has been written about it in the books, since it occurs at the beginning of every work (...) and at every act, with what suits that act. So when reciting, you say: "In the name of Allah I recite"; when eating: "In the name of Allah I eat"; when drinking: "In the name of Allah I drink"; and when slaughtering: "In the name of Allah I slaughter"; as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Then let him slaughter in the name of Allah"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7400) and Muslim (1960 / 1), from the hadith of Jundub ibn 'Abdullah al-Bajali.]].

They estimated it as a verb, not a noun. Why? They estimated it as a verb (fi'l), not a noun (masdar); meaning, they said "I recite" and did not say "my recitation in the name of Allah." Rather they said the estimate is: "In the name of Allah I recite," not "In the name of Allah my recitation." For example?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. Continuity in the sense of stability and permanence; the verb indicates renewal and occurrence. This is one point, and it is a meaningful benefit.

Also, the original in governing is the verb. Therefore it is the one that is fitting to estimate rather than the noun, because the governing of the noun is a branch, not an origin. The active participle, for example, governs like the verb because it resembles it.

So we now say: it is estimated as a verb, because it is a naming accompanying an action, and the verb requires renewal and occurrence. This is the first point.

Second: because the origin in governing is what? The verb. It is the one that is strong enough to govern when elided.

Good. And they estimated it (...); meaning, they said one should say: "In the name of Allah I recite," not "I recite in the name of Allah." Why?
* Student: First: seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah the Exalted. Second: that fronting the object (mu'mal) implies restriction (hasr).
* The Shaykh: Correct: seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah, and second: implying restriction, because fronting the object indicates restriction.

They also estimated it as specific; meaning, they did not say, for example, when you want to perform wudu': "In the name of Allah I begin," or when you want to recite: "In the name of Allah I begin"; because it is more indicative of what? Of the intended meaning.

So the prepositional phrase with its genitive is dependent on an elided element, which is a specific, delayed verb.

The basmalah often occurs. When you want to perform wudu' you say: "In the name of Allah." What is the estimate?
* Student: "In the name of Allah I perform wudu'."
* The Shaykh: "In the name of Allah I perform wudu'." Better than estimating "my wudu' is in the name of Allah," for example, and better than estimating "In the name of Allah I begin." So one estimates the specific verb as delayed.

As for "Allah," it is a proper name for the Holy Essence, the Essence of Allah, glorified and exalted, and it is exclusive to Him. Its origin is al-Ilah, but due to frequent use they dropped the hamzah, just as they dropped the hamzah in "al-Nas" (the people), whose origin is "al-Anas."

So al-Ilah is the origin, and "Ilah" is on the pattern fi'āl in the sense of maf'ul; i.e., ma'luh, meaning worshipped. This word is therefore derived, and its origin is al-Ilah, and al-Uluhiyyah is worship.

And His saying "al-Rahman" is also one of the names specific to Allah, the Exalted. It is a sifah mushabbahah (attributive adjective of quality). We estimated it as a sifah mushabbahah because it is on its pattern, like fa'lan on the pattern of ghadban. Moreover, the sifah mushabbahah indicates stability and continuity, unlike the active participle.

This form "al-Rahman" came for the vastness of Allah's mercy, and some scholars explained it with this: "al-Rahman" is the One with all-encompassing mercy.

"Al-Rahim" is on the pattern fa'il. From what is it derived? From mercy also, but it indicates the action, i.e., the delivery of mercy to the one shown mercy. The first, "al-Rahman," indicates the attribute; the second indicates the act. For this reason He, exalted, said: ﴿The Most Merciful, established above the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha 5] when He intended the absolute attribute, and said: ﴿And He is ever merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab 43] when He intended the delivery of mercy to the one shown mercy.

So the conclusion now is that when "al-Rahman" and "al-Rahim" are combined, "al-Rahman" is explained as indicating the attribute more than the act, and "al-Rahim" indicates the act more than the attribute, though each of them indicates the attribute of mercy. This is when they are combined. When they are separate, their meaning is one.

* * *

"In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Merciful" ("﴿Blessed﴾" [al-Furqan 1] "exalted"). The author explained "Blessed" as "exalted," and there is no doubt that this explanation has some deficiency, because ﴿Blessed﴾ indicates exaltedness, and indeed abundance of good, its vastness, and its permanence; so its meaning is that His goodness is abundant, great, and continuous for the servants.

And His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan 1] is part of the blessing, which is among the attributes of Allah, the Exalted: that He ﴿sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾, Muhammad ﷺ.

"Nazzala" (the form fa''ala) indicates sending down gradually, and likewise the Noble Qur'an was sent down upon the Prophet ﷺ gradually, while the earlier scriptures were sent down all at once; as He said in this surah: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?" Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby, and We have spaced it out in gradual distinctness﴾ [al-Furqan 32].

And His saying: ﴿He sent down the Criterion﴾ indicates that this Qur'an is the speech of Allah.

If someone says: there is no proof in this that it is the speech of Allah, because Allah says: ﴿He sent down water from the sky﴾ [al-An'am 99], and the water, which is rain, is not an attribute of Allah, is it not so? Therefore, when Allah says that He sent down the Qur'an, it does not necessarily follow that the Qur'an is one of His attributes, because Allah ascribes sending down and revelation to what is not of His attribute.

The answer to that is: if Allah ascribes the sending down of something to Himself, then if that thing is an entity subsisting by itself, or an attribute in an entity subsisting by itself, it is not one of Allah's attributes. If it is an entity subsisting by itself, it is not one of Allah's attributes; or if it is an attribute in an entity subsisting by its own essence, it is not one of Allah's attributes.

And if it is an attribute that cannot subsist by itself, meaning it is not an entity subsisting by itself (...), an attribute in an entity subsisting by its own essence, then it necessarily follows that it is what?
* Student: An attribute.
* The Shaykh: An attribute of Allah. The Qur'an is speech. Can speech be an entity subsisting by itself?
* Student: It is not possible.
* The Shaykh: It is not possible. Here it was not ascribed to any of the people so that we could say it is an attribute in an entity subsisting by its own essence, which would then imply it was created in the entity in which it subsists. Thus it is determined, and what is determined? That it is the speech of Allah and one of His attributes. For this reason the People of the Sunnah and the Community used verses like this to prove that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah.
* It is also derived from His saying ﴿He sent down the Criterion﴾ that Allah is above in the heavens; the point of derivation is that sending down happens from a height, and since Allah sent down the Criterion, this indicates the highness of Allah, blessed and exalted.

And His saying: ﴿the Criterion﴾ is the Qur'an. It is described thus because it distinguishes between good and evil, between truth and falsehood, between the people of truth and the people of falsehood, and the people of good and the people of evil. So it is a criterion in every matter.

Just as it is a criterion in itself (...) it distinguishes, so whoever is of its people is given this quality: if he is of its people, adheres to it, and acts by it, he is given this quality and comes to have the ability to distinguish between truth and falsehood; because of the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion﴾ [al-Anfal 29].

﴿He sent down the Criterion﴾: if the Qur'an is a criterion between truth and falsehood and between good and evil, it necessarily follows that it is clear and evident, with no ambiguity and no difficulty in it, is it not so?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: How does this necessarily follow? Because if it contained ambiguity or confusion, it would not be a criterion; for how can what is confused be a criterion?! The criterion must be clear, clarifying, and manifest.

If someone says: Allah says: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech, a Book consistent [and paired]﴾ [al-Zumar 23], ﴿a Book consistent﴾, and this implies there is ambiguity in it.

We say: what is meant by "mutashabih" here is that some of it agrees with other parts, resembling one another in perfection and goodness; this is the meaning of mutashabih, as in His saying: ﴿and they were given it in resemblance﴾ [al-Baqarah 25], i.e., agreeing and similar. Likewise the Qur'an is mutashabih, meaning that part of it resembles another in goodness, agrees with it, and does not contradict it.

As for His saying: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are precise [muhkamat] ... and others [that are] unspecific [mutashabihat]﴾ [Al 'Imran 7], Allah has made clear that the muhkamat are the reference; ﴿they are the foundation of the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran 7]. Since they are the foundation of the Book, it necessarily follows that the mutashabih must be referred to what? To the muhkam. And when the mutashabih is referred to the muhkam, all becomes muhkam. This principle that Allah mentioned is the one held by those firm in knowledge, and it is what relieves a person from possibilities, because in the Qur'an and the Sunnah there always come texts that have possibilities: they may mean this and may mean that, while we have other texts that are clear, explicit, and free of difficulty. So what is obligatory for us? It is obligatory that we interpret this ambiguous text by the muhkam, i.e., by what agrees with it and does not contradict it, so that everything becomes muhkam.

﴿He sent down the Criterion﴾: we said that this verse indicates what? That the whole Qur'an is clear and explicit, with no difficulty; because it cannot be a criterion except in this way. And we answered what we raised from His saying: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech, a Book consistent [and paired]﴾ [al-Zumar 23]: the agreement and resemblance in perfection and judgment.

﴿He sent down the Criterion upon His servant⁠..⁠
* Student: Shaykh, an example of referring the mutashabih to the muhkam.
* The Shaykh: Yes. An example of referring the mutashabih to the muhkam is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid 4]. It may appear to a person that Allah is with us in His essence; but we have muhkam texts that indicate Allah's highness, and that essential togetherness in which Allah is with us in every place is impossible. So this is from the muhkam and the mutashabih; for this reason those in whose hearts is deviation follow this mutashabih, abandon the muhkam, and say that Allah is with us in His essence in every place. This is an example in news.

An example in ruling: the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "When one of you enters the mosque, let him not sit until he has prayed two rak'ahs"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1163) from Abu Qatadah al-Ansari, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. A man entered on Friday while he was delivering the khutbah, and sat. He said: "Have you prayed?" He said: No. He said: "Stand and pray two rak'ahs"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (931) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]. This is muhkam and clear (...) on the request for the two rak'ahs for everyone who enters the mosque, is it not so? That he should not sit until he has prayed two rak'ahs.

And there is in it the hadith of the three men who came to the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, among his companions: one of them sat, one entered the circle, and the third left[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (66) and Muslim (2176 / 26), from Abu Waqid al-Laythi, that while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sitting in the mosque with people around him, three men came; two came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and one went away. He said: they stood before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; one of them saw a gap in the circle and sat in it, the other sat behind them, and the third turned and left. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ finished, he said: "Shall I not tell you about the three men? As for one of them, he sought refuge with Allah, so Allah sheltered him; as for the other, he felt shy, so Allah was shy of him; and as for the other, he turned away, so Allah turned away from him."]]. In the hadith there is nothing indicating that any of them prayed two rak'ahs. So this is mutashabih, because it may indicate that it is not required, which is the sunnah of greeting the mosque. But we cannot abandon the muhkam hadith for the sake of this possibility; because of the possibility that these three men prayed while the Prophet saw them and did not object, and because of the possibility that they were without wudu', and other possibilities. Therefore we do not abandon the muhkam for the sake of this mutashabih, and the examples of this are many.

And His saying: ﴿upon His servant﴾: who is His servant? Muhammad ﷺ. This servanthood is the most distinguished of the servanthoods by which people are described, because servanthood is divided into three kinds: general, specific, and most specific.

The general is that which includes all creation, as in: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he will come to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93]; all creation are the servants of Allah. And also: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you﴾ [al-Hijr 42], where He excepted those among His servants who follow him.

The second: specific, as in His saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan 63].

The third, the most specific, is the servanthood of prophethood, as in His saying about Nuh: ﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾ [al-Isra' 3], and His saying about Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾. This is more specific than the first, because it is servanthood specific to a particular responsibility, which is prophethood.

Describing a human as a servant of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and ascribing him to Allah: is this an honor or a humiliation?
* The students: An honor.
* The Shaykh: An honor. There is no doubt that he has all the pride in being a servant of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Even a person loves to be ascribed to the servanthood of another human being if he loves that person. For this reason a poet says of his beloved:

"Do not call me except by 'O servant of her'..." [verse incomplete in the source]

That is, do not say: "O Muhammad, O Bakr, O Khalid, O Ali." No, there is a name more noble to him, which is that you say: "O servant of so-and-so," because he takes pride in being her servant.

So the servanthood of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is without doubt a source of pride for the worshipper when it is ascribed to Allah.

﴿upon His servant﴾ Muhammad ﷺ.

He says: (﴿the Criterion﴾ the Qur'an, because it distinguishes between truth and falsehood), and likewise between good and evil. (﴿upon His servant﴾ Muhammad ﷺ ﴿that he may be to the worlds﴾ i.e., mankind and jinn, not the angels.)

To whom does the pronoun in ﴿that he may be﴾ refer?
* Student: To Muhammad.
* The Shaykh: To Muhammad. ﴿He sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be﴾, i.e., Muhammad ﷺ; by the saying of Allah: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings, and a warner, and as one who invites to Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab 45, 46]; so the warner is Muhammad ﷺ.

It is possible that the pronoun in ﴿that he may be﴾ refers to the Criterion being a warner to the worlds, by His saying: ﴿that I may warn you thereby and whoever it reaches﴾ [al-An'am 19]; so warning is attributed to the Qur'an. But this is not the stronger view; the stronger view is the first. First: because the pronoun refers to the nearest preceding mention, which is directly before ﴿that he may be﴾, namely ﴿His servant﴾. Second: because Allah described the Prophet ﷺ with this in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings, and a warner﴾.

And His saying: ﴿to the worlds﴾: the world ('alam). The author says: "mankind and jinn, not the angels." As for mankind, it is clear; as for the jinn, likewise the texts indicate that the Prophet ﷺ was sent to them. What is the evidence for this?
* Student: His saying, Exalted: "And We have certainly directed to you [a company] of the jinn..."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 1–2 (part 2 of 3):

* The Shaykh: ﴿And when We turned towards you a company of the jinn, listening to the Quran﴾ [al-Ahqaf 29], and ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened and said: Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Quran﴾ [al-Jinn 1]. Likewise, the Prophet ﷺ said to them: "Every bone over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, you will find it with the most meat on it"[[Narrated by Muslim (450/15) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) with the wording: "For you, every bone over which the name of Allah has been mentioned that falls into your hands, [you will find it] with the most meat on it..." the hadith.]], and so he placed them under the rulings of the Shari'ah.

As for the angels, the evidence that he is not a messenger to them is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Say: If there were in the earth angels walking securely, We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger﴾ [al-Isra 95]. The verse indicates that angels are sent to by angels, and the Prophet ﷺ is not an angel. This requires that he not be a messenger to the angels. But must the angels believe in him or not?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Without doubt they believe in him. There is no doubt that they believe in the Messenger ﷺ, but he was not sent to them, nor was he charged with conveying to them, peace and blessings be upon him.

So ﴿to be a warner to the worlds﴾ is from the category of the general term intended in a specific sense, because the angels are among the worlds; ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah 2]. Everything other than Allah is a world ('alam).

As for His saying ﴿a warner﴾: the nadhir is one who announces or informs of what causes fear, and the bashir is one who informs of what gladdens. So the nadhir is one who informs of what causes fear. On this basis, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, informs of what causes fear, and this does not preclude that he is also a bashir (bringer of glad tidings). Allah has mentioned both states in His saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah who sent down to His servant the Book and did not make therein any crookedness (1), [but made it] straight, to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward (2), abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Kahf 1–3]. Therefore, limiting oneself to glad tidings or warning in one place does not necessitate negating the other. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is described by both.

* A student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, this is by way of warning. But it is restricted, like: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran 21]. Some of them said: this is by way of mockery toward them, meaning (...) with punishment, which is not normally announced as good news. And some say: No, when it is restricted by something, it is restricted by it; but when unrestricted, it is in the good.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿to be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan 1].

* What is derived from the noble verse, ﴿li-yakun (that he may be)﴾: it establishes wisdom in the acts of Allah, because the lam in His saying ﴿li-yakun﴾ is for causation (ta'lil). If it is for causation, this indicates that it conveys wisdom, since the 'illah (cause, reason) is what motivates a thing or is its purpose; that is, the 'illah is either final (ghā'iyyah) or motivating (bā'ithah), and each of them indicates wisdom.

* And His saying ﴿to be a warner to the worlds﴾: from it is derived the universality of the Prophet's ﷺ mission, and that whoever says he is a messenger only to the Arabs is a disbeliever in him. Take care, O people! Those who said he was a messenger to the Arabs said: Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿It is He who raised among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 2]. This requires that he is a messenger only to the Arabs, and that the Children of Israel are not obligated to follow the Messenger ﷺ. So what is the answer to this doubt? This is among the ambiguous (mutashabihah) verses.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. Therefore we say: ﴿among the unlettered﴾ is not (...). If the intent were to restrict them, He would have said: "He it is who sent to the unlettered," as in His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾ [al-Nisa 79]: "We sent you to mankind." But ﴿among the unlettered﴾ — it is true that the Messenger was sent among them, he was sent among them, not to them only; he was sent among them for them and for others; ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾.

When I say, for example: "So-and-so was sent in this country," or for instance: "Allah created in this country a generous man," or "a scholar," or what is similar to that, is he only for the country? No. His place is in the country, that is correct, but what comes from him is general. Thus restriction by place or restriction by time does not indicate restriction of the call. From it is derived the universality of the mission of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

* And from it is also derived: the excellence of the Messenger ﷺ, in that he was charged with the message to all creation; because this is evidence of his excellence and that he is worthy of this great task, is it not? If you send a person to reconcile two individuals, this is evidence of his merit; but if you send a person to reconcile between two groups or two nations, this increases his merit. For this reason, none attains this last task except one who is deserving of it. So the fact that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent to all of the (...) is evidence of his excellence, since he carried the message to all creation.

Then there is in it also evidence of Allah's favour upon him, because everyone who benefits from his message accrues to him, that is, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, a share of his reward. Is that not so?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: "Whoever guides to good has a reward like that of its doer, without that diminishing anything from his reward."[[The statement "Whoever guides to good has a reward like that of its doer" is narrated by Muslim (1893/133) from Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him). As for "without that diminishing anything from his reward," it is from another hadith narrated by Muslim (1017/69) and al-Darimi (529), with the wording of al-Darimi, from the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali (may Allah be pleased with him): "Whoever establishes a good practice, and it is acted upon after him, he will have a reward like the reward of those who act upon it, without that diminishing anything from their reward..." the hadith.]] Therefore, if you teach a person and he acts upon your knowledge and teaches another, and that one teaches another, and another, you will receive reward and merit in proportion to those who benefited from it.

﴿to be a warner to the worlds (1). He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Furqan 1, 2].

(﴿a warner﴾: one who frightens from the punishment of Allah, the Exalted.)

(﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and who has not taken a son, and has no partner in the dominion, and created everything﴾, of a nature to be created, ﴿and determined for it a measure﴾ [al-Furqan 2]: He made it proportionate.)

﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: this is an attribute of His saying ﴿He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the sending down of the Criterion, which is legislation and organization. Then He followed it with His saying ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, indicating that it is obligatory to act upon what came in this Criterion, because it came from whom? From the Owner of the heavens and the earth, and the owner has the right to dispose of his property, by legislating for it whatever He wills and organizing for it whatever He wills. This is the benefit of His saying ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens﴾ after His saying ﴿He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾. So He brought the legislation first, or the constitution of legislation, as they say, then after that He brought the generality of dominion, because when He, glory be to Him, is the general owner of the heavens and the earth, it necessarily follows that what He has legislated is binding upon those who are owned.

﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. Now, is this dominion ownership of the substances only, or ownership of substances and disposal? It is ownership of substances and disposal. Why? Because ownership may be of the thing without the right of disposal over it, and it may be of the right of disposal without the thing itself; that is, a person may own the disposal of a thing without its essence, or own the essence of a thing without the right to dispose of it.

The owner of a thing to which no one else's right is attached owns the substance and the disposal of it. The one for whom an endowment (waqf) is made owns the substance but does not have full disposal of it: he may not sell it, nor give it away, nor is it inherited from him. The renter owns the usufruct, the right to dispose of the usufruct only, without the substance.

As for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, He has the dominion of the heavens and the earth, their substances and the disposal of them.

Now, did He not mention the dominion of those in them, in ﴿the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, because the heavens and the earth include all who are in them; for those in the heavens and the earth are from the heavens and the earth, their origin is from the heavens and the earth. Man was created from clay, and the other animals, as it appears, Allah knows best, though we do not know anything about them, were created from the earth. But what matters is that we know our origin; as for these, Allah created them for us: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is in the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 29] (...).

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and He has not taken a son﴾. ﴿A son﴾ means a begotten one. The phrase ﴿and has not taken a son﴾ is more general than His saying ﴿He neither begets nor is begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas 3]. Nevertheless, Allah negated of Himself the taking of a son and begetting. He, glory be to Him, did not beget and did not take a son from among His servants. In this is a refutation of whose saying? 

* A student: The Christians.

* The Shaykh: The saying of the Christians who said: the Messiah is the son of Allah; and the saying of the Jews who said: 'Uzayr is the son of Allah; and of the polytheists who said: the angels are the daughters of Allah. So Allah, glory be to Him, did not beget anything, and did not take any of His creation as a son; ﴿and has not taken a son, and has no partner in the dominion﴾.

Now, we mentioned earlier that when Allah negates an attribute from Himself, the purpose is not merely negating the attribute, but negating the attribute and affirming the perfection of its opposite. So what is the opposite here?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes: the perfection of His power and His self-sufficiency, and that He has no need of a son, due to the perfection of His independence from others. One only needs a son or takes a son if he is in need of one; but whoever is independent of it, capable of what he wills, does not take a son.

﴿and has no partner in the dominion﴾. Yes, Allah, glory be to Him, has no partner in the dominion; no one shares it with Him, not any of the angels, not any of the prophets, not any of those beneath them. The dominion belongs to Allah alone, with no partner in it.

In this is a refutation of those who associate partners with Allah in lordship (rububiyyah), such as those who say that some saints (awliya') dispose of the universe. These are without doubt in error, and they are also liars in what they report; for they are wrong in their creed and lying in what they relate. Allah, glory be to Him, has no partner in His dominion.

And His saying: ﴿and has no partner in the dominion﴾. If someone says: Do we not own our houses, own our clothes, and own our livestock? Does this necessitate that Allah has a partner?

The answer: No. Because our ownership of these things is not absolute ownership. It is true that I own my house, own my garment, own my car, and own my livestock, but my ownership of these things is not absolute; the proof is that I am restricted by the Shari'ah in disposing of these things. Do I have the right, for example, to neglect them so that I burn them, or do I not have that right?

* A student: It is forbidden.

* The Shaykh: I do not have that right; it is forbidden for me. I do not have the right, for example, to burden an animal in carrying and riding and other things. Therefore my being an owner (...) does not make me a partner of Allah, the Exalted, in His dominion; because this ownership of mine is restricted according to the permission of the Lawgiver to me. I do not dispose of it except as Allah, the Exalted, has permitted.

﴿and has no partner in the dominion, and created everything﴾. The commentator says: (of a nature to be created).

﴿and created everything﴾ indicates generality, but the commentator restricted it by his saying: (of a nature to be created). Why did he restrict it by his saying: (of a nature to be created)?

* A student: So that the Qur'an is not included.

* The Shaykh: Yes, so that the Qur'an, or Himself for example, is not included. If someone says: Did Allah create Himself? This is impossible; it is impossible that He creates Himself. Yet he still says: (of a nature to be created). As for what is not of a nature to be created, such as the essence of Allah and the attributes of Allah, this is not included from the outset, because Allah is the Creator, and the Creator is other than the created, and the attributes of the Creator are not created, because the attribute follows the essence. For this reason it is as if the author, when he says (of a nature to be created), alerts you so that you may answer with this word those who said that the Qur'an is created, and you say: the Qur'an is not of a nature to be created, because it is among the attributes of Allah, the Exalted, and the attributes of Allah, the Exalted, are not created.

But we should not restrict the verse by this; we say: He created everything. Can the Creator be the created, or other than the uncreated? It is not possible. So if it is not possible, this indicates that Allah, the Exalted, is not created, and that His attributes are also not created, because the attribute follows the described. Then there is no need to say: of a nature to be created; for if we say: of a nature to be created, we have restricted the noble verse.

The one who says the Qur'an is created may argue against us, saying: Who told you that the verse is restricted by this?

So we say: ﴿and created everything﴾ absolutely and generally, and this does not necessitate that the Qur'an be created, because the Creator is other than the created, and the Qur'an is among the attributes of Allah, and the attributes of the Creator are certainly not created, because the attributes follow the essence.

So now, if the Mu'tazilah and the Jahmiyyah, who say that the Qur'an is created, argue against us, how do we answer them? We answer them with one of two ways:

The first way: what the author indicated, namely that it is said: this is from the category of the general term intended in a specific sense; that is, everything that is of a nature to be created. This is one way, and many of the early scholars answered with it. They said: If someone says the Qur'an is created, and cites His saying ﴿and created everything﴾, then say to him: Allah said about the wind of 'Ad: ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾, yet it did not destroy the sky, nor the earth, nor the dwellings; ﴿so that nothing could be seen but their dwellings﴾ [al-Ahqaf 25].

Another group of scholars says: No, the verse is general, and the Qur'an is not included at all, so that we would need to exclude it. Why? Because if He is the Creator, the Creator is other than the created, and the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, and the speech of Allah is among His attributes, and the attributes of the Creator are not created; for the attribute follows what? The described.

﴿and created everything and determined for it a measure﴾. What does the particle fa (then) indicate? It indicates sequence.

And (qaddarahu) means (sawwarahu, shaped it), because creation may exist without proportioning; so Allah created everything and then determined it, that is, proportioned it.

The evidence that taqdir here means proportioning is His saying: ﴿He who created and proportioned﴾ [al-A'la 2]. On this basis, the sequence in His saying ﴿and created everything, then determined it﴾ is the sequence according to reality: it is a real sequence, because proportioning comes after creating; when you produce a building, first you produce the frame, then you introduce the adjustments and refinements. Likewise Allah, glory be to Him, created everything and then determined it; that is, proportioned it with a proportioning fitting to what it was created for.

Some scholars said: the meaning of ﴿qaddarahu﴾ is "qadaahu" (He decreed it), so the verse indicates both decree and creation. According to this view, which takes taqdir to mean qada' (decree), there is a non-factual sequence in the verse. The reason: taqdir in the sense of qada' precedes creation, does it not? For Allah decrees first and then creates second.

But which of the two is better? The better view is that the sequence is factual, and that creation comes before determination. This is also indicated by the noble verse: ﴿the One who created and then proportioned﴾. His saying ﴿created, then proportioned﴾ shows this, for the Qur'an explains one part of itself by another, and we take taqdir here to mean taswiyah (proportioning).

As for the sequence coming contrary to the factual order: although this occurs in the Arabic language, it is contrary to what is customary. Otherwise it has been said: whoever repented, then his father repented, and after that his grandfather repented, so (...) the grandfather is the first, and in sequence here he is the last. But the closer and more appropriate view is the one the author adopted, namely that taqdir here means taswiyah, because the speech of Allah explains one part of it by another (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 1–2 (part 1 of 3):

The basmalah has already been discussed, and much has been written about it in the books, since it occurs at the beginning of every work (...) and at every act, with what suits that act. So when reciting, you say: "In the name of Allah I recite"; when eating: "In the name of Allah I eat"; when drinking: "In the name of Allah I drink"; and when slaughtering: "In the name of Allah I slaughter"; as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Then let him slaughter in the name of Allah"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7400) and Muslim (1960 / 1), from the hadith of Jundub ibn 'Abdullah al-Bajali.]].

They estimated it as a verb, not a noun. Why? They estimated it as a verb (fi'l), not a noun (masdar); meaning, they said "I recite" and did not say "my recitation in the name of Allah." Rather they said the estimate is: "In the name of Allah I recite," not "In the name of Allah my recitation." For example?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. Continuity in the sense of stability and permanence; the verb indicates renewal and occurrence. This is one point, and it is a meaningful benefit.

Also, the original in governing is the verb. Therefore it is the one that is fitting to estimate rather than the noun, because the governing of the noun is a branch, not an origin. The active participle, for example, governs like the verb because it resembles it.

So we now say: it is estimated as a verb, because it is a naming accompanying an action, and the verb requires renewal and occurrence. This is the first point.

Second: because the origin in governing is what? The verb. It is the one that is strong enough to govern when elided.

Good. And they estimated it (...); meaning, they said one should say: "In the name of Allah I recite," not "I recite in the name of Allah." Why?
* Student: First: seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah the Exalted. Second: that fronting the object (mu'mal) implies restriction (hasr).
* The Shaykh: Correct: seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah, and second: implying restriction, because fronting the object indicates restriction.

They also estimated it as specific; meaning, they did not say, for example, when you want to perform wudu': "In the name of Allah I begin," or when you want to recite: "In the name of Allah I begin"; because it is more indicative of what? Of the intended meaning.

So the prepositional phrase with its genitive is dependent on an elided element, which is a specific, delayed verb.

The basmalah often occurs. When you want to perform wudu' you say: "In the name of Allah." What is the estimate?
* Student: "In the name of Allah I perform wudu'."
* The Shaykh: "In the name of Allah I perform wudu'." Better than estimating "my wudu' is in the name of Allah," for example, and better than estimating "In the name of Allah I begin." So one estimates the specific verb as delayed.

As for "Allah," it is a proper name for the Holy Essence, the Essence of Allah, glorified and exalted, and it is exclusive to Him. Its origin is al-Ilah, but due to frequent use they dropped the hamzah, just as they dropped the hamzah in "al-Nas" (the people), whose origin is "al-Anas."

So al-Ilah is the origin, and "Ilah" is on the pattern fi'āl in the sense of maf'ul; i.e., ma'luh, meaning worshipped. This word is therefore derived, and its origin is al-Ilah, and al-Uluhiyyah is worship.

And His saying "al-Rahman" is also one of the names specific to Allah, the Exalted. It is a sifah mushabbahah (attributive adjective of quality). We estimated it as a sifah mushabbahah because it is on its pattern, like fa'lan on the pattern of ghadban. Moreover, the sifah mushabbahah indicates stability and continuity, unlike the active participle.

This form "al-Rahman" came for the vastness of Allah's mercy, and some scholars explained it with this: "al-Rahman" is the One with all-encompassing mercy.

"Al-Rahim" is on the pattern fa'il. From what is it derived? From mercy also, but it indicates the action, i.e., the delivery of mercy to the one shown mercy. The first, "al-Rahman," indicates the attribute; the second indicates the act. For this reason He, exalted, said: ﴿The Most Merciful, established above the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha 5] when He intended the absolute attribute, and said: ﴿And He is ever merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab 43] when He intended the delivery of mercy to the one shown mercy.

So the conclusion now is that when "al-Rahman" and "al-Rahim" are combined, "al-Rahman" is explained as indicating the attribute more than the act, and "al-Rahim" indicates the act more than the attribute, though each of them indicates the attribute of mercy. This is when they are combined. When they are separate, their meaning is one.

* * *

"In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Merciful" ("﴿Blessed﴾" [al-Furqan 1] "exalted"). The author explained "Blessed" as "exalted," and there is no doubt that this explanation has some deficiency, because ﴿Blessed﴾ indicates exaltedness, and indeed abundance of good, its vastness, and its permanence; so its meaning is that His goodness is abundant, great, and continuous for the servants.

And His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan 1] is part of the blessing, which is among the attributes of Allah, the Exalted: that He ﴿sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾, Muhammad ﷺ.

"Nazzala" (the form fa''ala) indicates sending down gradually, and likewise the Noble Qur'an was sent down upon the Prophet ﷺ gradually, while the earlier scriptures were sent down all at once; as He said in this surah: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?" Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby, and We have spaced it out in gradual distinctness﴾ [al-Furqan 32].

And His saying: ﴿He sent down the Criterion﴾ indicates that this Qur'an is the speech of Allah.

If someone says: there is no proof in this that it is the speech of Allah, because Allah says: ﴿He sent down water from the sky﴾ [al-An'am 99], and the water, which is rain, is not an attribute of Allah, is it not so? Therefore, when Allah says that He sent down the Qur'an, it does not necessarily follow that the Qur'an is one of His attributes, because Allah ascribes sending down and revelation to what is not of His attribute.

The answer to that is: if Allah ascribes the sending down of something to Himself, then if that thing is an entity subsisting by itself, or an attribute in an entity subsisting by itself, it is not one of Allah's attributes. If it is an entity subsisting by itself, it is not one of Allah's attributes; or if it is an attribute in an entity subsisting by its own essence, it is not one of Allah's attributes.

And if it is an attribute that cannot subsist by itself, meaning it is not an entity subsisting by itself (...), an attribute in an entity subsisting by its own essence, then it necessarily follows that it is what?
* Student: An attribute.
* The Shaykh: An attribute of Allah. The Qur'an is speech. Can speech be an entity subsisting by itself?
* Student: It is not possible.
* The Shaykh: It is not possible. Here it was not ascribed to any of the people so that we could say it is an attribute in an entity subsisting by its own essence, which would then imply it was created in the entity in which it subsists. Thus it is determined, and what is determined? That it is the speech of Allah and one of His attributes. For this reason the People of the Sunnah and the Community used verses like this to prove that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah.
* It is also derived from His saying ﴿He sent down the Criterion﴾ that Allah is above in the heavens; the point of derivation is that sending down happens from a height, and since Allah sent down the Criterion, this indicates the highness of Allah, blessed and exalted.

And His saying: ﴿the Criterion﴾ is the Qur'an. It is described thus because it distinguishes between good and evil, between truth and falsehood, between the people of truth and the people of falsehood, and the people of good and the people of evil. So it is a criterion in every matter.

Just as it is a criterion in itself (...) it distinguishes, so whoever is of its people is given this quality: if he is of its people, adheres to it, and acts by it, he is given this quality and comes to have the ability to distinguish between truth and falsehood; because of the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion﴾ [al-Anfal 29].

﴿He sent down the Criterion﴾: if the Qur'an is a criterion between truth and falsehood and between good and evil, it necessarily follows that it is clear and evident, with no ambiguity and no difficulty in it, is it not so?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: How does this necessarily follow? Because if it contained ambiguity or confusion, it would not be a criterion; for how can what is confused be a criterion?! The criterion must be clear, clarifying, and manifest.

If someone says: Allah says: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech, a Book consistent [and paired]﴾ [al-Zumar 23], ﴿a Book consistent﴾, and this implies there is ambiguity in it.

We say: what is meant by "mutashabih" here is that some of it agrees with other parts, resembling one another in perfection and goodness; this is the meaning of mutashabih, as in His saying: ﴿and they were given it in resemblance﴾ [al-Baqarah 25], i.e., agreeing and similar. Likewise the Qur'an is mutashabih, meaning that part of it resembles another in goodness, agrees with it, and does not contradict it.

As for His saying: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are precise [muhkamat] ... and others [that are] unspecific [mutashabihat]﴾ [Al 'Imran 7], Allah has made clear that the muhkamat are the reference; ﴿they are the foundation of the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran 7]. Since they are the foundation of the Book, it necessarily follows that the mutashabih must be referred to what? To the muhkam. And when the mutashabih is referred to the muhkam, all becomes muhkam. This principle that Allah mentioned is the one held by those firm in knowledge, and it is what relieves a person from possibilities, because in the Qur'an and the Sunnah there always come texts that have possibilities: they may mean this and may mean that, while we have other texts that are clear, explicit, and free of difficulty. So what is obligatory for us? It is obligatory that we interpret this ambiguous text by the muhkam, i.e., by what agrees with it and does not contradict it, so that everything becomes muhkam.

﴿He sent down the Criterion﴾: we said that this verse indicates what? That the whole Qur'an is clear and explicit, with no difficulty; because it cannot be a criterion except in this way. And we answered what we raised from His saying: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech, a Book consistent [and paired]﴾ [al-Zumar 23]: the agreement and resemblance in perfection and judgment.

﴿He sent down the Criterion upon His servant⁠..⁠
* Student: Shaykh, an example of referring the mutashabih to the muhkam.
* The Shaykh: Yes. An example of referring the mutashabih to the muhkam is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid 4]. It may appear to a person that Allah is with us in His essence; but we have muhkam texts that indicate Allah's highness, and that essential togetherness in which Allah is with us in every place is impossible. So this is from the muhkam and the mutashabih; for this reason those in whose hearts is deviation follow this mutashabih, abandon the muhkam, and say that Allah is with us in His essence in every place. This is an example in news.

An example in ruling: the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "When one of you enters the mosque, let him not sit until he has prayed two rak'ahs"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1163) from Abu Qatadah al-Ansari, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. A man entered on Friday while he was delivering the khutbah, and sat. He said: "Have you prayed?" He said: No. He said: "Stand and pray two rak'ahs"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (931) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]. This is muhkam and clear (...) on the request for the two rak'ahs for everyone who enters the mosque, is it not so? That he should not sit until he has prayed two rak'ahs.

And there is in it the hadith of the three men who came to the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, among his companions: one of them sat, one entered the circle, and the third left[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (66) and Muslim (2176 / 26), from Abu Waqid al-Laythi, that while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sitting in the mosque with people around him, three men came; two came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and one went away. He said: they stood before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; one of them saw a gap in the circle and sat in it, the other sat behind them, and the third turned and left. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ finished, he said: "Shall I not tell you about the three men? As for one of them, he sought refuge with Allah, so Allah sheltered him; as for the other, he felt shy, so Allah was shy of him; and as for the other, he turned away, so Allah turned away from him."]]. In the hadith there is nothing indicating that any of them prayed two rak'ahs. So this is mutashabih, because it may indicate that it is not required, which is the sunnah of greeting the mosque. But we cannot abandon the muhkam hadith for the sake of this possibility; because of the possibility that these three men prayed while the Prophet saw them and did not object, and because of the possibility that they were without wudu', and other possibilities. Therefore we do not abandon the muhkam for the sake of this mutashabih, and the examples of this are many.

And His saying: ﴿upon His servant﴾: who is His servant? Muhammad ﷺ. This servanthood is the most distinguished of the servanthoods by which people are described, because servanthood is divided into three kinds: general, specific, and most specific.

The general is that which includes all creation, as in: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he will come to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93]; all creation are the servants of Allah. And also: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you﴾ [al-Hijr 42], where He excepted those among His servants who follow him.

The second: specific, as in His saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan 63].

The third, the most specific, is the servanthood of prophethood, as in His saying about Nuh: ﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾ [al-Isra' 3], and His saying about Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾. This is more specific than the first, because it is servanthood specific to a particular responsibility, which is prophethood.

Describing a human as a servant of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and ascribing him to Allah: is this an honor or a humiliation?
* The students: An honor.
* The Shaykh: An honor. There is no doubt that he has all the pride in being a servant of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Even a person loves to be ascribed to the servanthood of another human being if he loves that person. For this reason a poet says of his beloved:

"Do not call me except by 'O servant of her'..." [verse incomplete in the source]

That is, do not say: "O Muhammad, O Bakr, O Khalid, O Ali." No, there is a name more noble to him, which is that you say: "O servant of so-and-so," because he takes pride in being her servant.

So the servanthood of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is without doubt a source of pride for the worshipper when it is ascribed to Allah.

﴿upon His servant﴾ Muhammad ﷺ.

He says: (﴿the Criterion﴾ the Qur'an, because it distinguishes between truth and falsehood), and likewise between good and evil. (﴿upon His servant﴾ Muhammad ﷺ ﴿that he may be to the worlds﴾ i.e., mankind and jinn, not the angels.)

To whom does the pronoun in ﴿that he may be﴾ refer?
* Student: To Muhammad.
* The Shaykh: To Muhammad. ﴿He sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be﴾, i.e., Muhammad ﷺ; by the saying of Allah: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings, and a warner, and as one who invites to Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab 45, 46]; so the warner is Muhammad ﷺ.

It is possible that the pronoun in ﴿that he may be﴾ refers to the Criterion being a warner to the worlds, by His saying: ﴿that I may warn you thereby and whoever it reaches﴾ [al-An'am 19]; so warning is attributed to the Qur'an. But this is not the stronger view; the stronger view is the first. First: because the pronoun refers to the nearest preceding mention, which is directly before ﴿that he may be﴾, namely ﴿His servant﴾. Second: because Allah described the Prophet ﷺ with this in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings, and a warner﴾.

And His saying: ﴿to the worlds﴾: the world ('alam). The author says: "mankind and jinn, not the angels." As for mankind, it is clear; as for the jinn, likewise the texts indicate that the Prophet ﷺ was sent to them. What is the evidence for this?
* Student: His saying, Exalted: "And We have certainly directed to you [a company] of the jinn..."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 1–2 (part 2 of 3):

* The Shaykh: ﴿And when We turned towards you a company of the jinn, listening to the Quran﴾ [al-Ahqaf 29], and ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened and said: Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Quran﴾ [al-Jinn 1]. Likewise, the Prophet ﷺ said to them: "Every bone over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, you will find it with the most meat on it"[[Narrated by Muslim (450/15) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) with the wording: "For you, every bone over which the name of Allah has been mentioned that falls into your hands, [you will find it] with the most meat on it..." the hadith.]], and so he placed them under the rulings of the Shari'ah.

As for the angels, the evidence that he is not a messenger to them is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Say: If there were in the earth angels walking securely, We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger﴾ [al-Isra 95]. The verse indicates that angels are sent to by angels, and the Prophet ﷺ is not an angel. This requires that he not be a messenger to the angels. But must the angels believe in him or not?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Without doubt they believe in him. There is no doubt that they believe in the Messenger ﷺ, but he was not sent to them, nor was he charged with conveying to them, peace and blessings be upon him.

So ﴿to be a warner to the worlds﴾ is from the category of the general term intended in a specific sense, because the angels are among the worlds; ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah 2]. Everything other than Allah is a world ('alam).

As for His saying ﴿a warner﴾: the nadhir is one who announces or informs of what causes fear, and the bashir is one who informs of what gladdens. So the nadhir is one who informs of what causes fear. On this basis, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, informs of what causes fear, and this does not preclude that he is also a bashir (bringer of glad tidings). Allah has mentioned both states in His saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah who sent down to His servant the Book and did not make therein any crookedness (1), [but made it] straight, to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward (2), abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Kahf 1–3]. Therefore, limiting oneself to glad tidings or warning in one place does not necessitate negating the other. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is described by both.

* A student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, this is by way of warning. But it is restricted, like: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran 21]. Some of them said: this is by way of mockery toward them, meaning (...) with punishment, which is not normally announced as good news. And some say: No, when it is restricted by something, it is restricted by it; but when unrestricted, it is in the good.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿to be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan 1].

* What is derived from the noble verse, ﴿li-yakun (that he may be)﴾: it establishes wisdom in the acts of Allah, because the lam in His saying ﴿li-yakun﴾ is for causation (ta'lil). If it is for causation, this indicates that it conveys wisdom, since the 'illah (cause, reason) is what motivates a thing or is its purpose; that is, the 'illah is either final (ghā'iyyah) or motivating (bā'ithah), and each of them indicates wisdom.

* And His saying ﴿to be a warner to the worlds﴾: from it is derived the universality of the Prophet's ﷺ mission, and that whoever says he is a messenger only to the Arabs is a disbeliever in him. Take care, O people! Those who said he was a messenger to the Arabs said: Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿It is He who raised among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 2]. This requires that he is a messenger only to the Arabs, and that the Children of Israel are not obligated to follow the Messenger ﷺ. So what is the answer to this doubt? This is among the ambiguous (mutashabihah) verses.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. Therefore we say: ﴿among the unlettered﴾ is not (...). If the intent were to restrict them, He would have said: "He it is who sent to the unlettered," as in His saying: ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾ [al-Nisa 79]: "We sent you to mankind." But ﴿among the unlettered﴾ — it is true that the Messenger was sent among them, he was sent among them, not to them only; he was sent among them for them and for others; ﴿And We have sent you to mankind as a messenger﴾.

When I say, for example: "So-and-so was sent in this country," or for instance: "Allah created in this country a generous man," or "a scholar," or what is similar to that, is he only for the country? No. His place is in the country, that is correct, but what comes from him is general. Thus restriction by place or restriction by time does not indicate restriction of the call. From it is derived the universality of the mission of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

* And from it is also derived: the excellence of the Messenger ﷺ, in that he was charged with the message to all creation; because this is evidence of his excellence and that he is worthy of this great task, is it not? If you send a person to reconcile two individuals, this is evidence of his merit; but if you send a person to reconcile between two groups or two nations, this increases his merit. For this reason, none attains this last task except one who is deserving of it. So the fact that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent to all of the (...) is evidence of his excellence, since he carried the message to all creation.

Then there is in it also evidence of Allah's favour upon him, because everyone who benefits from his message accrues to him, that is, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, a share of his reward. Is that not so?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: "Whoever guides to good has a reward like that of its doer, without that diminishing anything from his reward."[[The statement "Whoever guides to good has a reward like that of its doer" is narrated by Muslim (1893/133) from Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him). As for "without that diminishing anything from his reward," it is from another hadith narrated by Muslim (1017/69) and al-Darimi (529), with the wording of al-Darimi, from the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali (may Allah be pleased with him): "Whoever establishes a good practice, and it is acted upon after him, he will have a reward like the reward of those who act upon it, without that diminishing anything from their reward..." the hadith.]] Therefore, if you teach a person and he acts upon your knowledge and teaches another, and that one teaches another, and another, you will receive reward and merit in proportion to those who benefited from it.

﴿to be a warner to the worlds (1). He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Furqan 1, 2].

(﴿a warner﴾: one who frightens from the punishment of Allah, the Exalted.)

(﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and who has not taken a son, and has no partner in the dominion, and created everything﴾, of a nature to be created, ﴿and determined for it a measure﴾ [al-Furqan 2]: He made it proportionate.)

﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: this is an attribute of His saying ﴿He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the sending down of the Criterion, which is legislation and organization. Then He followed it with His saying ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, indicating that it is obligatory to act upon what came in this Criterion, because it came from whom? From the Owner of the heavens and the earth, and the owner has the right to dispose of his property, by legislating for it whatever He wills and organizing for it whatever He wills. This is the benefit of His saying ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens﴾ after His saying ﴿He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾. So He brought the legislation first, or the constitution of legislation, as they say, then after that He brought the generality of dominion, because when He, glory be to Him, is the general owner of the heavens and the earth, it necessarily follows that what He has legislated is binding upon those who are owned.

﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. Now, is this dominion ownership of the substances only, or ownership of substances and disposal? It is ownership of substances and disposal. Why? Because ownership may be of the thing without the right of disposal over it, and it may be of the right of disposal without the thing itself; that is, a person may own the disposal of a thing without its essence, or own the essence of a thing without the right to dispose of it.

The owner of a thing to which no one else's right is attached owns the substance and the disposal of it. The one for whom an endowment (waqf) is made owns the substance but does not have full disposal of it: he may not sell it, nor give it away, nor is it inherited from him. The renter owns the usufruct, the right to dispose of the usufruct only, without the substance.

As for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, He has the dominion of the heavens and the earth, their substances and the disposal of them.

Now, did He not mention the dominion of those in them, in ﴿the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, because the heavens and the earth include all who are in them; for those in the heavens and the earth are from the heavens and the earth, their origin is from the heavens and the earth. Man was created from clay, and the other animals, as it appears, Allah knows best, though we do not know anything about them, were created from the earth. But what matters is that we know our origin; as for these, Allah created them for us: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is in the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 29] (...).

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and He has not taken a son﴾. ﴿A son﴾ means a begotten one. The phrase ﴿and has not taken a son﴾ is more general than His saying ﴿He neither begets nor is begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas 3]. Nevertheless, Allah negated of Himself the taking of a son and begetting. He, glory be to Him, did not beget and did not take a son from among His servants. In this is a refutation of whose saying? 

* A student: The Christians.

* The Shaykh: The saying of the Christians who said: the Messiah is the son of Allah; and the saying of the Jews who said: 'Uzayr is the son of Allah; and of the polytheists who said: the angels are the daughters of Allah. So Allah, glory be to Him, did not beget anything, and did not take any of His creation as a son; ﴿and has not taken a son, and has no partner in the dominion﴾.

Now, we mentioned earlier that when Allah negates an attribute from Himself, the purpose is not merely negating the attribute, but negating the attribute and affirming the perfection of its opposite. So what is the opposite here?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes: the perfection of His power and His self-sufficiency, and that He has no need of a son, due to the perfection of His independence from others. One only needs a son or takes a son if he is in need of one; but whoever is independent of it, capable of what he wills, does not take a son.

﴿and has no partner in the dominion﴾. Yes, Allah, glory be to Him, has no partner in the dominion; no one shares it with Him, not any of the angels, not any of the prophets, not any of those beneath them. The dominion belongs to Allah alone, with no partner in it.

In this is a refutation of those who associate partners with Allah in lordship (rububiyyah), such as those who say that some saints (awliya') dispose of the universe. These are without doubt in error, and they are also liars in what they report; for they are wrong in their creed and lying in what they relate. Allah, glory be to Him, has no partner in His dominion.

And His saying: ﴿and has no partner in the dominion﴾. If someone says: Do we not own our houses, own our clothes, and own our livestock? Does this necessitate that Allah has a partner?

The answer: No. Because our ownership of these things is not absolute ownership. It is true that I own my house, own my garment, own my car, and own my livestock, but my ownership of these things is not absolute; the proof is that I am restricted by the Shari'ah in disposing of these things. Do I have the right, for example, to neglect them so that I burn them, or do I not have that right?

* A student: It is forbidden.

* The Shaykh: I do not have that right; it is forbidden for me. I do not have the right, for example, to burden an animal in carrying and riding and other things. Therefore my being an owner (...) does not make me a partner of Allah, the Exalted, in His dominion; because this ownership of mine is restricted according to the permission of the Lawgiver to me. I do not dispose of it except as Allah, the Exalted, has permitted.

﴿and has no partner in the dominion, and created everything﴾. The commentator says: (of a nature to be created).

﴿and created everything﴾ indicates generality, but the commentator restricted it by his saying: (of a nature to be created). Why did he restrict it by his saying: (of a nature to be created)?

* A student: So that the Qur'an is not included.

* The Shaykh: Yes, so that the Qur'an, or Himself for example, is not included. If someone says: Did Allah create Himself? This is impossible; it is impossible that He creates Himself. Yet he still says: (of a nature to be created). As for what is not of a nature to be created, such as the essence of Allah and the attributes of Allah, this is not included from the outset, because Allah is the Creator, and the Creator is other than the created, and the attributes of the Creator are not created, because the attribute follows the essence. For this reason it is as if the author, when he says (of a nature to be created), alerts you so that you may answer with this word those who said that the Qur'an is created, and you say: the Qur'an is not of a nature to be created, because it is among the attributes of Allah, the Exalted, and the attributes of Allah, the Exalted, are not created.

But we should not restrict the verse by this; we say: He created everything. Can the Creator be the created, or other than the uncreated? It is not possible. So if it is not possible, this indicates that Allah, the Exalted, is not created, and that His attributes are also not created, because the attribute follows the described. Then there is no need to say: of a nature to be created; for if we say: of a nature to be created, we have restricted the noble verse.

The one who says the Qur'an is created may argue against us, saying: Who told you that the verse is restricted by this?

So we say: ﴿and created everything﴾ absolutely and generally, and this does not necessitate that the Qur'an be created, because the Creator is other than the created, and the Qur'an is among the attributes of Allah, and the attributes of the Creator are certainly not created, because the attributes follow the essence.

So now, if the Mu'tazilah and the Jahmiyyah, who say that the Qur'an is created, argue against us, how do we answer them? We answer them with one of two ways:

The first way: what the author indicated, namely that it is said: this is from the category of the general term intended in a specific sense; that is, everything that is of a nature to be created. This is one way, and many of the early scholars answered with it. They said: If someone says the Qur'an is created, and cites His saying ﴿and created everything﴾, then say to him: Allah said about the wind of 'Ad: ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾, yet it did not destroy the sky, nor the earth, nor the dwellings; ﴿so that nothing could be seen but their dwellings﴾ [al-Ahqaf 25].

Another group of scholars says: No, the verse is general, and the Qur'an is not included at all, so that we would need to exclude it. Why? Because if He is the Creator, the Creator is other than the created, and the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, and the speech of Allah is among His attributes, and the attributes of the Creator are not created; for the attribute follows what? The described.

﴿and created everything and determined for it a measure﴾. What does the particle fa (then) indicate? It indicates sequence.

And (qaddarahu) means (sawwarahu, shaped it), because creation may exist without proportioning; so Allah created everything and then determined it, that is, proportioned it.

The evidence that taqdir here means proportioning is His saying: ﴿He who created and proportioned﴾ [al-A'la 2]. On this basis, the sequence in His saying ﴿and created everything, then determined it﴾ is the sequence according to reality: it is a real sequence, because proportioning comes after creating; when you produce a building, first you produce the frame, then you introduce the adjustments and refinements. Likewise Allah, glory be to Him, created everything and then determined it; that is, proportioned it with a proportioning fitting to what it was created for.

Some scholars said: the meaning of ﴿qaddarahu﴾ is "qadaahu" (He decreed it), so the verse indicates both decree and creation. According to this view, which takes taqdir to mean qada' (decree), there is a non-factual sequence in the verse. The reason: taqdir in the sense of qada' precedes creation, does it not? For Allah decrees first and then creates second.

But which of the two is better? The better view is that the sequence is factual, and that creation comes before determination. This is also indicated by the noble verse: ﴿the One who created and then proportioned﴾. His saying ﴿created, then proportioned﴾ shows this, for the Qur'an explains one part of itself by another, and we take taqdir here to mean taswiyah (proportioning).

As for the sequence coming contrary to the factual order: although this occurs in the Arabic language, it is contrary to what is customary. Otherwise it has been said: whoever repented, then his father repented, and after that his grandfather repented, so (...) the grandfather is the first, and in sequence here he is the last. But the closer and more appropriate view is the one the author adopted, namely that taqdir here means taswiyah, because the speech of Allah explains one part of it by another (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 3–9 (part 1 of 5):

(...) The verse now. First, the revelation of the Qur'an was mentioned (...).
* Student: (...) ﴿So they have committed injustice and falsehood (4). And they say, "Myths of the former peoples, which he has had written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening." (5) Say, "It was sent down by He who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth. Indeed, He is ever Forgiving and Merciful." (6) And they say, "What is with this messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets? Why was an angel not sent down to him to be a warner along with him? (7) Or a treasure be thrown to him, or he be given a garden from which to eat?" And the wrongdoers say, "You follow none but a man affected by magic." (8) See how they have coined for you comparisons, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.﴾ [Al-Furqan 4–9].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from Satan, the accursed. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they have taken, besides Him, gods that create nothing, while they themselves are created﴾ [Al-Furqan 3].
(﴿And they have taken﴾ means: the disbelievers. ﴿besides Him﴾ means: besides Allah.) As for the first pronoun, ﴿they have taken﴾, no explicit antecedent has been mentioned for it, but its referent is known from the context; that is, ﴿they have taken besides Him﴾ — who are they?
* Student: The disbelievers.
* The Shaykh: The disbelievers who took them. It has no antecedent in wording, but its referent is known from the situation.
As for ﴿besides Him﴾, its referent is clear from what preceded, because Allah spoke of Himself in His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾, up to His saying: ﴿and they have taken besides Him﴾.
The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah praised Himself with what He praised Himself with, it was appropriate to mention those idols that were taken besides Him — meaning besides Allah — as gods, so that their state would be made clear, because things are made clear by the attributes they possess.
﴿And they have taken besides Him gods﴾: the word ﴿gods﴾ is the plural of (ilah, god). These gods were gods only by their taking, but in reality they are not gods, because they do not deserve worship. Is that not so?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Due to the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other? Is for you the male and for Him the female? That, then, is an unjust division. They are not but names you have named them, you and your fathers; Allah has sent down no authority for them﴾ [An-Najm 19–23]. And Yusuf said: ﴿Are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer? What you worship besides Him are but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾ [Yusuf 39, 40]. So they are gods in name and in their belief, but in reality they are not gods; meaning they do not deserve to be gods. Is it clear, O brothers?
So if someone says: how did Allah here establish that they are gods, ﴿they have taken besides Him gods﴾, when all the prophets, peace be upon them, said to their peoples: ﴿Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾ [Hud 61], and Allah, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [Al-Baqarah 163]. How do we reconcile this negation with this affirmation?
We say: we reconcile this negation and this affirmation in that the negation is with regard to reality and fact, for there is no god except Allah, and there is no doubt about that; and the affirmation is according to what? According to the actions of these people, in that they made these into gods, that is, objects of worship; and there is no doubt that they are worshipped, but they do not deserve to be worshipped. So, with regard to what is deserved, there is negation, and with regard to what actually happens, there is affirmation. Is the matter clear or not?
With regard to what is deserved, there is negation; that is, no one deserves, and no one is truly a god, except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. As for belief and action, some people believe and act so as to take another god alongside Allah, and the reality of these gods is that they are nothing. It is true that they are worshipped, called upon, bowed to, prostrated to, and vowed to, but in reality they do not deserve this, so they are not gods.
Then Allah explained these taken gods: ﴿they create nothing﴾, and their not creating is a proof of their powerlessness, and their powerlessness is a proof that they are not gods, because a god must necessarily be capable, since capability is part of perfection; and this incapacity which these gods are characterized by prevents them from being gods.
Second: ﴿while they themselves are created﴾. Who is ﴿while they themselves are created﴾? The gods. So they are originated after they were not, and the Lord must be primordial, nothing preceding Him; for the Lord deserving worship must be a creator, and if He is created, He is originated, and if He is originated, then whoever came before Him is not of His creation. Thus, in His saying ﴿they create nothing﴾ there is an explanation of their unfitness for divinity in terms of what? The absence of ability.
﴿while they themselves are created﴾ also makes it unfit for them to be gods, in two respects:
First: origination, for they are originated, and a god cannot be originated.
Second: whoever came before them and preceded them is not of their creation, supposing they could create, and this is a proof of their unfitness for divinity.
﴿They create nothing, while they themselves are created, and they do not control for themselves any harm or benefit, and they do not control death or life or resurrection﴾ [Al-Furqan 3]. The author says: (﴿they do not control for themselves any harm﴾, meaning: its repelling). We say: its repelling and its bringing as well. What prevents it?! If they wished to harm themselves, they would not harm themselves, and if they wished to repel harm from themselves, they would not repel it. So keeping the verse general is better: ﴿they do not control for themselves any harm﴾, meaning: neither bringing harm nor repelling it. Even harm that might be easy, if they wished it for themselves they could not do it. That is, if these idols wished to destroy themselves, could they do it or not?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: If they wished to make themselves sick, if they were the kind that can become sick, would they have that power or not? They do not. And if someone wished to attack them, could they repel him or not?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: They cannot. That is why Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿O mankind, a parable has been presented, so listen to it﴾, and this indicates its importance; Allah's command to us to listen to this parable indicates its importance.
The parable: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah will never create a fly, even if they gather together for it﴾. The fly, which is among the weakest and feeblest of creatures — if they gathered together to create it, they could not.
Another matter: ﴿And if the fly should snatch away from them something, they could not rescue it from it﴾, despite its weakness, ﴿weak are the seeker and the sought﴾ [Al-Hajj 73].
