But here ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ is more eloquent and complete, because the flowing of water in its rivers is a visual delight through which a person takes pleasure when he sees it, in addition to the abundance of water in the garden, which is a cause of its abundant growth and vigour.
As for his saying: ﴿and will appoint for you palaces﴾, there are two readings: ﴿wayaj'al﴾ with sukun (jazm), and ﴿wayaj'alu﴾ with raf' (damma).
On the reading with sukun, what is it coordinated with? With the response of the condition: ﴿in shaa'a ja'ala﴾, ﴿wayaj'al﴾. On the reading with raf', the author says: (as a new clause). But it is not restricted to that even with the reading of raf'; it is as if he says: "and He will appoint for you palaces," which is not the case. That is, do not understand this matter from it: "as a new clause" is in terms of i'rab, not in terms of meaning, because the meaning is joined to what precedes; but grammatically it permits jazm, following the form of the verb, and permits raf' (as a new clause), making it the coordination of one clause to another.
Ibn Malik says in his Alfiyya:
"And after a past verb, your raf' of the response is good..."
That is: if the conditional verb is past, raising the response (jaza') when it is present is good.
"...and its raf' after a present verb is weak."
That is: weak. It is permissible but weak.
From these verses is learned: Allah's care for His Messenger ﷺ in defending him. Allah's care for the Messenger in defending him is not care for him alone, but extends to the Ummah as well, because that removes the doubts by which the falsifiers argue, and removing doubts from the Ummah is one of Allah's mercies towards them. And Allah is the Granter of success. (...)

* * *

﴿Nay, they deny the Hour, and We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blaze﴾ [al-Furqan 11]. When Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned what these people had done against Him, against His revelation, and against His Messenger, and the answer to that, He mentioned another matter, which is their denial of the Hour, and He introduced it with (bal) (nay), which indicates transition. This transition is not a cancellation of what came before, but the addition of another matter to it, namely His saying: ﴿Nay, they deny the Hour﴾.

What is meant by ﴿the Hour﴾ is the Day of Resurrection. The word (the Hour) is used in the language for every important matter, as if there were no hour except this one indicated by this time. Otherwise, in origin it applies to any period of time, short or long, but it is used often for what happens in it of an important matter, as is the case here.

﴿They denied it﴾: denial of the Hour includes denial of its occurrence outright, by saying: there is no resurrection, or denial of the matters that occur in it, such as the reckoning, the books, the bridge (sirat), the Pool (hawd), the intercession, and the like; because belief in the Last Day includes belief in its occurrence and in what occurs in it. So if a person denies it outright, he has denied it, and if he affirms it but denies what occurs in it, he is also a denier of it.

Allah, mighty and majestic, says: (﴿And We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blaze﴾: a fire kindled, i.e., intensely hot.)

﴿We have prepared﴾ means: We have made ready. ﴿For those who deny the Hour﴾ includes them and others; therefore He used ﴿man﴾ (whoever), which indicates generality, and did not say "and We have prepared for them." This is the placing of an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, and it was previously stated yesterday that among the benefits of placing an explicit noun in place of a pronoun is generality and the explicit statement of the cause of the ruling.

So His saying: ﴿for those who deny﴾ ... ﴿a blaze﴾ is as if it were the reason for the ruling that is His saying: ﴿We have prepared﴾ ... ﴿a blaze﴾, because they denied the Hour.

His saying, exalted: ﴿And We have prepared for those who deny﴾: From it is derived that the Fire is now created, and this is so, and the texts of the Book and the Sunnah indicate it. Allah, exalted, said about the people of Pharaoh: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾ [Ghafir 46], and this is an explicit text that it is created. And in the sound hadiths there is what indicates it, such as: "The Fire complained to its Lord, so He permitted it two breaths: a breath in winter and a breath in summer."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (536) and Muslim (617/186), the wording is his, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

As for His saying: ﴿a blaze﴾, the author said: (a fire kindled), thus making fa'il (a form like "fa'eel") to mean maf'ul: kindled. It may also mean fa'il: blazing, burning whoever enters it. The meanings are not contradictory, because if it is kindled, i.e., intensely heated, or it itself blazes and consumes people, then this and that are mutually implicated.

(﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they hear its raging and roaring﴾ [al-Furqan 12]: boiling like the angry man when his chest boils with anger, ﴿and roaring﴾: a violent sound; or the hearing of its raging is seeing it and knowing it.)

He says: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place﴾: the subject is the blaze, and this is evidence that it sees, and this seeing must be taken in its literal meaning. It is not possible to say that this is a metaphor and a figurative meaning, because it is permissible that Allah create in it the faculty of sight, even though it is not by custom a thing that sees. Allah, glorified and exalted, is capable of all things, just as the earth hears and speaks: ﴿On that day it will report its news﴾ [al-Zalzalah 4], and no tree or clod hears the voice of the caller to prayer without bearing witness for him on the Day of Resurrection.[[Ibn Khuzaymah (389) narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him: "If you are in the desert, raise your voice with the call; for I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'No tree, no clod, no stone, no jinn, and no human hears his voice but bears witness for him.'"]]

So we say: there is no metaphor in this verse; it is on its literal meaning, and the Fire sees, because Allah has informed that it sees: ﴿when it sees them﴾. And what prevents Allah from creating this faculty in it?

Also by the evidence of ﴿they hear its raging﴾: raging is well known to occur only from beings possessing awareness, but despite this we must say that in this verse it is on its apparent meaning, and that it rages, and its raging produces a sound, like the raging of an angry person, when his chest is filled with anger, you hear from him a sound of anger.

This is evidence of the intensity of its wrath, may Allah protect us, against its people, and that, as Allah said in Surah Tabarak: ﴿When they are thrown into it, they hear from it a roaring, while it boils up. It almost bursts with rage﴾ [al-Mulk 7-8]. So what do you think of a thing into which a person is cast, while it is full of rage and wrath against him? What will it do to him? This is evidence of the severity of its punishment, may Allah protect us, and that it shows them no mercy and spares them nothing and no covenant.

(﴿They hear from it a raging﴾: boiling like the angry man when his chest boils with anger, ﴿and roaring﴾.) This is from a distant place: what does this indicate about this raging and roaring, that it is severe or light? Severe. As long as it is heard from a distant place, it is severe.

The author says: (or the hearing of its raging is seeing it and knowing it). This is not correct, though it is possible; but the first meaning, that seeing be taken literally, is the obligation. There has passed among us from the rules of tafsir, indeed from the rules of every speech, that it must be taken in its apparent and literal sense unless there is evidence that diverts from the literal or the apparent; and it is not just any evidence: there must be sound evidence. As for what a person thinks is evidence and is not, this is not accepted.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: That is, if they see it.
* Student: That is, the wording ﴿when it sees them﴾: if its customers see them, that is?
* Shaykh: No, that is not correct; this is in fact a distortion (tahrif), because we said it is permissible that Allah create in it the faculty of sight.
* Student: There are weak hadiths restricting the verse (...)?
* Shaykh: On what?
* Student: Weak hadiths; it is said it has two eyes[[al-Tabarani in al-Kabir (7599) narrated from Abu Umamah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in Hell between my two eyes." That was difficult for his companions, and they said: O Messenger of Allah, we narrate from you a hadith and add and subtract? He said: "That is not what I mean; I mean the one who lies about me, speaking, seeking thereby to disgrace Islam." They said: O Messenger of Allah, you said: between my two eyes, and does Hell have an eye? He said: "Yes. Have you not heard Him say: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they hear its raging and roaring﴾ [al-Furqan 12]? So do they see them except with two eyes?"]] (...).
* Shaykh: We do not; these hadiths are weak.
* Student: They support us, in a sense (...)?
* Shaykh: No, we do not need to support them. Support is not needed while the wording is explicit: ﴿and Allah is over all things competent﴾ [al-Baqarah 284]. The One who created the eye in a human: is it impossible for Him to create it in the Fire?
* Student: It is not impossible.
* Shaykh: It is not impossible. But some people, when their minds do not grasp a matter, go and distort it to what they can grasp.

Furthermore, we must also know that the conditions of the Hereafter cannot be measured by the conditions of this world. We know that people will be gathered: some of them have their light going before them, and some are in darkness; and they are in one flat place, the caller makes them hear and the sight reaches them. We know that some people sweat, so that the sweat reaches their ankles, their knees, and their waists, and some are bridled by it; yet they are in one place. The conditions of the Hereafter can never be measured by the conditions of this world.

He says: (﴿And when they are cast into a narrow place of it, bound together﴾ [al-Furqan 13]: with the shaddah and without it), meaning: two Sab'i readings, (that they will be constricted, and ﴿from it﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial) of ﴿a place﴾, because originally it is an attribute of it; ﴿muqarranin﴾ ...) and so on.

﴿When they are cast﴾: in this is evidence that they, may Allah protect us, are not treated with mercy, but are thrown and cast down.

His saying: ﴿a place﴾ is an adverbial complement, governed by ﴿were cast﴾. His saying: ﴿from it﴾ is originally an attribute, but the rule among the grammarians is that when a prepositional phrase precedes the noun it qualifies, it becomes a ḥāl of it, because an attribute does not precede what it qualifies. For example, you say: a man came on a camel riding; so you parse "riding" as a ḥāl. But if you put it before "man": a rider came, it would have to be an attribute in meaning.

Likewise the prepositional phrase: if you say: a man came on a camel, "on a camel" is an attribute of "man". If you put "on a camel" first: came on a camel a man, that attribute must be a ḥāl. Why? Because an attribute does not precede the thing qualified. That is why he said: (and ﴿from it﴾ is a ḥāl of ﴿a place﴾), because originally it is an attribute of it.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed: narrow.
* And in this also, ﴿And when they are cast from it into a narrow place﴾: is evidence that this place from which they are cast will not be spacious but will be constricted upon them. This is before entering it; how then when they enter it?!

It is possible that the very places in which they are in the Fire itself are narrow, when they are cast into a place of it that is narrow; so this ﴿min﴾ would be close in meaning to ﴿fiha﴾ (in it).

(﴿Muqarranin﴾: shackled, their hands bound to their necks in chains; the shaddah is for intensification.) The shaddah in His saying ﴿muqarranin﴾: because the root of (muqarran) is qarana; that is, it is derived from qurrina, so he is muqarran; its origin is from qarana without shaddah: I qarantu this man, aqrinuhu, so he is maqrun; but it came with the shaddah for intensification, or for emphasis in this binding: that they are bound with severity. So when they are ﴿cast from it into a narrow place, bound together, they call there for destruction﴾ (ruin, so it is said to them) ﴿Do not call today for one destruction, but call for many destructions﴾ [al-Furqan 14].

This is in truth a clear depiction of the condition of the Fire and its people on the Day of Resurrection: that before they enter it they hear its raging and roaring, and this without doubt unnerves their hearts and terrifies them.

Then, when they are cast into it, they are not cast in honour, but cast down. Then they are not cast loose, but bound together, meaning their hands gathered to their necks.

Then, when they are cast in this condition, they call for destruction, may Allah protect us: ﴿they call there for destruction﴾, meaning they say: "Woe to us! Our destruction!" and similar. So it is said to them: ﴿Do not call today for one destruction, but call for many destructions﴾. This is by way of reproach, because the custom is that when a man calls for destruction in this world, he is pitied; but there they are not pitied. It is said to them: your calling for destruction benefits you nothing, so call for many destructions. The punishment will continue: ﴿and call for many destructions﴾.

This entire passage, which all stands as the commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin, is the cause for the people of the Fire, may God save us from it, to suffer two kinds of torment: a torment of the heart and a torment of the body. The torment of the heart may at times be more severe than the torment of the body, God forbid. They are not honoured, neither by deed, nor by welcome, nor by speech.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is correct that what has been mentioned of them above indicates that they do not believe in the Resurrection (al-ba'th), because whoever believes in the Resurrection must act for it. But this is in fact among the things they said. Among what they said is that they denied the Resurrection, so it is in addition to what came before. However, yes, we should say: why was it introduced with (bal, "rather"), without the waw (and), even though the faults and evil qualities mentioned before were all introduced with the waw, while this one was introduced with (bal)?
This may suggest that one of the causes of their earlier statements is that they denied the Hour. That is, they do not have faith in the Hour, and had they believed in it, they would not have said what came before.

* Student: His saying: ﴿a narrow place﴾, is the meaning "they will be thrown (...)"?
* Shaykh: We have said that it has two possibilities. Either the meaning is that they will be cast from a narrow place upon their entry, or the meaning is that the place itself in the Fire will be narrow, meaning it will be constricted upon them, because each one of them, God forbid, will be in a coffin, as the hadith (prophetic report) has come: in a closed coffin.[[Ibn Abi Shaybah (35414) narrated from Suwayd ibn Ghaflah, who said: When God wishes to make the people of the Fire forget, He places for each person among them a coffin of fire according to his size, then locks it upon him with locks of fire, so that no vein of his beats except that there is a nail of fire in it. Then He places that coffin inside another coffin of fire, locks it with locks of fire, and then a fire is kindled between them. So none of them sees that there is anyone in the Fire other than himself. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿They will have above them canopies of fire, and below them canopies﴾ [al-Zumar 39:16], and His saying: ﴿They will have from Hell a bed, and above them coverings. Thus We recompense the wrongdoers﴾ [al-A'raf 7:41].]]

* Student: What is narrated from (...) that some parts of his body are enlarged?
* Shaykh: Indeed, he himself is enlarged, but there is nothing preventing that he is enlarged while in a narrow place. This enlargement of his may be among the causes of the constriction.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No. It is apparently possible. Some of them may acknowledge this, but he associates partners with God.

But God, glorified and exalted is He, attributes actions to the whole nation, even to the point that He sometimes addresses the latter part of a nation with what its earlier part did, because it is satisfied with it and approves of it. Look, for example, at how God addresses the Children of Israel in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) with what their forefathers did: ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed over it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:72], and ﴿So repent to your Creator and kill your selves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:54]. Although this address does not apply to these people, because they are not the ones who did it, nevertheless the one nation whose part does an action is considered as having done it by all of them, because they are satisfied with it.

God, the Exalted, said: (﴿Say: Is that﴾, meaning the mentioned threat and description of the Fire, ﴿better, or the Garden of Eternity which the God-fearing have been promised﴾, that is, in His knowledge, ﴿it shall be for them a recompense﴾, a reward, ﴿and a destination﴾, a return).

What is the address in ﴿Say﴾ directed to? To the Messenger (ﷺ), and likewise to others. For this reason we may say: the address is to everyone who can be addressed, meaning the Messenger (ﷺ) and others. But the closer view is that it is directed to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Nevertheless, the address to the Messenger (ﷺ) includes him and his nation, unless evidence specifies it for him. So each of us can say something like this. He says to the deniers who were promised the Fire: Is that mentioned threat, which must certainly befall, better, or the Garden of Eternity? And what is the answer? The Garden of Eternity, without doubt.

Here there is a difficulty: he said ﴿better﴾, although that has no good in it at all, so how can it be compared with that which is absolutely good?

The answer: this is a matter of condescension toward the opponent (tanazzul ma'a al-khasm), and it is fine when dealing with an opponent to make such a comparison. God, the Exalted, has compared two things between which there is a greater difference than the difference between the threat to the people of the Fire and the promise to the people of Paradise. He said: ﴿Is God better, or what they associate?﴾ [al-Naml 27:59]. It is known that God is better, and that no sensible person could compare this with that. But since those addressed were equating others with God, it became a matter of condescension toward them that we address them with this and say: ﴿Is God better, or what they associate?﴾.

﴿Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity?﴾ He added it to ﴿Eternity﴾ by the idafa of the described to its attribute (idafat al-mawsuf ila sifatih), meaning the Garden which is the place of eternity. And ﴿Eternity (al-khuld)﴾ means remaining. God, the Exalted, has very often stated the everlastingness (al-ta'bid) of their eternity.

As for the people of the Fire, everlastingness is mentioned in three verses of the Qur'an: in Surat al-Nisa', in Surat al-Ahzab, and in Surat al-Jinn. In Surat al-Nisa': ﴿Indeed, God would not forgive them, nor would He guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever. And that is ever easy for God﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:168-169]. In Surat al-Ahzab: ﴿Indeed, God has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze, abiding therein forever; they will not find any protector or helper﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:64-65]. In Surat al-Jinn: ﴿And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn 72:23].

In this there is a clear refutation of the one who says that the torment of the Fire is not everlasting. Among those who inclined to this view, which is one of the strangest views, is Ibn al-Qayyim, may God have mercy on him, for he tended to hold that the torment of the Fire is not everlasting and must come to an end. But he did not say that it ends and then the people of the Fire move to Paradise. No, rather it ends in the sense that it and its people perish.

The correct view, about which there is no doubt, is what the majority of the People of the Sunnah (ahl al-sunnah) hold, and consensus (ijma') has been reported on it: that the Fire and its people are everlasting. This does not contradict the mercy of God, mighty and majestic, because God, the Exalted, has given them a warning and established the proof against them. They are the ones who brought ruin upon themselves.

* Student: The exception, may God be good to you, in Hud?
* Shaykh: The exception in Hud, because it is an exception from His saying: ﴿As long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾ [Hud 11:107]. If it were restricted to the duration of the heavens and the earth, it would have an end. But when He said: ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, this is not outside the duration of the heavens and the earth. This is the meaning of the exception.

* Student: In another verse (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes: ﴿abiding therein, except what God wills﴾ [al-An'am 6:128]. We say: this exception, ﴿except what God wills﴾, the texts indicate that He does not will that they not be everlasting. So this exception seems to indicate that if God willed, He could prevent the torment from them, and that it is not a matter obligatory upon Him, but rather it is within His will. Therefore the exception is explained by the clear and explicit verses, that He does not will to lift the torment from them, because He has informed us, and God does not break His word, that their torment is everlasting.

* Student: Ibn al-Qayyim (...)?
* Shaykh: Who?
* Student: Ibn al-Qayyim.
* Shaykh: No, at the beginning of his words he firmly asserted this.
* Student: In Hadi al-Arwah (...).
* Shaykh: No, he mentioned it in Shifa' al-Alil. He mentioned it there and asserted it at the beginning of the discussion, then he cited the narrations (athar) on this matter.

* Student: The explanation that He is ﴿the Doer of what He wills﴾ [Hud 11:107] (...)?
* Shaykh: No. It seems to hint that if someone said: how does God, glorified and exalted, do this, given that it is a perpetual torment and His mercy encompasses all things? So He said: ﴿Doer of what He wills﴾, just as He said: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾ [Hud 11:108].

In truth, these matters, although these possibilities may have some basis, nevertheless, since we have clear, firm texts, it is obligatory upon the believer to refer the ambiguous (mutashabih) to the firm (muhkam), since in these three verses the matters are merely possibilities, whereas we have something that admits of no possibility, which is the explicit statement of everlastingness. And you know that this is a report (khabar), and a report does not admit negation or (...).

* Student: Alright, O Shaykh, (...) the non-fulfilment of a threat without the non-fulfilment of a promise.
* Shaykh: Yes. And even if they said: God praises Himself that He does not break His promise and that His report is true. The threat by which God praises Himself is that which falls under His will, other than associating partners with Him. For example, we have a threat for sins below shirk, so if God pardons them, that is good, and He is praised for it, glorified and exalted is He.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Who is it about?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but 'Umar and others than 'Umar are addressed by His saying: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, we need not concern ourselves with it. Even if it were explicit, if he said: they will come out, we say: they will not come out. Since there are explicit verses, what is the obstacle? And ﴿remaining therein for ages, tasting therein neither coolness nor drink﴾ [al-Naba' 78:23-24], this also does not indicate limitation, because ﴿ages (ahqab)﴾ means: long, having no end, this is the meaning. And a person, if he imagined that he would remain in the Fire not for ages but for one second, and he were sensible, he would avoid the deeds of the people of the Fire. So how about those who remain in it for ages?! It does not indicate limitation. Whoever claims that it indicates limitation and says that these ages are restricted by what follows, meaning: ﴿ages, tasting therein neither coolness nor drink﴾, and other ages in which they taste, this is not correct. Rather the meaning is intensification of this, that they remain therein for vast, long eras that have no end.

(﴿Or the Garden of Eternity which the God-fearing have been promised﴾.) The author brought in (ha), what is (ha)? It is the second object of ﴿promised﴾, because (wa'ada, "to promise") is one of the verbs that take two objects whose original structure is not subject and predicate. So the first object is omitted, and the second object, the deputy subject, is ﴿the God-fearing﴾. We have often mentioned before that the muttaqi (God-fearing person) is one who takes a shield against the torment of God by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, and that this is the most comprehensive of what has been said about taqwa and the most suitable to its wording, since it derives from (ittaqa), from protection (wiqaya).

And His saying: ﴿the God-fearing have been promised﴾, who promised them? God, glorified and exalted is He promised them, and the agent is omitted here because it is known, as in His saying: ﴿and man was created weak﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:28], and the Creator is God, glorified and exalted is He.

And His saying: (﴿it shall be for them﴾ in His knowledge). The author, may God have mercy on him, restricted the existence to His knowledge, because (kana, "was") is a past tense verb, and the Garden has been a destination, or will it be a destination? It will be a destination. Therefore he restricted the existence, which he expressed by the past tense verb, restricting it to God's knowledge, meaning not according to actual reality, because in reality it has not been, but will be. But this is based on the view that (kana) is meant to denote time. However, if a person examines its uses in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, he finds that sometimes it denotes mere occurrence and not time, because the verb, as you know, denotes both time and meaning. So (kana) always comes to denote only the meaning. That is: ﴿which the God-fearing have been promised﴾, and it is for them a recompense and a destination. Based on this, there is no need for the estimation that the author mentioned. This is the clearer view. ﴿which the God-fearing have been promised﴾, that is: and it is for them a recompense and a destination. We need not estimate that it was in God's knowledge. Rather, it is ﴿kanat﴾, that is: it is a recompense. So we strip (kana) of indicating time, and when we strip it of this, as it often occurs in the Arabic language, we are spared this estimation which the author brought.

* Student: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed God was ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:11]?
* Shaykh: It is similar, stripped of time. This is stripped of time, because God has not ceased and will not cease to be Forgiving and Merciful.
* Student: We said: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, ﴿Indeed God was Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:23]. When we bring (kana) and say that what is meant by it is time and occurrence, like God's forgiveness and mercy in the past, but now He is not Forgiving and Merciful, that is the case. But in these instances what is meant is mere occurrence, that is, He is characterized by forgiveness and mercy. This verse is similar, and (kana) always indicates mere occurrence and not time.
* Student: (...) the ends of verses (ru'us al-ayat)?
* Shaykh: What do you mean?
* Student: So it is said: God is Forgiving and Merciful (...)?
* Shaykh: No. It is possible, but it is not necessary. That is, sometimes they come fitting and sometimes not fitting.

The discussion of (kana), everyone: this is the point. In the Arabic language (kana) does not always denote time, but denotes the absolute occurrence of the event. That is, this matter is the reality. Here, ﴿they have been for them a recompense and a destination﴾. It is known that the God-fearing have not now entered Paradise nor arrived there, but they will arrive. Therefore the author needed to estimate: (in His knowledge), that is, it was in God's knowledge. But we say: there is no need for this estimate, because (kana) is stripped of indicating time.

And His saying: ﴿a recompense and a destination﴾. He says: (a reward). The one who made this reward for them is God, glorified and exalted is He. (﴿and a destination﴾, a return). From when does it become a destination? From the Day of Resurrection or from their death?

* Student: From their death.
* Shaykh: From the moment they die. ﴿Those whom the angels take in a good state, saying: Peace be upon you; enter Paradise﴾ [al-Nahl 16:32]. But of course it is not the entry into the Paradise that is in the heavens, and therefore a door to Paradise is opened for him, a bed from Paradise is spread for him, and he is clothed in garments from Paradise. So the God-fearing, from the moment they die, enter Paradise, just as the people of the Hellfire, from the moment they die, taste the torment of Hellfire.

For this reason, in books of exhortation, yesterday I heard someone reading in books of exhortation, they bring up death, worms, and such things, and that worms eat him and pus, and what is similar to that. In truth this only applies to the body. When people feel this, they do not rejoice at death; they shrink from it greatly. What a person should be admonished with is what concerns his soul, so it is said, for example: if he dies and is not among the God-fearing, he will have such and such torment, and so on to the end. And if he is among the God-fearing, he will be in bliss and among the people of Paradise, so that the believer may rejoice. But when we go and direct people only to fear of the sensory, material matter, this in truth harms people. When a person hears this, does he become reassured about death? No, never. He shrinks from it. But when he hears that if he is a believer he enters Paradise from the moment he dies, yes, you find him, perhaps I would not say he rejoices at death, but he is glad at this promise that awaits him.

This is what people should be raised upon. They should not be told only about material matters. For this reason, if you contemplate the whole Qur'an, you will find that these material matters have no mention in it. What is mentioned in the Qur'an is what concerns the soul of bliss and torment, to the point that a person rejoices, is glad, and works for this bliss, and fears, dreads, and flees from this Hellfire.

This matter, we wanted to point it out because it is found often in books of exhortation (wa'z), just as many things that encourage what the Sharia has forbidden are found in them. For example, they mention some worshippers who are excused by their ignorance, who would stand in prayer the whole night throughout their lives, and they said: "So-and-so remained for forty years praying Fajr with the ablution of 'Isha'." What do they intend by this? Encouragement. This is contrary to what the Messenger ﷺ commanded, so this is from opposition (muhadda) to Allah and His Messenger. They bring forth reprehensible matters that they do not know. I will explain this to you, because you hear what I hear. If, for example, a reciter from among the imams recites from such books, then we must speak with him. Not before the people like this, no, because the common folk, as you know, are common folk, and they are with their imam. It may be that he is right, and they will rise against you. But it is possible, when you are alone with him, to say to him, "My brother," addressing him calmly: "You are an imam who is followed, and the common folk say, 'What is said in the prayer niche (mihrab) is correct.' You must know that this is contrary to the Sharia, and explain to him as much as you can, so that the imams who are followed now will be upon the truth."

* Student: Are the hadiths about the squeezing of the grave (ḍaghṭat al-qabr) authentic? [Among them is what Ibn Hibban (2466) narrated from 'A'isha, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The grave has a squeezing; if anyone were to be saved from it, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh would have been saved from it."] (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, but as for the squeezing of the grave, I do not know about its authenticity. It is mentioned in the story of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, but I do not recall now whether it is authentic. It is certainly not in the Two Sahihs, but I do not know whether it reaches the level of authenticity or not. Yet whatever it is, the squeezing of the grave is nothing compared to what they say and describe of the condition of the dead. They focus on the matter of the body, to the point that people, whatever their good deeds, fall into despair (qunut).
* Student: O Shaykh, is the decay or the preservation of the body a sign of righteousness or not?
* Shaykh: By Allah, the apparent matter is that its preservation indicates righteousness, because it does not occur except as a karamah (a noble gift of Allah to a righteous person). The original rule is that bodies are consumed by the earth, except the prophets, for the earth does not consume them. [Abu Dawud (1047) narrated from Aws ibn Aws, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Among the best of your days is Friday. On it Adam was created, on it he was taken, on it is the blowing (of the Trumpet), and on it is the blast (of the Trumpet). So increase your sending of blessings upon me on it, for your blessings are presented to me." He said: They said, "O Messenger of Allah, how will our blessings be presented to you when you have decayed?" (they say: "decayed" meaning "become worn away") He said: "Indeed Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden the earth to consume the bodies of the prophets."]
* Student: And the martyrs?
* Shaykh: No, the martyrs' case is not established. The matter concerns the prophets.
* Student: Alright, and their going (away)?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: It does not indicate that the person is not among the people of goodness. It does not indicate that, but it may occur as a karamah for some people of goodness.
* Student: But the hadith is not authentic?
* Shaykh: The martyrs, no.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, only the bodies of the prophets are not consumed.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is by way of karamah, and likewise the story of 'Umar when they dug up the graves, yes. But among the martyrs of Uhud, there are some whom the earth has consumed.
* Student: Glory be to Allah!
* Shaykh: Some of his body was consumed, not all of his body. (...)
(﴿They shall have it as a reward and a final destination﴾, "a destination" meaning a place of return; ﴿They will have therein whatever they wish, abiding eternally﴾ [al-Furqan 16]: "abiding" is a necessary state (hal lazimah).) What is the necessary state? 
* Student: ﴿Abiding eternally﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Abiding eternally﴾.
As for His saying ﴿They will have therein whatever they wish﴾, this verse indicates that whatever they wish is theirs. In Surah Qaf, Allah says: ﴿They will have therein whatever they wish, and with Us is more﴾ [Qaf 35]; that is, with Allah there is more than what a person wishes, because a person, however far his understanding and will reach, is limited. He may wish for some things while some of the bliss remains hidden from him, so Allah completes it for him. For this reason He said: ﴿They will have therein whatever they wish﴾.
As for His saying ﴿abiding eternally﴾: what is the meaning of "necessary state" (hal lazimah)? That is, is there a necessary state and a transient state (hal 'aridah)?
The answer: Yes. If the state is not necessary for its bearer, then it is a transient state (...). "The man came riding" is a transient state, because he may come without riding, on foot. And if it is necessary...
The angels were more numerous, and every heaven has more angels than the heaven beneath it.
Likewise, these angels who encompass the world: each circle is more numerous than the circle before it. They are sent down as a demonstration of the greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and of the encompassing of creation. Then the saying of Allah, the Exalted, becomes true: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass. You will not pass except with authority﴾ [al-Rahman 33]; because they will not be able, with the angels encompassing them, to flee from the terrors of this Day.
As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿tanzil﴾ (descending), it is the verbal noun of "nuzzila" (was sent down). As we previously mentioned, it indicates that they descend gradually, not all at once. So the angels of the lowest heaven descend first, then the second, then the third, up to the seventh.
We pointed to the verse in Surah al-Rahman to repel the saying of some people who interpret it as referring to these artificial satellites or the space vehicles by which people have ascended into space. They claim that Allah's saying ﴿except with authority﴾ means "except with knowledge," and that this knowledge brought them to passage. This is without doubt a distortion of the Qur'an. There is no need for us to strain and say that everything that happens has a witness in the Qur'an. There is no need for this strain, because the witness of these events is their occurrence. Whenever they occur, we believe in them, whether the Qur'an indicated them or was silent about them, except when the Qur'an indicates their negation, in which case it is not permissible for us to believe them.
All of these inventions and these crafts fall within His saying: ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl 8], after He said: ﴿and horses, mules, and donkeys for you to ride and as adornment﴾ [al-Nahl 8]. He said: ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾. This verse includes everything that has occurred and everything that will occur of such matters. As for distorting the Qur'an to conform to this reality, that is forbidden to us and not permissible.
As for His saying ﴿authority﴾ [al-Rahman 33], it does not mean knowledge. It means the power (sultah) by which you are enabled to pass through. The sultan (authority) in every context is according to its context. Its origin is: the power by which a person is enabled to reach what he wants. For example, if a claimant makes a claim, we say, "You have no sultan in this," meaning you have no proof, as Allah says: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾ [Yunus 68]; that is, you have no evidence, because evidence is an authority by which the claimant is enabled to establish his claim.
Then the verse ﴿if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Rahman 33]: these people have not passed beyond the regions of the heavens. Even if we say they passed beyond the regions of the earth or left the earth's atmosphere, they are still unable to pass beyond the regions of the heavens.
Then the verse is clearly a challenge: ﴿if you are able﴾. Is a challenge with something possible correct or not?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: A challenge with something possible is not correct, because it nullifies the challenge.
Then His saying ﴿there will be sent upon you both a flame of fire and molten copper﴾ [al-Rahman 35] is contradicted by reality. Reality refutes the claim of these people, because they flew into space and reached what they reached, and no flame of fire or copper was sent upon them.
The point is that my intention in all this is that some people, who are knowledgeable in natural sciences, try to find a specific proof from the Qur'an for every event. This is not permissible, because it diverts the Qur'an from what Allah intended by it, and it implies that people would play with the Qur'an.
Then they may cite the noble verses as support for the theories they have seen, and afterwards other theories come that nullify them, so the Qur'an would then appear false according to what the earlier ones cited. We, praise be to Allah, are free of this matter. These events that occur from human craftsmanship do not need proof from the Qur'an, because their reality establishes them.
* Student: They want to establish the miraculousness (i'jaz) of the Qur'an (...)?
* Shaykh: Does the miraculousness of the Qur'an suffice for us to say: ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾?
* Student: Alright, and the facts (...)?
* Shaykh: If the Qur'an indicates them, there is no harm. But to distort the Qur'an in order to subject it to indicating this matter, no.
As for, for example, if the development of the embryo in its creation is cited, and someone cites the noble verse and the authentic hadith for it, there is no harm. What the Qur'an indicates, the Qur'an indicates. But something for which the Qur'an is distorted, no.
* Student: He said, for example: (...)?
* Shaykh: This too is incorrect, because the conditions of the Hereafter are not measured by the conditions of this world. For example, if a person's skin were now burned and peeled off, and we burned the flesh, there is no contradiction: we burned the flesh, and the person is undoubtedly tormented. He is tormented without doubt, and we do not (...) test it.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Correct, this is reasonable, and most of the interior of the body generally has no sensation. For this reason a person does not feel the food descending into his stomach.
* Student: Some (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, there is no contradiction. ﴿We have not neglected in the Book anything﴾ [al-An'am 38]. What is meant by "the Book"?
* Student: The Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).
* Shaykh: The Preserved Tablet. ﴿And there is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its wings, but they are communities like you. We have not neglected in the Book anything. Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾ [al-An'am 38]. But ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [al-Nahl 89] is clearer, if they wish to cite evidence: ﴿an explanation of all things﴾. However, we know that explanation (tibyan) is either general (mujmal) or detailed (mufassal). The well-known story about Shaykh Muhammad 'Abduh with the Christian man, when he asked him how the food served to him at the restaurant is prepared, said: "The Qur'an is an explanation of all things. So how is this food made? Where in the Qur'an is it found how it is made?" He said: "This is found in the Qur'an." He summoned the cook and said to him, "How do you make this food?" He said, "I make it with such and such." He said, "This is the way in the Qur'an, for Allah says: ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl 43], and every people's remembrance is specific to them. I asked this man because I do not know." So the Qur'an may guide us to a thing directly or through the means and method.
* Student: The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl 8]: what is intended by it? (...)?
* Shaykh: Everything we do not know. That is, Allah, the Exalted, creates everything we do not know. In our time, we...
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Upon all these events, yes.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, a person does not know before they occur, a person does not know.
* Student: After their occurrence he knows them.
* Shaykh: After their occurrence he knows them, because He said: ﴿and horses, mules, and donkeys for you to ride and as adornment﴾ [al-Nahl 8], and this is a known thing. ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl 8]; that is, things you do not know. Indeed Allah, the Exalted, created things that they did not know in the time of the Messenger ﷺ, and He will create things that we do not know in their time.
* Student: That is, for example (...)?
* Shaykh: Until the end of time, Allah, the Exalted, will create something that those before do not know, but whoever lives to it knows it, because His creating it means it exists. And what exists must be known, because Allah is speaking about a matter that will be for us: ﴿and horses, mules, and donkeys for you to ride and as adornment﴾ [al-Nahl 8]. So if He is speaking about a matter that will be for us, it means we will know it when Allah creates it.
* Student: Allah's saying: ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾ [al-Anbiya' 7] (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, everything you do not know, the way to reach it is to ask its people of remembrance.
* Student: But who is meant by the people of remembrance?
* Shaykh: The people of knowledge. But is the intended meaning people of religious knowledge, or people of every knowledge according to its field? Suppose you restrict it to religious knowledge. Let us suppose we restrict it to religious knowledge: should other matters not be measured by it?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: (...), so it either indicates generality, and is comprehensive of such a matter by implicit inclusion (dalalat al-tadammun), or by comprehensiveness in meaning, not in wording, which is analogy (qiyas).
* Student: But the context does not indicate that it (...)?
* Shaykh: The verse is ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know, [with clear proofs and scriptures]﴾ [al-Nahl 43–44]. This is one verse, and it indicates that the intended meaning is religious knowledge: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed; so ask the people of remembrance﴾ [al-Nahl 43], no.
And in the second verse, ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾ [al-Anbiya' 7], it is general, and He did not say ﴿with clear proofs and scriptures﴾. As I told you: if it is comprehensive of everything, and the people of each remembrance are according to their field, then it is comprehensive. Otherwise, it is comprehensive by comprehensiveness in meaning, which is analogy. So we say: if Allah referred us to the people of religious remembrance to know the religious ruling, then likewise we turn to people of non-religious knowledge to know that knowledge.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, but as we have just mentioned: generality may be lexical comprehensiveness or comprehensiveness in meaning, and they are not equal. But who is praised? The people of religious knowledge.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Lexical comprehensiveness means that this wording indicates this matter specifically, that is, among the individual items it denotes. Comprehensiveness in meaning means that this wording does not include what is mentioned, but it is analogized to what is mentioned in it, so this is generality in meaning, because the reason (illah) is the same in all of them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 10–24 (part 1 of 3):

Allah, blessed and exalted, says: (﴿Blessed is He﴾: abundance of good. ﴿He who, if He wills, will give you better than that﴾ [al-Furqan 10].)

Let us see: at the beginning of the surah, how did the author explain ﴿tabaraka﴾ [al-Furqan 1]?
* Student: (Exalted).
* Shaykh: As (exalted). Here he explains it as (its good is abundant). So does this mean that this word is subject to context, that it is explained as "exalted" in one context and as "its good is abundant" in another?
The apparent practice of the author is that this is so: this word (tabaraka), if it occurs in one context, is explained according to what that context requires, and if it occurs in another context, it is explained according to what that context requires. But we have pointed out previously that although it indicates exaltation, it also indicates abundance of good, because it derives from barakah (blessing), and barakah is abundance of good together with its permanence. It is derived from al-birkah (birkah), which is the gathering place of water, where there is water that is stable and abundant.
﴿Tabaraka alladhi﴾ means: exalted, together with abundance of good things. ﴿alladhi in shaa'a ja'ala laka khayran min dhalika﴾ and so on.
The relative clause here is conditional, or not? The clause to which the relative pronoun is joined is conditional, namely ﴿in shaa'a ja'ala﴾. From this we learn that the relative clause may come in conditional form, and if it does, there must be a conditional verb and a conditional response. Then we say: the clause consisting of the conditional verb and its response, which is the relative clause, has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis).
﴿Tabaraka alladhi﴾, and what is meant by it is Allah, glorified and exalted: (﴿if He wills, will give you better than that﴾ which they said of the treasure and the garden). What is the good? He substituted for it his saying: (﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, i.e., in this world, because He wills to give them to him in the Hereafter), ﴿and will appoint for you palaces﴾ likewise, and in one reading with the nominative, as a new clause (...) and so on.

The author's saying: (i.e., in this world, because He wills to give them to him in the Hereafter) has no basis, because the context makes this restriction unnecessary: these people are proposing that the matters they seek be for them in the Hereafter or in this world?
* Student: In this world.
* Shaykh: In this world. So Allah says: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that﴾. The restriction the author mentions seems to be an answer to an objection that might be raised against us, namely that Allah has willed to give His Messenger the Garden of the Hereafter. We restrict the verse to this world. We say: there is no need for this restriction, because they do not want Allah to give him a treasure and a garden in the Hereafter; they want them to be his in this world. So Allah says: If Allah had willed to give you that, He would have given you better than it, namely these gardens. They say: ﴿or he has a garden from which he eats﴾, and what Allah would give in its place if He willed is ﴿gardens﴾, not one garden.
Also, ﴿from which he eats﴾: a garden may be eaten from while having no rivers in it; the palms and trees may be watered by their roots. But here ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ is more eloquent and complete, because the flowing of water in its rivers is a visual delight through which a person takes pleasure when he sees it, in addition to the abundance of water in the garden, which is a cause of its abundant growth and vigour.
As for his saying: ﴿and will appoint for you palaces﴾, there are two readings: ﴿wayaj'al﴾ with sukun (jazm), and ﴿wayaj'alu﴾ with raf' (damma).
On the reading with sukun, what is it coordinated with? With the response of the condition: ﴿in shaa'a ja'ala﴾, ﴿wayaj'al﴾. On the reading with raf', the author says: (as a new clause). But it is not restricted to that even with the reading of raf'; it is as if he says: "and He will appoint for you palaces," which is not the case. That is, do not understand this matter from it: "as a new clause" is in terms of i'rab, not in terms of meaning, because the meaning is joined to what precedes; but grammatically it permits jazm, following the form of the verb, and permits raf' (as a new clause), making it the coordination of one clause to another.
Ibn Malik says in his Alfiyya:
"And after a past verb, your raf' of the response is good..."
That is: if the conditional verb is past, raising the response (jaza') when it is present is good.
"...and its raf' after a present verb is weak."
That is: weak. It is permissible but weak.
From these verses is learned: Allah's care for His Messenger ﷺ in defending him. Allah's care for the Messenger in defending him is not care for him alone, but extends to the Ummah as well, because that removes the doubts by which the falsifiers argue, and removing doubts from the Ummah is one of Allah's mercies towards them. And Allah is the Granter of success. (...)

* * *

﴿Nay, they deny the Hour, and We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blaze﴾ [al-Furqan 11]. When Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned what these people had done against Him, against His revelation, and against His Messenger, and the answer to that, He mentioned another matter, which is their denial of the Hour, and He introduced it with (bal) (nay), which indicates transition. This transition is not a cancellation of what came before, but the addition of another matter to it, namely His saying: ﴿Nay, they deny the Hour﴾.

What is meant by ﴿the Hour﴾ is the Day of Resurrection. The word (the Hour) is used in the language for every important matter, as if there were no hour except this one indicated by this time. Otherwise, in origin it applies to any period of time, short or long, but it is used often for what happens in it of an important matter, as is the case here.

﴿They denied it﴾: denial of the Hour includes denial of its occurrence outright, by saying: there is no resurrection, or denial of the matters that occur in it, such as the reckoning, the books, the bridge (sirat), the Pool (hawd), the intercession, and the like; because belief in the Last Day includes belief in its occurrence and in what occurs in it. So if a person denies it outright, he has denied it, and if he affirms it but denies what occurs in it, he is also a denier of it.

Allah, mighty and majestic, says: (﴿And We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blaze﴾: a fire kindled, i.e., intensely hot.)

﴿We have prepared﴾ means: We have made ready. ﴿For those who deny the Hour﴾ includes them and others; therefore He used ﴿man﴾ (whoever), which indicates generality, and did not say "and We have prepared for them." This is the placing of an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, and it was previously stated yesterday that among the benefits of placing an explicit noun in place of a pronoun is generality and the explicit statement of the cause of the ruling.

So His saying: ﴿for those who deny﴾ ... ﴿a blaze﴾ is as if it were the reason for the ruling that is His saying: ﴿We have prepared﴾ ... ﴿a blaze﴾, because they denied the Hour.

His saying, exalted: ﴿And We have prepared for those who deny﴾: From it is derived that the Fire is now created, and this is so, and the texts of the Book and the Sunnah indicate it. Allah, exalted, said about the people of Pharaoh: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾ [Ghafir 46], and this is an explicit text that it is created. And in the sound hadiths there is what indicates it, such as: "The Fire complained to its Lord, so He permitted it two breaths: a breath in winter and a breath in summer."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (536) and Muslim (617/186), the wording is his, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

As for His saying: ﴿a blaze﴾, the author said: (a fire kindled), thus making fa'il (a form like "fa'eel") to mean maf'ul: kindled. It may also mean fa'il: blazing, burning whoever enters it. The meanings are not contradictory, because if it is kindled, i.e., intensely heated, or it itself blazes and consumes people, then this and that are mutually implicated.

(﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they hear its raging and roaring﴾ [al-Furqan 12]: boiling like the angry man when his chest boils with anger, ﴿and roaring﴾: a violent sound; or the hearing of its raging is seeing it and knowing it.)

He says: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place﴾: the subject is the blaze, and this is evidence that it sees, and this seeing must be taken in its literal meaning. It is not possible to say that this is a metaphor and a figurative meaning, because it is permissible that Allah create in it the faculty of sight, even though it is not by custom a thing that sees. Allah, glorified and exalted, is capable of all things, just as the earth hears and speaks: ﴿On that day it will report its news﴾ [al-Zalzalah 4], and no tree or clod hears the voice of the caller to prayer without bearing witness for him on the Day of Resurrection.[[Ibn Khuzaymah (389) narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him: "If you are in the desert, raise your voice with the call; for I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'No tree, no clod, no stone, no jinn, and no human hears his voice but bears witness for him.'"]]

So we say: there is no metaphor in this verse; it is on its literal meaning, and the Fire sees, because Allah has informed that it sees: ﴿when it sees them﴾. And what prevents Allah from creating this faculty in it?

Also by the evidence of ﴿they hear its raging﴾: raging is well known to occur only from beings possessing awareness, but despite this we must say that in this verse it is on its apparent meaning, and that it rages, and its raging produces a sound, like the raging of an angry person, when his chest is filled with anger, you hear from him a sound of anger.

This is evidence of the intensity of its wrath, may Allah protect us, against its people, and that, as Allah said in Surah Tabarak: ﴿When they are thrown into it, they hear from it a roaring, while it boils up. It almost bursts with rage﴾ [al-Mulk 7-8]. So what do you think of a thing into which a person is cast, while it is full of rage and wrath against him? What will it do to him? This is evidence of the severity of its punishment, may Allah protect us, and that it shows them no mercy and spares them nothing and no covenant.

(﴿They hear from it a raging﴾: boiling like the angry man when his chest boils with anger, ﴿and roaring﴾.) This is from a distant place: what does this indicate about this raging and roaring, that it is severe or light? Severe. As long as it is heard from a distant place, it is severe.

The author says: (or the hearing of its raging is seeing it and knowing it). This is not correct, though it is possible; but the first meaning, that seeing be taken literally, is the obligation. There has passed among us from the rules of tafsir, indeed from the rules of every speech, that it must be taken in its apparent and literal sense unless there is evidence that diverts from the literal or the apparent; and it is not just any evidence: there must be sound evidence. As for what a person thinks is evidence and is not, this is not accepted.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: That is, if they see it.
* Student: That is, the wording ﴿when it sees them﴾: if its customers see them, that is?
* Shaykh: No, that is not correct; this is in fact a distortion (tahrif), because we said it is permissible that Allah create in it the faculty of sight.
* Student: There are weak hadiths restricting the verse (...)?
* Shaykh: On what?
* Student: Weak hadiths; it is said it has two eyes[[al-Tabarani in al-Kabir (7599) narrated from Abu Umamah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in Hell between my two eyes." That was difficult for his companions, and they said: O Messenger of Allah, we narrate from you a hadith and add and subtract? He said: "That is not what I mean; I mean the one who lies about me, speaking, seeking thereby to disgrace Islam." They said: O Messenger of Allah, you said: between my two eyes, and does Hell have an eye? He said: "Yes. Have you not heard Him say: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they hear its raging and roaring﴾ [al-Furqan 12]? So do they see them except with two eyes?"]] (...).
* Shaykh: We do not; these hadiths are weak.
* Student: They support us, in a sense (...)?
* Shaykh: No, we do not need to support them. Support is not needed while the wording is explicit: ﴿and Allah is over all things competent﴾ [al-Baqarah 284]. The One who created the eye in a human: is it impossible for Him to create it in the Fire?
* Student: It is not impossible.
* Shaykh: It is not impossible. But some people, when their minds do not grasp a matter, go and distort it to what they can grasp.

Furthermore, we must also know that the conditions of the Hereafter cannot be measured by the conditions of this world. We know that people will be gathered: some of them have their light going before them, and some are in darkness; and they are in one flat place, the caller makes them hear and the sight reaches them. We know that some people sweat, so that the sweat reaches their ankles, their knees, and their waists, and some are bridled by it; yet they are in one place. The conditions of the Hereafter can never be measured by the conditions of this world.

He says: (﴿And when they are cast into a narrow place of it, bound together﴾ [al-Furqan 13]: with the shaddah and without it), meaning: two Sab'i readings, (that they will be constricted, and ﴿from it﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial) of ﴿a place﴾, because originally it is an attribute of it; ﴿muqarranin﴾ ...) and so on.

﴿When they are cast﴾: in this is evidence that they, may Allah protect us, are not treated with mercy, but are thrown and cast down.

His saying: ﴿a place﴾ is an adverbial complement, governed by ﴿were cast﴾. His saying: ﴿from it﴾ is originally an attribute, but the rule among the grammarians is that when a prepositional phrase precedes the noun it qualifies, it becomes a ḥāl of it, because an attribute does not precede what it qualifies. For example, you say: a man came on a camel riding; so you parse "riding" as a ḥāl. But if you put it before "man": a rider came, it would have to be an attribute in meaning.

Likewise the prepositional phrase: if you say: a man came on a camel, "on a camel" is an attribute of "man". If you put "on a camel" first: came on a camel a man, that attribute must be a ḥāl. Why? Because an attribute does not precede the thing qualified. That is why he said: (and ﴿from it﴾ is a ḥāl of ﴿a place﴾), because originally it is an attribute of it.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed: narrow.
* And in this also, ﴿And when they are cast from it into a narrow place﴾: is evidence that this place from which they are cast will not be spacious but will be constricted upon them. This is before entering it; how then when they enter it?!

It is possible that the very places in which they are in the Fire itself are narrow, when they are cast into a place of it that is narrow; so this ﴿min﴾ would be close in meaning to ﴿fiha﴾ (in it).

(﴿Muqarranin﴾: shackled, their hands bound to their necks in chains; the shaddah is for intensification.) The shaddah in His saying ﴿muqarranin﴾: because the root of (muqarran) is qarana; that is, it is derived from qurrina, so he is muqarran; its origin is from qarana without shaddah: I qarantu this man, aqrinuhu, so he is maqrun; but it came with the shaddah for intensification, or for emphasis in this binding: that they are bound with severity. So when they are ﴿cast from it into a narrow place, bound together, they call there for destruction﴾ (ruin, so it is said to them) ﴿Do not call today for one destruction, but call for many destructions﴾ [al-Furqan 14].

This is in truth a clear depiction of the condition of the Fire and its people on the Day of Resurrection: that before they enter it they hear its raging and roaring, and this without doubt unnerves their hearts and terrifies them.

Then, when they are cast into it, they are not cast in honour, but cast down. Then they are not cast loose, but bound together, meaning their hands gathered to their necks.

Then, when they are cast in this condition, they call for destruction, may Allah protect us: ﴿they call there for destruction﴾, meaning they say: "Woe to us! Our destruction!" and similar. So it is said to them: ﴿Do not call today for one destruction, but call for many destructions﴾. This is by way of reproach, because the custom is that when a man calls for destruction in this world, he is pitied; but there they are not pitied. It is said to them: your calling for destruction benefits you nothing, so call for many destructions. The punishment will continue: ﴿and call for many destructions﴾.

This entire passage, which all stands as the commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin, is the cause for the people of the Fire, may God save us from it, to suffer two kinds of torment: a torment of the heart and a torment of the body. The torment of the heart may at times be more severe than the torment of the body, God forbid. They are not honoured, neither by deed, nor by welcome, nor by speech.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is correct that what has been mentioned of them above indicates that they do not believe in the Resurrection (al-ba'th), because whoever believes in the Resurrection must act for it. But this is in fact among the things they said. Among what they said is that they denied the Resurrection, so it is in addition to what came before. However, yes, we should say: why was it introduced with (bal, "rather"), without the waw (and), even though the faults and evil qualities mentioned before were all introduced with the waw, while this one was introduced with (bal)?
This may suggest that one of the causes of their earlier statements is that they denied the Hour. That is, they do not have faith in the Hour, and had they believed in it, they would not have said what came before.

* Student: His saying: ﴿a narrow place﴾, is the meaning "they will be thrown (...)"?
* Shaykh: We have said that it has two possibilities. Either the meaning is that they will be cast from a narrow place upon their entry, or the meaning is that the place itself in the Fire will be narrow, meaning it will be constricted upon them, because each one of them, God forbid, will be in a coffin, as the hadith (prophetic report) has come: in a closed coffin.[[Ibn Abi Shaybah (35414) narrated from Suwayd ibn Ghaflah, who said: When God wishes to make the people of the Fire forget, He places for each person among them a coffin of fire according to his size, then locks it upon him with locks of fire, so that no vein of his beats except that there is a nail of fire in it. Then He places that coffin inside another coffin of fire, locks it with locks of fire, and then a fire is kindled between them. So none of them sees that there is anyone in the Fire other than himself. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿They will have above them canopies of fire, and below them canopies﴾ [al-Zumar 39:16], and His saying: ﴿They will have from Hell a bed, and above them coverings. Thus We recompense the wrongdoers﴾ [al-A'raf 7:41].]]

* Student: What is narrated from (...) that some parts of his body are enlarged?
* Shaykh: Indeed, he himself is enlarged, but there is nothing preventing that he is enlarged while in a narrow place. This enlargement of his may be among the causes of the constriction.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No. It is apparently possible. Some of them may acknowledge this, but he associates partners with God.

But God, glorified and exalted is He, attributes actions to the whole nation, even to the point that He sometimes addresses the latter part of a nation with what its earlier part did, because it is satisfied with it and approves of it. Look, for example, at how God addresses the Children of Israel in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) with what their forefathers did: ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed over it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:72], and ﴿So repent to your Creator and kill your selves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:54]. Although this address does not apply to these people, because they are not the ones who did it, nevertheless the one nation whose part does an action is considered as having done it by all of them, because they are satisfied with it.

God, the Exalted, said: (﴿Say: Is that﴾, meaning the mentioned threat and description of the Fire, ﴿better, or the Garden of Eternity which the God-fearing have been promised﴾, that is, in His knowledge, ﴿it shall be for them a recompense﴾, a reward, ﴿and a destination﴾, a return).

What is the address in ﴿Say﴾ directed to? To the Messenger (ﷺ), and likewise to others. For this reason we may say: the address is to everyone who can be addressed, meaning the Messenger (ﷺ) and others. But the closer view is that it is directed to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Nevertheless, the address to the Messenger (ﷺ) includes him and his nation, unless evidence specifies it for him. So each of us can say something like this. He says to the deniers who were promised the Fire: Is that mentioned threat, which must certainly befall, better, or the Garden of Eternity? And what is the answer? The Garden of Eternity, without doubt.

Here there is a difficulty: he said ﴿better﴾, although that has no good in it at all, so how can it be compared with that which is absolutely good?

The answer: this is a matter of condescension toward the opponent (tanazzul ma'a al-khasm), and it is fine when dealing with an opponent to make such a comparison. God, the Exalted, has compared two things between which there is a greater difference than the difference between the threat to the people of the Fire and the promise to the people of Paradise. He said: ﴿Is God better, or what they associate?﴾ [al-Naml 27:59]. It is known that God is better, and that no sensible person could compare this with that. But since those addressed were equating others with God, it became a matter of condescension toward them that we address them with this and say: ﴿Is God better, or what they associate?﴾.

﴿Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity?﴾ He added it to ﴿Eternity﴾ by the idafa of the described to its attribute (idafat al-mawsuf ila sifatih), meaning the Garden which is the place of eternity. And ﴿Eternity (al-khuld)﴾ means remaining. God, the Exalted, has very often stated the everlastingness (al-ta'bid) of their eternity.

As for the people of the Fire, everlastingness is mentioned in three verses of the Qur'an: in Surat al-Nisa', in Surat al-Ahzab, and in Surat al-Jinn. In Surat al-Nisa': ﴿Indeed, God would not forgive them, nor would He guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever. And that is ever easy for God﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:168-169]. In Surat al-Ahzab: ﴿Indeed, God has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze, abiding therein forever; they will not find any protector or helper﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:64-65]. In Surat al-Jinn: ﴿And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn 72:23].

In this there is a clear refutation of the one who says that the torment of the Fire is not everlasting. Among those who inclined to this view, which is one of the strangest views, is Ibn al-Qayyim, may God have mercy on him, for he tended to hold that the torment of the Fire is not everlasting and must come to an end. But he did not say that it ends and then the people of the Fire move to Paradise. No, rather it ends in the sense that it and its people perish.

The correct view, about which there is no doubt, is what the majority of the People of the Sunnah (ahl al-sunnah) hold, and consensus (ijma') has been reported on it: that the Fire and its people are everlasting. This does not contradict the mercy of God, mighty and majestic, because God, the Exalted, has given them a warning and established the proof against them. They are the ones who brought ruin upon themselves.

* Student: The exception, may God be good to you, in Hud?
* Shaykh: The exception in Hud, because it is an exception from His saying: ﴿As long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾ [Hud 11:107]. If it were restricted to the duration of the heavens and the earth, it would have an end. But when He said: ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, this is not outside the duration of the heavens and the earth. This is the meaning of the exception.

* Student: In another verse (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes: ﴿abiding therein, except what God wills﴾ [al-An'am 6:128]. We say: this exception, ﴿except what God wills﴾, the texts indicate that He does not will that they not be everlasting. So this exception seems to indicate that if God willed, He could prevent the torment from them, and that it is not a matter obligatory upon Him, but rather it is within His will. Therefore the exception is explained by the clear and explicit verses, that He does not will to lift the torment from them, because He has informed us, and God does not break His word, that their torment is everlasting.

* Student: Ibn al-Qayyim (...)?
* Shaykh: Who?
* Student: Ibn al-Qayyim.
* Shaykh: No, at the beginning of his words he firmly asserted this.
* Student: In Hadi al-Arwah (...).
* Shaykh: No, he mentioned it in Shifa' al-Alil. He mentioned it there and asserted it at the beginning of the discussion, then he cited the narrations (athar) on this matter.

* Student: The explanation that He is ﴿the Doer of what He wills﴾ [Hud 11:107] (...)?
* Shaykh: No. It seems to hint that if someone said: how does God, glorified and exalted, do this, given that it is a perpetual torment and His mercy encompasses all things? So He said: ﴿Doer of what He wills﴾, just as He said: ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾ [Hud 11:108].

In truth, these matters, although these possibilities may have some basis, nevertheless, since we have clear, firm texts, it is obligatory upon the believer to refer the ambiguous (mutashabih) to the firm (muhkam), since in these three verses the matters are merely possibilities, whereas we have something that admits of no possibility, which is the explicit statement of everlastingness. And you know that this is a report (khabar), and a report does not admit negation or (...).

* Student: Alright, O Shaykh, (...) the non-fulfilment of a threat without the non-fulfilment of a promise.
* Shaykh: Yes. And even if they said: God praises Himself that He does not break His promise and that His report is true. The threat by which God praises Himself is that which falls under His will, other than associating partners with Him. For example, we have a threat for sins below shirk, so if God pardons them, that is good, and He is praised for it, glorified and exalted is He.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Who is it about?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but 'Umar and others than 'Umar are addressed by His saying: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, we need not concern ourselves with it. Even if it were explicit, if he said: they will come out, we say: they will not come out. Since there are explicit verses, what is the obstacle? And ﴿remaining therein for ages, tasting therein neither coolness nor drink﴾ [al-Naba' 78:23-24], this also does not indicate limitation, because ﴿ages (ahqab)﴾ means: long, having no end, this is the meaning. And a person, if he imagined that he would remain in the Fire not for ages but for one second, and he were sensible, he would avoid the deeds of the people of the Fire. So how about those who remain in it for ages?! It does not indicate limitation. Whoever claims that it indicates limitation and says that these ages are restricted by what follows, meaning: ﴿ages, tasting therein neither coolness nor drink﴾, and other ages in which they taste, this is not correct. Rather the meaning is intensification of this, that they remain therein for vast, long eras that have no end.

(﴿Or the Garden of Eternity which the God-fearing have been promised﴾.) The author brought in (ha), what is (ha)? It is the second object of ﴿promised﴾, because (wa'ada, "to promise") is one of the verbs that take two objects whose original structure is not subject and predicate. So the first object is omitted, and the second object, the deputy subject, is ﴿the God-fearing﴾. We have often mentioned before that the muttaqi (God-fearing person) is one who takes a shield against the torment of God by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, and that this is the most comprehensive of what has been said about taqwa and the most suitable to its wording, since it derives from (ittaqa), from protection (wiqaya).

And His saying: ﴿the God-fearing have been promised﴾, who promised them? God, glorified and exalted is He promised them, and the agent is omitted here because it is known, as in His saying: ﴿and man was created weak﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:28], and the Creator is God, glorified and exalted is He.

And His saying: (﴿it shall be for them﴾ in His knowledge). The author, may God have mercy on him, restricted the existence to His knowledge, because (kana, "was") is a past tense verb, and the Garden has been a destination, or will it be a destination? It will be a destination. Therefore he restricted the existence, which he expressed by the past tense verb, restricting it to God's knowledge, meaning not according to actual reality, because in reality it has not been, but will be. But this is based on the view that (kana) is meant to denote time. However, if a person examines its uses in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, he finds that sometimes it denotes mere occurrence and not time, because the verb, as you know, denotes both time and meaning. So (kana) always comes to denote only the meaning. That is: ﴿which the God-fearing have been promised﴾, and it is for them a recompense and a destination. Based on this, there is no need for the estimation that the author mentioned. This is the clearer view. ﴿which the God-fearing have been promised﴾, that is: and it is for them a recompense and a destination. We need not estimate that it was in God's knowledge. Rather, it is ﴿kanat﴾, that is: it is a recompense. So we strip (kana) of indicating time, and when we strip it of this, as it often occurs in the Arabic language, we are spared this estimation which the author brought.

* Student: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed God was ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:11]?
* Shaykh: It is similar, stripped of time. This is stripped of time, because God has not ceased and will not cease to be Forgiving and Merciful.
* Student: We said: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, ﴿Indeed God was Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:23]. When we bring (kana) and say that what is meant by it is time and occurrence, like God's forgiveness and mercy in the past, but now He is not Forgiving and Merciful, that is the case. But in these instances what is meant is mere occurrence, that is, He is characterized by forgiveness and mercy. This verse is similar, and (kana) always indicates mere occurrence and not time.
* Student: (...) the ends of verses (ru'us al-ayat)?
* Shaykh: What do you mean?
* Student: So it is said: God is Forgiving and Merciful (...)?
* Shaykh: No. It is possible, but it is not necessary. That is, sometimes they come fitting and sometimes not fitting.

The discussion of (kana), everyone: this is the point. In the Arabic language (kana) does not always denote time, but denotes the absolute occurrence of the event. That is, this matter is the reality. Here, ﴿they have been for them a recompense and a destination﴾. It is known that the God-fearing have not now entered Paradise nor arrived there, but they will arrive. Therefore the author needed to estimate: (in His knowledge), that is, it was in God's knowledge. But we say: there is no need for this estimate, because (kana) is stripped of indicating time.

And His saying: ﴿a recompense and a destination﴾. He says: (a reward). The one who made this reward for them is God, glorified and exalted is He. (﴿and a destination﴾, a return). From when does it become a destination? From the Day of Resurrection or from their death?

* Student: From their death.
* Shaykh: From the moment they die. ﴿Those whom the angels take in a good state, saying: Peace be upon you; enter Paradise﴾ [al-Nahl 16:32].
