I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the preceding verses, Allah Exalted ordered that this great Day be mentioned, the Day when the sky will be split open with clouds at the descent of Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

* In the verse is the affirmation of Allah's descent, because this splitting occurs for His descent. The purpose of mentioning it is warning against it and preparing for it, because whenever a thing is mentioned, a person takes precaution against it and prepares for it. In what preceded, Allah described the Day of Resurrection as difficult, with a description restricted to the disbelievers, and in another verse He described it with an unrestricted description as difficult.

We mentioned previously that although it is difficult, it is easy for the believers. So the unrestricted description of that day is that it is difficult, but those who are affected by it and for whom it is difficult are the disbelievers, not the believers.

Then Allah Exalted ordered that the condition of the criminals on that day be mentioned: the regret, the great remorse, and the biting of hands: ﴿And on the Day the wrongdoer will bite his hands﴾. And whom did the author (Ibn Kathir) restrict the verse to? To ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt. The correct view is that it is general to every wrongdoer, because the original state is that a general expression remains general until there is evidence that it is specific.

Here, ﴿And on the Day the wrongdoer will bite⁠﴾ is general, to ʿUqbah and to others.

He says: (﴿He will say, "Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger⁠﴾ — Muhammad — ﴿a path⁠﴾, meaning a way to guidance.)

﴿He will say⁠﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from ﴿the wrongdoer⁠﴾, meaning that he bites, and this is evidence of regret in action. And ﴿He will say, "Oh, I wish⁠﴾ (...) the vocative. The sign of a noun is the vocative: ﴿yā⁠﴾ enters only upon a noun, but if it enters upon a particle as here, or upon a verb, it conveys only alerting. This is one of the two views on its grammatical analysis (iʿrāb).

The second view is that it is a vocative particle and the addressed person is omitted, and the estimate in such a verse is: "O Lord, I wish," or "O people, I wish."

But we say: the original state is non-estimation, and if the original state is non-estimation, then it is better that we not estimate anything here and that we make ﴿yā⁠﴾ for alerting, for mere alerting. It is for mere alerting because the original use of the vocative, what is its origin? It is for alerting. When you say, "O so-and-so," you alert him so that he pays attention to you and turns his face toward you. So it is for alerting, and there is no need to estimate the addressed person.

And His saying: ﴿Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger⁠﴾: (layta) is for wishing, and wishing is the request for what cannot be attained or what is difficult to attain. Something whose attainment is impossible or difficult is called a wish:

"Would that youth would return one day, so that I could tell it what old age has done." 

This is impossible. And the poor man says: "I wish I had wealth so that I could give it in charity." This is difficult, not impossible.

﴿Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger⁠﴾: which of the two categories is it?
* Student: This is impossible.
* Shaykh: This is impossible, because the matter has passed.

﴿Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger⁠﴾: that is, I would have followed ﴿a way⁠﴾, which is the path leading to Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

The author's saying (﴿with the Messenger⁠﴾ — Muhammad) is based on the premise that the verse is aimed at ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt. In this case, the definite article (al) is for mental reference (ʿahd dhihnī). Which kind of reference?
* Student: Mental.
* Shaykh: Mental reference. And if we take the general view, which is the stronger one, then what is meant by ﴿the Messenger⁠﴾ here is whoever was sent to his people, so the definite article is for the category, for generality, because what is meant by it is the category of messenger, including Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and others.

(﴿Oh, woe to me⁠﴾: its alif is a substitute for the ya' of possession, meaning "my woe," and its meaning is "my ruin." ﴿I wish I had not taken so-and-so⁠﴾, that is, Ubayy, ﴿as a close friend⁠﴾.) ... and so on.

﴿Oh, woe to me⁠﴾: ﴿yā⁠﴾ is a vocative particle, and ﴿woe to me⁠﴾ is the addressed term. Its origin is "waylatī," then the yā was changed into an alif, so it became ﴿yā waylatā⁠﴾. This is permissible in the language: it is permissible to say "yā waylatī" and "yā waylatā." Woe (wayl) means ruin, and it is as if he says: "O my ruin, come!" ﴿I wish I had not taken⁠﴾... and so on.

In the first wish he did not say ﴿Oh, woe to me⁠﴾, but in the second wish he said ﴿Oh, woe to me⁠﴾, because his grief had increased. The first time he expresses his grief for the first time, and the second for the second time, so that is more intense in grief; therefore he said ﴿Oh, woe to me⁠﴾.

And his saying: ﴿I wish I had not taken⁠﴾, I had not made ﴿so-and-so⁠﴾ — ﴿so-and-so⁠﴾ is a noun of a category used to refer to any one human being, and "so-and-so" (feminine) is used for any one female human being. He did not mention ﴿so-and-so⁠﴾ by name here, because, as we have indicated, it is general. For ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt, the one meant by "so-and-so" would be Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and for others it is whoever led him astray from the remembrance of Allah.

﴿I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend⁠﴾. The khalīl is the beloved whose love has reached the furthest point, because khullah (close friendship) is the highest type of love, and it is so called because love penetrates the pathways of the body, as the poet said:

"You have penetrated the pathway of the spirit in me, and for this the khalīl was named khalīl."

On this basis, khullah is higher than mahabbah (love). Through this we know the error of those who say: "Muhammad is the beloved (ḥabīb) of Allah, Ibrahim is the friend (khalīl) of Allah, and Musa is the one who spoke with Allah (kalīm Allah)," because these have lowered the rank of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, by describing him as the beloved of Allah while describing Ibrahim as the friend of Allah. Khullah is higher, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the khalīl of Allah just as Ibrahim is the khalīl of Allah. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Indeed Allah has taken me as a khalīl just as He took Ibrahim as a khalīl" [Muslim (532/23) and Ibn Hibban, and the wording is his (6425), from the hadith of Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Bajali, may Allah be pleased with him]. As for Musa being the kalīm of Allah, we also say: Muhammad is the kalīm of Allah, and if Musa was the kalīm of Allah on earth, then Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the kalīm of Allah in the heavens.

(﴿He had led me astray from the Reminder⁠﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿after it had come to me⁠﴾.)

﴿He had led me astray from the Reminder, after it had come to me⁠﴾. The lām is a preface to an oath, and qad is for confirmation, so the sentence is emphatic. With how many emphases?
* Student: With qad and (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, I said: with how many?
* Student: ﴿He had led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me⁠﴾ is emphatic.
* Shaykh: Fine, and what are they?
* Student: The oath and qad.
* Shaykh: Where is the oath?
* Student: The oath...
* Shaykh: The oath and qad. Qad is known and present; and the oath?
* Student: Because this lām is called a preface to the oath, that is, the answer of an oath (...).
* Shaykh: Fine, (...) is emphatic with three emphases: the oath, the lām, and qad. He emphasizes on this Day that this close friend led him astray, an emphasis intended to blame himself. But that will not benefit him now. If this emphasis had been in the world, it would have benefited him; but now it does not benefit him, and it only increases his grief.

"He had led me astray from the Reminder": the author says: (that is, the Qur'an), and this is based on his view that what was previously mentioned refers to the wrongdoer or to Ibn Abi Muʿayt, so the reminder is the Qur'an. If we take the general view, which is the stronger, then the Reminder means the Book revealed to that Messenger; in the time of Musa it was the Torah, in the time of ʿIsa the Gospel, and similarly in other eras the books revealed to the messengers.

﴿He had led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me⁠﴾ [Al-Furqan 29]. This time-clause has its great benefit: that is, after the Reminder had reached me, I knew it and understood it, and then misguidance occurred. This is more forceful than if he had been led astray from an expected matter that did not occur. This is an actual matter; he acknowledges that the Reminder came to him and the proof was established against him, and this close friend led him astray after it came to him.

(...by turning him away from belief in it. Allah Exalted said: ﴿And Satan is ever, for man, a deserter⁠﴾ — for the disbeliever — "for man, for the disbeliever" (or "for the disbeliever"?)
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (The disbeliever is a deserter ﴿deserter⁠﴾ by leaving him and disowning him in time of trial.)

His saying: "Allah Exalted said: ﴿And Satan is ever, for man, a deserter⁠﴾ [Al-Furqan 29]", as if the author holds that this sentence is not part of the speech of the wrongdoer, and that the speech of the wrongdoer ends at ﴿after it had come to me⁠﴾. On this basis it is proper to stop: ﴿He had led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me⁠﴾, and you pause, then resume and say: ﴿And Satan is ever, for man, a deserter⁠﴾.

His saying: ﴿Satan⁠﴾ is meant as a category, because there are many devils; Allah Exalted said: ﴿And the devils did not bring it down⁠﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 210], and He said: ﴿Its shoots are as if they were the heads of devils⁠﴾ [As-Saffat 65]. So what is meant here is the category. They are of various kinds, and apparently, and Allah knows best, each type of sin has a devil: the devil of polytheism, the devil of denial, the devil of miserliness, and others; for every kind there is a devil. This is what appears, and Allah knows best.

His saying: ﴿for man⁠﴾: what is meant by it, according to the author's statement, is "the disbeliever," and it is either ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt or general; because this statement is from the words of Allah, not from the words of the wrongdoer, from the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It may be general to the disbeliever and the believer, since Satan also misleads the believer and then abandons him afterward.

So the apparent meaning is that what is meant by ﴿man⁠﴾ here is the category, that is, believer or disbeliever. We said this is apparent because just as he misleads disbelievers into disbelief, so he misleads believers into sin.

His saying: ﴿a deserter⁠﴾ is either an adjective of quality (ṣifah mushabbahah) or an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālaghah). On either of the two, the description of Satan in relation to man is desertion, or the desertion of Satan toward man is constant, because intensiveness implies frequency. Desertion means: humiliating a person in a situation where he needs support; this is desertion, namely that you abandon a person in a situation where he needs help. When we reflect on what Allah mentioned about Satan in the Qur'an, we find that he deserts man in times of need for support: he made the Quraysh attractive so that they went out to fight the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and they went out, ﴿but when the two hosts sighted each other, he turned back on his heels and said: "Indeed, I am free of you; indeed, I see what you do not see"⁠﴾ [Al-Anfal 48]. He made disbelief attractive to man: ﴿Like Satan when he says to man, "Disbelieve," and when he disbelieves, says, "Indeed, I am free of you"⁠﴾ [Al-Hashr 16]. This is in this world. In the Hereafter: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided: "Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I failed you. I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me. Indeed, I disbelieved in what you associated with me before"⁠﴾ [Ibrahim 22]. This too is a great desertion: Satan in the times of support deserts man and disowns him.

As for this description, ﴿And Satan is ever⁠﴾: do we say that (kāna) refers to what is in Allah's knowledge, or to what occurred in the past and ended?
* Student: In Allah's knowledge.
* Student: We say: (kāna) does not indicate time.
* Shaykh: This passed us recently (...).
* Student: No, it is detached from time.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 25–31 (part 3 of 4):

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is stripped of time. That is, (kāna) comes without being intended to denote time; what is intended is the general attribution of the quality. Like: ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [an-Nisa' 96], ﴿And Allah is ever over all things Capable﴾ [al-Ahzab 27]. It does not mean "was in the past"; (...) the meaning is that this is a continuous attribute of Allah.
And likewise here: ﴿And Satan is ever a deserter of man﴾. It does not mean that Satan was a deserter of man in the past and then became no longer a deserter; rather, the meaning is that this is a quality constantly attached to Satan in relation to man.
* A student: Is it not (...) ﴿And (kāna)﴾, meaning in this world?
* The Shaykh: No, it is in this world and the Hereafter. Even in the Hereafter: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided﴾ [Ibrahim 22], which we recited just now.
Alright, and here?
* A student: O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Sometimes it is intended to indicate time, and sometimes it is intended merely as the event; that is, stripped of time. So you say, for example: Zayd was standing, meaning in the past, then he sat down. And you say: Allah was Forgiving, Merciful; this does not mean in the past, rather the meaning is that forgiveness and mercy are His attributes.
Here, Satan's attribute of forsaking the children of Adam is constant; it does not mean only in the past. Allah, blessed and exalted, has informed us that Satan is a deserter of man so that we take him as an enemy and do not be deceived by him, for he will forsake us at a time when we need his help, so we beware of him.
If someone says: What is the sign that something is from Satan, or that this act is from the commands of Satan? How do we know, for example, that Satan commanded us with this and that this is the work of Satan?
* A student: (...) as the Shari'ah has brought it.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: If it contradicts it, then it is from the commands of Satan.
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is the criterion: ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to immorality﴾ [al-Baqarah 268]. So when we see that the self wants us to fall into this act, if it contradicts the Shari'ah, we know that this is from the command of Satan, and it becomes obligatory for us to beware of it, because we know that this Satan will forsake us at a time when we need victory. This is the distinguishing mark between what is from the command of Satan and what is from the command of Allah, blessed and exalted.
(﴿And the Messenger said﴾, Muhammad.)
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, the self that commands evil obeys the command of Satan, because you yourself do not feel that Satan, for example, descended upon you and brought you; but your self commands you to this, so it obeys the command of Satan.
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, meaning it makes it like an intermediary between him and the heart of a person.
(﴿And the Messenger said﴾, Muhammad, ﴿O my Lord, indeed my people﴾, meaning the Quraysh, ﴿have taken this Qur'an as abandoned﴾ [al-Furqan 30]).
Here the author also restricted it to the Prophet ﷺ, and here we may agree with the author that it is specific to the Prophet ﷺ, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾ [al-Furqan 31]; because the purpose of this sentence is consolation, and this is what supports what the author said.
As for the matter of ﴿the Qur'an﴾, the word Qur'an is applied to the verbal noun, so it includes everything that is recited of the Torah, the Gospel and other books. But what makes it specific to what was revealed to Muhammad ﷺ is what follows it.
* A student: The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿this Qur'an﴾ (...)?
* The Shaykh: Where?
* The student: (...).
* A student: At His saying: ﴿have taken this Qur'an﴾ [al-Furqan 30]?
* The Shaykh: Yes, because the Messenger says it while the Qur'an is before him. For example, if Musa said it while the Torah was before him, it would be correct for him to point to it.
(﴿O my Lord, indeed my people﴾, the Quraysh), and he attributed them to himself, because that is more emphatic in rebuking them. How so? Because the actual situation requires that his people be the first of people to believe him and to accept what he brought; but the matter was the opposite. This is similar to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿By the star when it descends, your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ [an-Najm 1, 2], where He attributed them to him, as if He says: You should be the first to believe in it because he is your companion. Likewise: ﴿Nun. By the pen and what they inscribe, you are not, by the favour of your Lord, a madman﴾ [al-Qalam 1, 2].
The point is that the attribution here is intended to increase the rebuke; instead of saying "indeed the Quraysh," He said ﴿indeed my people﴾ to intensify the rebuke of them, since being his people entails that they should believe in him and accept what he brought.
(﴿have taken this Qur'an as abandoned﴾, mahjur, left aside), derived from hajr, and hajr is leaving a thing out of aversion to it. So they took it ﴿as abandoned﴾.
(...) abandoned, meaning they do not pay attention to it. This is more eloquent than saying: My people abandoned the Qur'an. The reason: "hajarū" is a verb, and a verbal sentence does not indicate permanence and continuity, but "ittakhadhūhu mahjūran" is a nominal sentence, since the pronoun and ﴿mahjūran﴾ originally are subject and predicate. So it is as if they made this Qur'an, which deserves care and turning toward it, into a matter ﴿abandoned﴾, an object of aversion, as if it did not deserve turning toward at all. They made it one of the abandoned matters that it is not its nature to be approached. This is more eloquent than their having abandoned it, because they might abandon it while it deserves to be accepted; but when they take it as abandoned, their taking it as abandoned means they abandoned it while it deserved to be abandoned. Is that clear?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Good. What is the difference between (they abandoned it) and (they took it as abandoned)?
* The student: (They abandoned it) means (...).
* The Shaykh: That is: it may be that they abandoned it while it did not deserve to be abandoned.
* The student: But "they took it as abandoned" because they abandoned it while it was (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, and because a nominal sentence indicates permanence and continuity.
The abandonment of the Qur'an is divided into two types: verbal abandonment, which is leaving off its recitation out of aversion to it, and this is what the Prophet ﷺ warned against in his saying: «How wretched is it for one of you to say: I forgot such-and-such a verse; rather he says: I was made to forget»[[Related by al-Bukhari (5032), and Muslim, with the wording his (790/230), from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: «How wretched it is for a man to say: I forgot such-and-such a surah, or such-and-such a verse; rather he has been made to forget.»]]; because "nasiya" indicates desire and abandonment, while "nussītu" indicates that it is not by your choice, but a matter decreed upon you. This is abandonment of recitation.
The second type: abandonment of acting upon it; that is, a person recites it, does not neglect its recitation, but does not act upon it.
A third type may arise: the third type is verbal and practical abandonment, meaning he neither recites it nor acts upon it.
So the types are three: verbal abandonment, which is abandoning its recitation; practical abandonment, which is abandoning acting upon it; and verbal-practical abandonment. Which is the most severe?
* A student: The last.
* The Shaykh: The verbal-practical; after it, the practical; and the third, the verbal. Each of them is forbidden. Even verbal abandonment: if a person leaves its recitation out of aversion to it, it is not permissible. But if he leaves its recitation due to preoccupation with necessary matters, there is no harm in that. Yet a person cannot leave its recitation entirely, because he has the prayer, in which it is obligatory to recite Surat al-Fatihah. So absolute abandonment is impossible, since reciting al-Fatihah in prayer is among the most important things.
* A student: Abandoning the mushaf by touching it only, is it not forbidden?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not forbidden.
* The student: If he had a number of mushafs in the house (...).
* The Shaykh: There is no objection. But in case of need, it is not permissible for a person, for example, to hoard them while people need them. As for now, there is no need, so the warning found in the words of some scholars applied when mushafs were scarce, when a person had only one copy and kept it for himself, neither benefiting from it nor letting others benefit.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Abandoning reflection (tadabbur) is possible; it may be abandonment.
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, there is no doubt that this is an incomplete recitation, because Allah, the Exalted, commanded its reflection and informed that it was revealed only for reflection and remembrance: ﴿A Book We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses, and that those of understanding may be reminded﴾ [Sad 29].
* The student: Is it reflection on the meaning, or merely (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, tadabbur means that a person contemplates its meaning, thinks about it, and strives to reach its principles. That is tadabbur.
* The student: If a person is incapable (...)?
* The Shaykh: He should ask; and if he can himself consult books of tafsir, let him consult them.
﴿Indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as abandoned﴾. This is a complaint from the Messenger, peace be upon him, about his people, because he was distressed by them, so Allah revealed to him consolation and a response to his complaint: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾. The kāf is a noun meaning "like" (mithl), and it comes in the Qur'an frequently; whenever it comes, we parse it this way: as a noun meaning "like." As for its grammatical function, it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), and its governing verb is the verb after it; i.e., "and like that which We have made, We made for every prophet."
So these polytheists who made the Qur'an abandoned, cast it behind their backs, called to its abandonment, and mocked it, are not unprecedented among others; it has already been so for every prophet.
(﴿And thus﴾, as We have made for you an enemy among the polytheists of your people, ﴿We have made for every prophet﴾ before you ﴿an enemy from among the criminals﴾, the polytheists; so be patient as they were patient.) In this there is clear consolation for the Prophet ﷺ; a person is consoled when another has suffered a calamity like his. Al-Khansa' says while lamenting her brother Sakhr:
Were it not for the multitude of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself.
And they do not weep like my brother, but I console myself regarding him with consolation.
So when the Prophet, peace be upon him, knows that this is the custom of the people of the prophets before him, he is consoled and the matter becomes easier for him.
Allah, the Exalted, said: (﴿And sufficient is your Lord as a guide﴾ for you ﴿and a helper﴾, a helper for you against your enemies).
As for His saying: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord﴾, the bā' is said to be grammatically extra, and "Rabbika" is the subject of "kafā"; i.e., "and your Lord suffices." And ﴿hādiyan﴾ is a specification (tamyīz), meaning: His guidance and His help suffice; it is a tamyīz transferred from the subject, because tamyīz may be transferred from the subject and may be transferred from the object; ﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾ [al-Qamar 12] is transferred from the object, because the original is: and We caused springs to burst forth from the earth.
Here, ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as guide and helper﴾, the original is: and the guidance and help of your Lord sufficed, so it is a tamyīz transferred from the subject.
(﴿And sufficient is your Lord as guide and helper﴾, a helper for you against your enemies).
The connection of His saying ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as guide and helper﴾ is that the enemies of the messengers oppose them to mislead people and to prevent the guidance from reaching them. Likewise, they oppose the messengers with war, fighting and other things; so Allah, blessed and exalted, made clear that they cannot prevent Allah's guidance and help: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as guide and helper﴾.
For the second time I say: the polytheists who oppose the messengers intend two things: misleading people, and aggression against the messengers, even by war and fighting. So Allah, glorified and exalted, made clear that this attempt is nothing, because Allah, blessed and exalted, is sufficient as a guide, so these enemies cannot mislead anyone; and He is sufficient as a helper, so these enemies cannot eliminate the call of the messengers. This is the aspect of connection between His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the Messenger said: O my Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as abandoned.﴾
﴿And those who disbelieve say: Why was the Qur'an not revealed to him all at once?﴾ [al-Furqan 32].
Look, this surah has the character of speaking about the Qur'an and responding to those who deny it; because the surah begins: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan 1]. This Criterion, which Allah praised Himself for sending down to His Messenger, must be attended to and the opponents of it must be answered by the various methods that have passed us now.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it is extra only in terms of grammar.
* A student: That it has a meaning.
* The Shaykh: Yes, known to have a meaning, but only grammatically extra.
* In these verses we have recited:
* First: a description of the state of the wrongdoer on the Day of Resurrection, that he regrets greatly, and his regret appears by speech and by action. Where is the evidence that it is by speech?
* A student: The evidence that it is by speech is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O woe to me! Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend﴾ [al-Furqan 27–28].
* The Shaykh: Yes. And by action?
* The student: By action: ﴿And the day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands﴾.
* The Shaykh: Second benefit: a warning against the wrongdoing by which a person turns away from the religion of Allah. From where is it derived? A warning against the wrongdoing that causes a person to oppose the messengers?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, the purpose of this warning is not merely the story, but that a person should beware of this matter whose outcome for its doer is this state.
* Also in it: a warning against evil companions.
* A student: (...) ﴿O woe to me, would that I had not taken so-and-so﴾ (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿He had already led me astray﴾..
* The student: ﴿from the reminder﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Also in it: that the disbeliever, indeed all wrongdoers, on the Day of Resurrection will acknowledge the truth.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿from the reminder after﴾..
* The student: ﴿after it had come to me﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿after it had come to me﴾.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, so he now acknowledges that the reminder has come to him, and acknowledges that what came to him is a reminder by which a person is reminded.
* And in the verse: evidence of the state the Quraysh reached in obstinacy and arrogance. What do you say?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, but did they take it as abandoned, or did they abandon it?
* The student: They took it as abandoned.
* The Shaykh: And that is more eloquent than?
* The student: Than (they abandoned it).
* The Shaykh: Than (they abandoned it).
* Also in it: evidence of the greatness of this Qur'an.
* A student: From His saying: ﴿this Qur'an﴾.
* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿this Qur'an﴾, because the demonstrative indicates magnification; i.e., ﴿this Qur'an﴾, the great one that should not be abandoned, these people took as abandoned.
We mentioned that "they took it as abandoned" is more eloquent than "they abandoned it." How so?
* The student: Because "they took it as abandoned" means that they turned away from this Qur'an completely, and the meaning is not (...), although also they did not abandon it because of its being... If he had said "they abandoned it," they would have abandoned it while knowing there is benefit in it, but they left it. But ﴿mahjūran﴾ means they abandoned it and turned away from it entirely.
* The Shaykh: No, it is not that they turned away from it entirely; the meaning is their action...
* The student: Although there is nothing in it, meaning they made it something abandoned, meaning: there is nothing in it.
* The Shaykh: Meaning: they made it among the matters that...
* The student: It has no benefit.
* The Shaykh: Deserving to be abandoned; they took it as a matter to be abandoned, meaning an object of aversion and something left aside, in itself according to their claim.
* A student: This is one aspect, Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: This is one aspect; the second aspect?
* A student: ﴿Indeed my people﴾.
* The Shaykh: No. What do you say?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And they made it abandoned; the pronoun, as the first object, occupies the position of the subject, and ﴿mahjūran﴾ occupies the position of the predicate.
And in this is evidence of the monstrousness of this act by the Quraysh; in the verse is evidence of the monstrousness of this matter by the Quraysh...
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, other than that? Because this includes them and others. What do you say?

**Student:** His saying: ﴿my people﴾.

**Shaykh:** It has passed, but what about the (...)? The idafah (possessive construction) in...

**Student:** The Prophet's ﷺ complaint to Allah.

**Shaykh:** Yes, but with the wording ﴿my people﴾, the idafah. ﴿My people﴾ indicates how shameful this act was on their part, because it is expected that his own people would be the first to care for him and to accept what he brought. Isn't that so? But, regrettably, the matter has turned out to be the reverse.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 25, verses 25–31 (part 1 of 4):**

(﴿And the angels will be sent down, a descending﴾ is the Day of Resurrection. Its grammatical object is governed by a supposed verb "remember" (udhkur), which is understood. In one reading the shin of ﴿tashaqqaq﴾ is doubled, by assimilating the second taa into the original taa of the verb. In another reading it is ﴿wa-nunzilu﴾ with two nuns, the second one sukun, the lam damma, and ﴿al-malaʼikata﴾ in the accusative.)

There are now three readings.

First: the well-known reading we have, ﴿And the day the sky is split open with clouds, and the angels are sent down, a descending﴾ [al-Furqan 25].

Second reading: ﴿tashshaqqaq﴾. Its original form is ﴿tatashaqqaq﴾, and the taa was assimilated into the shin, so it became ﴿tashshaqqaq﴾.

Which is more eloquent: ﴿tashaqqaq﴾ or ﴿tashshaqqaq﴾? ﴿Tashshaqqaq﴾ is more eloquent.

As for ﴿nuzzila﴾, it has two canonical (sab'iyyah) readings. ﴿Nuzzila al-malaʼikatu﴾, taken as a past-tense verb with ﴿al-malaʼikatu﴾ as the deputy subject (nā'ib fā'il). And the second: ﴿nunzilu al-malaʼikata﴾, taken as a present-tense verb with ﴿al-malaʼikata﴾ as the direct object, and the subject is God.

The eloquence of the Qur'an is that its readings are useful either for explanation (tafsir) or for adding meaning. So the reading ﴿tashshaqqaq﴾ adds meaning, and the reading ﴿nunzilu al-malaʼikata﴾ provides explanation. This is because ﴿nuzzila al-malaʼikatu﴾ is in the passive voice, so the subject is unknown, whereas in ﴿wa-nunzilu al-malaʼikata﴾ the subject is known. Accordingly, if you are asked, "Who sends down the angels?", you say: it is God. The first proof is something clear to the mind, and another proof is from the wording of the verse in the second reading: ﴿nunzilu al-malaʼikata﴾.

(﴿The dominion that day is truly for the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan 26]: no one shares in it.)

﴿Al-mulku yawma'idhin al-haqq﴾: ﴿al-haqq﴾ is an adjective of ﴿al-mulku﴾. That is, ﴿al-mulk﴾, the established, affirmed, realized dominion on that day, belongs to God, glorified and exalted, ﴿lil-Rahman﴾ (to the Most Merciful). Dominion belongs to the Most Merciful, glorified and exalted, on that day and on other days. But His dominion, blessed and exalted, is more manifest and clearer on that day, because in this world there are kings, there are those who have authority to act, and there are those who are called "king". But in the Hereafter there is no king; people are on equal footing. God, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is God's, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Ghafir 16]. So dominion on that day belongs to no one except God, blessed and exalted.

In His saying ﴿lil-Rahman﴾ (rather than "to God"), there is an indication of the abundance of God's mercy on that day, as in the authentic hadith: "Indeed God, exalted is He, has a hundred mercies. He sent down one mercy from them, by which creation shows mercy to one another. When the Day of Resurrection comes, God, exalted is He, will complete it with the ninety-nine mercies He has with Him, and He will show mercy to the creatures with them."[[Muslim (2753/21) reported from Salman, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "God created a hundred mercies on the day He created the heavens and the earth, each mercy filling the space between heaven and earth. He placed one of them in the earth, and by it a mother is tender toward her child, and wild beasts and birds are tender toward one another. When the Day of Resurrection comes, He will complete them with this mercy."]] Thus there appears from God's mercy, glorified and exalted, on that day what does not appear on any other day. For this reason He expressed it with His saying: ﴿Al-mulku yawma'idhin al-haqqu lil-Rahman﴾.

It has already been noted that "al-Rahman" is an attribute that includes mercy, but it indicates the greatness and vastness of this mercy. Because the pattern (fa'lan), what does it indicate? It indicates an attribute that fills the one it describes, as one says ghadbān, meaning "filled with anger." For this reason some scholars explained "al-Rahman" as "the one of vast mercy," and "al-Rahim" as "the one whose mercy is specific to the believers." But the correct view is that "al-Rahman" is considered in terms of His attribute, and "al-Rahim" in terms of His act, that is, delivering mercy to whomever He wills. As for "al-Rahman," it is considered in terms of the attribute; therefore it came in the pattern fa'lan, because fa'lan is an adjective of resemblance (sifah mushabbahah).

﴿Al-mulku yawma'idhin al-haqqu lil-Rahman﴾. In this there is a warning and a caution against the domination of kings, for they must remember this day when their dominion will end and only the dominion of God, glorified and exalted, will remain.

In it there is also good news for people in general through the word "al-Rahman," since it points to the fact that He, glorified and exalted, manifests from His mercy on that day, and from His dominion, what does not appear on any other day.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah and other scholars used this verse as evidence for God's descent, glorified and exalted, to judge among His servants. What is the basis of the inference? What is the point of inference from the verse?

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No. It is true that if it were according to the requirement of judging between the servants, then as you said, because the King is the one who judges. But regarding His descent?
* Student: You mean from (...)?
* Shaykh: From the verse?
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: From the verse, let us look at the basis of inference.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Other than the King.
* Student: Other than the King.
* Shaykh: In reality, nothing in the wording of the verse indicates it. But the verse is explained by a hadith: that the sky is split open with clouds for the descent of God, glorified and exalted. So the inference cannot be completed merely from its wording, but only with the addition of what is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ in explaining the verse, that it is split open with clouds for the descent of God, blessed and exalted, to judge between His servants.[[Its meaning is reported in the long hadith of the Trumpet, recorded by Ishaq ibn Rahawayh (10) and al-Tabarani in al-Ahadith al-Tiwal (36), from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, with a weak chain. See Ithaf al-Khiyarah al-Maharah by al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar (1/187).]]
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed, but this is another verse, a different verse.
* In this verse there is evidence that the angels are in the heavens, from His saying: ﴿And the angels will be sent down, a descending﴾.
* And in it there is evidence of the greatness of God, blessed and exalted, and the abundance of His creation, because the angels descend and surround the creatures, which indicates their multitude.
* And also in it: preparation for this day, from which a person will find no escape. For, with the highest comparison belonging to God, if the troops of a king surrounded you from every side, in large numbers and in multiple rows, could you flee from his grip? Suppose, for example, and to God belongs the highest comparison, that people were gathered in a place, and the police forces came and surrounded them in rows, one row behind another. Could people flee from this? No. So it is with the Day of Resurrection: people cannot flee from that day, its horrors, and its judgments. In it is a warning about this day.

He said: (﴿And it was a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾, the day "was" difficult for the disbelievers, unlike the believers.)

Here God, glorified and exalted, restricted the hardship to the disbelievers: ﴿And it was a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾, that is, not for the believers. In another verse: ﴿That day will be a difficult day﴾ [al-Muddaththir 9], and He did not restrict it.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: It is said that the day itself is very difficult when considered in its own essence, but this hardship does not affect the believer, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿It is not easy for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Muddaththir 10]. Its implication is that for the believers it is easy. So, considering the day itself and its horrors, how do we describe it? As difficult for the disbelievers, difficult in its essence. Then this hardship does not extend to the believers; rather God, blessed and exalted, makes it easy for them, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And it was a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾, and by His saying: ﴿It is not easy for the disbelievers﴾.

The conclusion: considering the day itself, the day is difficult and severe, ﴿making children gray-haired﴾ [al-Muzzammil 17]. But considering what a person is affected by and its hardship, this applies to the disbelievers only, by His saying: ﴿It is not easy for the disbelievers﴾. As for the believer, it is easy for him.

In this there is evidence that it is difficult, but its difficulty is only for the disbelievers. It also shows that people differ in that standing, and that the ease and difficulty of that day depend on the state of the person. Whenever a person is stronger in faith and stronger in piety toward God, the day will be easier for him. For this reason it is established in the authentic hadith: "Seven [people] God will shade in His shade on a day when there is no shade but His shade,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6806) and Muslim (1031/91), from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him.]] and that "every person will be in the shade of his charity on the Day of Resurrection."[[Reported by Ahmad (17332) and Abu Nu'aym, and the wording is his (8/181), from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, may God be pleased with him.]] Accordingly we say: whenever a person is stronger in faith in God and stronger in piety toward God, the ease of that day will be proportionate to him.

Now, whenever a person is more defiant and more disbelieving, will it be more severe or not? Yes, it will be more severe and greater. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed that he saw 'Amr ibn Luhayy dragging his intestines in the Fire,[[Ibn Hibban (7490) reported from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: "The Fire was shown to me, and I saw in it 'Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Qam'ah ibn Khindif dragging his intestines in the Fire. He was the first to change the religion of Abraham and to dedicate the sawa'ib (she-camels set free)." ...the hadith.]] which indicates that the more a person's defiance and disbelief increase, the more the hardship of that day increases for him.

Furthermore, in the principles of jurisprudence: when a ruling is attached to an attribute, the effect of that ruling is proportionate to that attribute. So if hardship is attached to disbelief, the more disbelief there is, the more severe the hardship. And if ease is attached to faith, the stronger the faith, the stronger the ease.

The conclusion: every ruling attached to an attribute has an effect that varies according to that attribute.

* Student: The principle (...)?
* Shaykh: The principle is that we say: whenever a ruling is attached to an attribute, the effect of that ruling is proportionate to that attribute; that is, the influence of the attribute on the ruling is proportionate to the attribute.
* Student: What was reported from the prophets, all of them (...), is this evidence that at that time they are in severe fear?
* Shaykh: There is no doubt that there is severity and fear: ﴿a day that will make children gray-haired﴾ [al-Muzzammil 17]. But this severity and fear is borne by the person according to the faith he has; that is, it is not severe upon him in proportion to his faith. They fear, but it is not severe upon them; that is, they expect to fall into something, but they do not fall into it.

﴿And it was a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾.

Reflect on the saying of God, exalted: ﴿The dominion that day is truly for the Most Merciful, and it was a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾. Someone may say: where is the mercy with its hardship upon the disbelievers? It is said: the punishment of the disbelievers and its severity upon them is itself mercy. Mercy to whom? To the believers. For the believer sees his enemy, who used to mock him in this world, and God's justice is carried out against him. There is no doubt that this is joy and mercy for him, as God, exalted, said: ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers, on couches, looking on﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 34–35]. They are on their couches looking at those being punished, and they rejoice over them and laugh at them, just as their enemies in this world laughed at them and mocked them.

Furthermore, we also say: the execution of justice is considered mercy. In this world this is evident: when we carry out the prescribed punishment on a thief, or on an adulterer, or the like, it is mercy to people in general and to the one punished in particular. Even this one who is lashed or whose hand is cut off, it is mercy for him. How so? Because we prevent him from practicing the crime again whenever he remembers this pain, and because the prescribed punishment serves as an expiation for him, so he is not punished for it in the Hereafter, since God, exalted, does not combine two punishments for him.

﴿And the day the wrongdoer bites on his hands﴾ [al-Furqan 27] is coordinated with ﴿And the day the sky is split open﴾; that is, remember the day the wrongdoer bites on his hands.

﴿And the day the wrongdoer bites﴾. The author says "the polytheist (mushrik)." The verse may be said to be more general than polytheism, because wrongdoing (zulm) includes shirk and what is less than it. But let us look at the context now: does it specify that wrongdoing means shirk or not?

Then the author specified it further, saying: "'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt had pronounced the two testimonies, then turned back to please Ubayy ibn Khalaf."

His saying "and it is 'Uqbah" is a specification of a general statement. If the author intends to make this an example of what the verse applies to, the matter is easy. But if the author intends to make the verse a case of the general used to mean the specific, this is not accepted, because there is no evidence for it. There is no proof that the intended meaning is the specific; rather the verse is general, but it includes 'Uqbah and others.

His saying "﴿upon his hands﴾, out of regret and anguish": that is, on the Day of Resurrection he will say: ﴿Oh, I wish...﴾ and so on.

He bites on his hands. Biting the hand: what indicates it? It indicates regret and anguish. For this reason some people, when a matter escapes them, bite their hand and (...) with it like this, meaning that it has escaped them. This is evidence of anguish and regret, and how great is the grief and regret when he sees the believers in one state and the wrongdoers in another! This is the greatest of it.

His saying ﴿upon his hands﴾: the scholars of rhetoric (bayan) claimed that there is a figure of speech (majaz) in the verse, because a person does not bite his whole hand (...) he cannot. They say: the intended meaning of "hands" is the fingers, meaning that one cannot bite the whole hand.

But we say: in reality there is no figurative usage in the verse, because when the context indicates a meaning, that is the intended meaning. Everyone knows that the intended meaning of ﴿the wrongdoer bites on his hands﴾ is on his fingers. Everyone knows this. So the context did not indicate the whole hand from the outset, such that we would say it was moved from its meaning to a second meaning. And this which we have established is what led Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him, to deny the existence of figurative usage (majaz) in the Arabic language. For Shaykh al-Islam did not hold that figurative usage exists in the Arabic language at all, neither in the Qur'an nor elsewhere, because he says: the indication of a word upon a meaning is not intrinsic. That is, the word itself does not indicate the meaning by its own essence, but by context. The clearest example that shows this is shared words (al-alfaz al-mushtarakah), which are suitable for two or more meanings. What specifies the meaning? Context specifies it, and so too with other things. Based on this, he says: there is no figurative usage in the Arabic language, neither in the Qur'an nor elsewhere.

But you will find most people hold that figurative language (majaz) exists in the Qur'an and in other Arabic speech, while some scholars hold that there is no majaz in the Qur'an, though it exists in the Arabic language. What led these to a middle position is that they said: the criterion of majaz that no one disputes is that it can be negated (ṣiḥḥat nafyihi), that is, that the figurative sense can be denied. And there is nothing in the Qur'an that can be denied. Meaning: when you say, "I saw a lion reading," what is meant by "lion"? A brave man. It is as if you said, "I saw a brave man reading," but you expressed it with "lion" because bravery is more evident in it. They say: if you say, "I saw a lion reading," the listener may say, "This is not a lion," and deny it. Is this correct or not? It is correct, it is not a lion. So they say: if the major sign of majaz is that it can be denied, then there is nothing in the Qur'an that can be denied, whereas in other Arabic speech you can deny it without concern.

But when we return to what Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) said, namely that words' indication of meanings is not intrinsic, so that we would say that if they indicate another meaning in another place, then they are figurative. Rather, their indication of meanings depends on context.

On this basis, we say about the verse before us, ﴿And on the Day the wrongdoer will bite his hands﴾: is there majaz in it or not? There is no majaz, because no one can understand that what is meant originally is that he bites the whole hand. Everyone knows that what is meant by "bites on his hands" is that he bites what he normally bites, which is the fingers.

* Student: (...) ﴿And on the Day the wrongdoer will bite his hands﴾, and He did not say "his hands"?
* Shaykh: What is it?
* Student: ﴿ʿalā﴾ indicates the endpoint (...), the place of the biting. He did not say "yaʿaḍḍu yadayhi" (bites his hands). If he had said "yaʿaḍḍu yadayhi," could it be (...)?
* Shaykh: No, when you say ʿaḍḍa ʿalā yadayhi.
* Student: The place where he bites is on his hands, not on (...)?
* Shaykh: No, if it were (fī), for location, it would be possible, but you say ʿaḍḍtu ʿalā kadhā (I bit on such and such).
* Student: Even if it is fingers (...)?
* Shaykh: It is not apparent, even if he bites on his finger, he would bite on the tip of the finger, for example.
* Student: He bit on it; is it permissible to use it generally (...)?
* Shaykh: What do you say about this? He says that ﴿yaʿaḍḍu ʿalā yadayhi⁠﴾ means: on some of his hands, is that right?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: And that he derived the partiality from the word ʿalā, and did not say "yaʿaḍḍu yadayhi." But let us see whether ʿaḍḍa is transitive with ʿalā or with itself.
* Student: Even if you say he bites on the root of a tree.
* Shaykh: Yes, "and even if you were to bite on the root of a tree" [Al-Bukhari (7084) and Muslim (1847/51), from the hadith of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, may Allah be pleased with him].
* Student: It is not general, it is not (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but ʿaḍḍa is transitive by itself or with ʿalā? It is transitive by itself and with ʿalā: "Does one of you bite his brother as the stallion bites?" [Al-Bukhari (6892), from the hadith of ʿImran ibn Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording: "Does one of you bite his brother as a stallion bites?"], such as the man who bit another person's hand, pulled it out, and his teeth fell out. There is a possibility that we say it does not indicate totality, but even the word "hand" is not meant as the whole here. Even if it indicates partiality, it is not meant as the whole.
* Student: O Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: In the hadith (...)?
* Shaykh: Apparently it is not said, because he says only in the Qur'an. The Prophetic hadith may be narrated by meaning, so it is possible that a narrator changed the word.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, the negation of this word, not the basic meaning.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, apparently the regret over both hands is strongest whenever.
* Student: Both hands?
* Shaykh: Yes, (...).
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: I do not think it can be derived (...).
* Student: The saying of ʿAṭāʾ (...)?
* Shaykh: I think it is not authentic.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: I think its chain needs to reach ʿAṭāʾ, and then when it reaches ʿAṭāʾ it stops; meaning, it would not be accepted if he said it, because it is mursal (a report with a missing link).
* Student: The saying of the Exalted (...)?
* Shaykh: ﴿So We will not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Al-Kahf 105], meaning: no weight will be given to them.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, but they are not weighed in the way the sins of the believers are weighed, because the sins of believers are weighed for the purpose of balancing them against the good deeds, so whichever prevails is considered. As for those, it is only to establish the proof against them.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: This is correct, yes.
* Student: How do you mean?
* Shaykh: It means that if Allah were to call you to account for His blessings, you would be ruined, because if He called you to account for a single one of His blessings, all (...) would not match it.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, we do not say (...).

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the preceding verses, Allah Exalted ordered that this great Day be mentioned, the Day when the sky will be split open with clouds at the descent of Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

* In the verse is the affirmation of Allah's descent, because this splitting occurs for His descent. The purpose of mentioning it is warning against it and preparing for it, because whenever a thing is mentioned, a person takes precaution against it and prepares for it. In what preceded, Allah described the Day of Resurrection as difficult, with a description restricted to the disbelievers, and in another verse He described it with an unrestricted description as difficult.

We mentioned previously that although it is difficult, it is easy for the believers. So the unrestricted description of that day is that it is difficult, but those who are affected by it and for whom it is difficult are the disbelievers, not the believers.

Then Allah Exalted ordered that the condition of the criminals on that day be mentioned: the regret, the great remorse, and the biting of hands: ﴿And on the Day the wrongdoer will bite his hands﴾. And whom did the author (Ibn Kathir) restrict the verse to? To ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt. The correct view is that it is general to every wrongdoer, because the original state is that a general expression remains general until there is evidence that it is specific.

Here, ﴿And on the Day the wrongdoer will bite⁠﴾ is general, to ʿUqbah and to others.

He says: (﴿He will say, "Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger⁠﴾ — Muhammad — ﴿a path⁠﴾, meaning a way to guidance.)

﴿He will say⁠﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from ﴿the wrongdoer⁠﴾, meaning that he bites, and this is evidence of regret in action. And ﴿He will say, "Oh, I wish⁠﴾ (...) the vocative. The sign of a noun is the vocative: ﴿yā⁠﴾ enters only upon a noun, but if it enters upon a particle as here, or upon a verb, it conveys only alerting. This is one of the two views on its grammatical analysis (iʿrāb).

The second view is that it is a vocative particle and the addressed person is omitted, and the estimate in such a verse is: "O Lord, I wish," or "O people, I wish."

But we say: the original state is non-estimation, and if the original state is non-estimation, then it is better that we not estimate anything here and that we make ﴿yā⁠﴾ for alerting, for mere alerting. It is for mere alerting because the original use of the vocative, what is its origin? It is for alerting. When you say, "O so-and-so," you alert him so that he pays attention to you and turns his face toward you. So it is for alerting, and there is no need to estimate the addressed person.

And His saying: ﴿Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger⁠﴾: (layta) is for wishing, and wishing is the request for what cannot be attained or what is difficult to attain. Something whose attainment is impossible or difficult is called a wish:

"Would that youth would return one day, so that I could tell it what old age has done." 

This is impossible. And the poor man says: "I wish I had wealth so that I could give it in charity." This is difficult, not impossible.

﴿Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger⁠﴾: which of the two categories is it?
* Student: This is impossible.
* Shaykh: This is impossible, because the matter has passed.

﴿Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger⁠﴾: that is, I would have followed ﴿a way⁠﴾, which is the path leading to Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

The author's saying (﴿with the Messenger⁠﴾ — Muhammad) is based on the premise that the verse is aimed at ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt. In this case, the definite article (al) is for mental reference (ʿahd dhihnī). Which kind of reference?
* Student: Mental.
* Shaykh: Mental reference. And if we take the general view, which is the stronger one, then what is meant by ﴿the Messenger⁠﴾ here is whoever was sent to his people, so the definite article is for the category, for generality, because what is meant by it is the category of messenger, including Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and others.

(﴿Oh, woe to me⁠﴾: its alif is a substitute for the ya' of possession, meaning "my woe," and its meaning is "my ruin." ﴿I wish I had not taken so-and-so⁠﴾, that is, Ubayy, ﴿as a close friend⁠﴾.) ... and so on.

﴿Oh, woe to me⁠﴾: ﴿yā⁠﴾ is a vocative particle, and ﴿woe to me⁠﴾ is the addressed term. Its origin is "waylatī," then the yā was changed into an alif, so it became ﴿yā waylatā⁠﴾. This is permissible in the language: it is permissible to say "yā waylatī" and "yā waylatā." Woe (wayl) means ruin, and it is as if he says: "O my ruin, come!" ﴿I wish I had not taken⁠﴾... and so on.

In the first wish he did not say ﴿Oh, woe to me⁠﴾, but in the second wish he said ﴿Oh, woe to me⁠﴾, because his grief had increased. The first time he expresses his grief for the first time, and the second for the second time, so that is more intense in grief; therefore he said ﴿Oh, woe to me⁠﴾.

And his saying: ﴿I wish I had not taken⁠﴾, I had not made ﴿so-and-so⁠﴾ — ﴿so-and-so⁠﴾ is a noun of a category used to refer to any one human being, and "so-and-so" (feminine) is used for any one female human being. He did not mention ﴿so-and-so⁠﴾ by name here, because, as we have indicated, it is general. For ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt, the one meant by "so-and-so" would be Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and for others it is whoever led him astray from the remembrance of Allah.

﴿I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend⁠﴾. The khalīl is the beloved whose love has reached the furthest point, because khullah (close friendship) is the highest type of love, and it is so called because love penetrates the pathways of the body, as the poet said:

"You have penetrated the pathway of the spirit in me, and for this the khalīl was named khalīl."

On this basis, khullah is higher than mahabbah (love). Through this we know the error of those who say: "Muhammad is the beloved (ḥabīb) of Allah, Ibrahim is the friend (khalīl) of Allah, and Musa is the one who spoke with Allah (kalīm Allah)," because these have lowered the rank of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, by describing him as the beloved of Allah while describing Ibrahim as the friend of Allah. Khullah is higher, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the khalīl of Allah just as Ibrahim is the khalīl of Allah. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Indeed Allah has taken me as a khalīl just as He took Ibrahim as a khalīl" [Muslim (532/23) and Ibn Hibban, and the wording is his (6425), from the hadith of Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Bajali, may Allah be pleased with him]. As for Musa being the kalīm of Allah, we also say: Muhammad is the kalīm of Allah, and if Musa was the kalīm of Allah on earth, then Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the kalīm of Allah in the heavens.

(﴿He had led me astray from the Reminder⁠﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿after it had come to me⁠﴾.)

﴿He had led me astray from the Reminder, after it had come to me⁠﴾. The lām is a preface to an oath, and qad is for confirmation, so the sentence is emphatic. With how many emphases?
* Student: With qad and (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, I said: with how many?
* Student: ﴿He had led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me⁠﴾ is emphatic.
* Shaykh: Fine, and what are they?
* Student: The oath and qad.
* Shaykh: Where is the oath?
* Student: The oath...
* Shaykh: The oath and qad. Qad is known and present; and the oath?
* Student: Because this lām is called a preface to the oath, that is, the answer of an oath (...).
* Shaykh: Fine, (...) is emphatic with three emphases: the oath, the lām, and qad. He emphasizes on this Day that this close friend led him astray, an emphasis intended to blame himself. But that will not benefit him now. If this emphasis had been in the world, it would have benefited him; but now it does not benefit him, and it only increases his grief.

"He had led me astray from the Reminder": the author says: (that is, the Qur'an), and this is based on his view that what was previously mentioned refers to the wrongdoer or to Ibn Abi Muʿayt, so the reminder is the Qur'an. If we take the general view, which is the stronger, then the Reminder means the Book revealed to that Messenger; in the time of Musa it was the Torah, in the time of ʿIsa the Gospel, and similarly in other eras the books revealed to the messengers.

﴿He had led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me⁠﴾ [Al-Furqan 29]. This time-clause has its great benefit: that is, after the Reminder had reached me, I knew it and understood it, and then misguidance occurred. This is more forceful than if he had been led astray from an expected matter that did not occur. This is an actual matter; he acknowledges that the Reminder came to him and the proof was established against him, and this close friend led him astray after it came to him.

(...by turning him away from belief in it. Allah Exalted said: ﴿And Satan is ever, for man, a deserter⁠﴾ — for the disbeliever — "for man, for the disbeliever" (or "for the disbeliever"?)
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (The disbeliever is a deserter ﴿deserter⁠﴾ by leaving him and disowning him in time of trial.)

His saying: "Allah Exalted said: ﴿And Satan is ever, for man, a deserter⁠﴾ [Al-Furqan 29]", as if the author holds that this sentence is not part of the speech of the wrongdoer, and that the speech of the wrongdoer ends at ﴿after it had come to me⁠﴾. On this basis it is proper to stop: ﴿He had led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me⁠﴾, and you pause, then resume and say: ﴿And Satan is ever, for man, a deserter⁠﴾.

His saying: ﴿Satan⁠﴾ is meant as a category, because there are many devils; Allah Exalted said: ﴿And the devils did not bring it down⁠﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 210], and He said: ﴿Its shoots are as if they were the heads of devils⁠﴾ [As-Saffat 65]. So what is meant here is the category. They are of various kinds, and apparently, and Allah knows best, each type of sin has a devil: the devil of polytheism, the devil of denial, the devil of miserliness, and others; for every kind there is a devil. This is what appears, and Allah knows best.

His saying: ﴿for man⁠﴾: what is meant by it, according to the author's statement, is "the disbeliever," and it is either ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt or general; because this statement is from the words of Allah, not from the words of the wrongdoer, from the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It may be general to the disbeliever and the believer, since Satan also misleads the believer and then abandons him afterward.

So the apparent meaning is that what is meant by ﴿man⁠﴾ here is the category, that is, believer or disbeliever. We said this is apparent because just as he misleads disbelievers into disbelief, so he misleads believers into sin.

His saying: ﴿a deserter⁠﴾ is either an adjective of quality (ṣifah mushabbahah) or an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālaghah). On either of the two, the description of Satan in relation to man is desertion, or the desertion of Satan toward man is constant, because intensiveness implies frequency. Desertion means: humiliating a person in a situation where he needs support; this is desertion, namely that you abandon a person in a situation where he needs help. When we reflect on what Allah mentioned about Satan in the Qur'an, we find that he deserts man in times of need for support: he made the Quraysh attractive so that they went out to fight the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and they went out, ﴿but when the two hosts sighted each other, he turned back on his heels and said: "Indeed, I am free of you; indeed, I see what you do not see"⁠﴾ [Al-Anfal 48]. He made disbelief attractive to man: ﴿Like Satan when he says to man, "Disbelieve," and when he disbelieves, says, "Indeed, I am free of you"⁠﴾ [Al-Hashr 16]. This is in this world. In the Hereafter: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided: "Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I failed you. I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me. Indeed, I disbelieved in what you associated with me before"⁠﴾ [Ibrahim 22]. This too is a great desertion: Satan in the times of support deserts man and disowns him.

As for this description, ﴿And Satan is ever⁠﴾: do we say that (kāna) refers to what is in Allah's knowledge, or to what occurred in the past and ended?
* Student: In Allah's knowledge.
* Student: We say: (kāna) does not indicate time.
* Shaykh: This passed us recently (...).
* Student: No, it is detached from time.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 25–31 (part 3 of 4):

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is stripped of time. That is, (kāna) comes without being intended to denote time; what is intended is the general attribution of the quality. Like: ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [an-Nisa' 96], ﴿And Allah is ever over all things Capable﴾ [al-Ahzab 27]. It does not mean "was in the past"; (...) the meaning is that this is a continuous attribute of Allah.
And likewise here: ﴿And Satan is ever a deserter of man﴾. It does not mean that Satan was a deserter of man in the past and then became no longer a deserter; rather, the meaning is that this is a quality constantly attached to Satan in relation to man.
* A student: Is it not (...) ﴿And (kāna)﴾, meaning in this world?
* The Shaykh: No, it is in this world and the Hereafter. Even in the Hereafter: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided﴾ [Ibrahim 22], which we recited just now.
Alright, and here?
* A student: O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Sometimes it is intended to indicate time, and sometimes it is intended merely as the event; that is, stripped of time. So you say, for example: Zayd was standing, meaning in the past, then he sat down. And you say: Allah was Forgiving, Merciful; this does not mean in the past, rather the meaning is that forgiveness and mercy are His attributes.
Here, Satan's attribute of forsaking the children of Adam is constant; it does not mean only in the past. Allah, blessed and exalted, has informed us that Satan is a deserter of man so that we take him as an enemy and do not be deceived by him, for he will forsake us at a time when we need his help, so we beware of him.
If someone says: What is the sign that something is from Satan, or that this act is from the commands of Satan? How do we know, for example, that Satan commanded us with this and that this is the work of Satan?
* A student: (...) as the Shari'ah has brought it.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: If it contradicts it, then it is from the commands of Satan.
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is the criterion: ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to immorality﴾ [al-Baqarah 268]. So when we see that the self wants us to fall into this act, if it contradicts the Shari'ah, we know that this is from the command of Satan, and it becomes obligatory for us to beware of it, because we know that this Satan will forsake us at a time when we need victory. This is the distinguishing mark between what is from the command of Satan and what is from the command of Allah, blessed and exalted.
(﴿And the Messenger said﴾, Muhammad.)
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, the self that commands evil obeys the command of Satan, because you yourself do not feel that Satan, for example, descended upon you and brought you; but your self commands you to this, so it obeys the command of Satan.
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, meaning it makes it like an intermediary between him and the heart of a person.
(﴿And the Messenger said﴾, Muhammad, ﴿O my Lord, indeed my people﴾, meaning the Quraysh, ﴿have taken this Qur'an as abandoned﴾ [al-Furqan 30]).
Here the author also restricted it to the Prophet ﷺ, and here we may agree with the author that it is specific to the Prophet ﷺ, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾ [al-Furqan 31]; because the purpose of this sentence is consolation, and this is what supports what the author said.
As for the matter of ﴿the Qur'an﴾, the word Qur'an is applied to the verbal noun, so it includes everything that is recited of the Torah, the Gospel and other books. But what makes it specific to what was revealed to Muhammad ﷺ is what follows it.
* A student: The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿this Qur'an﴾ (...)?
* The Shaykh: Where?
* The student: (...).
* A student: At His saying: ﴿have taken this Qur'an﴾ [al-Furqan 30]?
* The Shaykh: Yes, because the Messenger says it while the Qur'an is before him. For example, if Musa said it while the Torah was before him, it would be correct for him to point to it.
(﴿O my Lord, indeed my people﴾, the Quraysh), and he attributed them to himself, because that is more emphatic in rebuking them. How so? Because the actual situation requires that his people be the first of people to believe him and to accept what he brought; but the matter was the opposite. This is similar to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿By the star when it descends, your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ [an-Najm 1, 2], where He attributed them to him, as if He says: You should be the first to believe in it because he is your companion. Likewise: ﴿Nun. By the pen and what they inscribe, you are not, by the favour of your Lord, a madman﴾ [al-Qalam 1, 2].
The point is that the attribution here is intended to increase the rebuke; instead of saying "indeed the Quraysh," He said ﴿indeed my people﴾ to intensify the rebuke of them, since being his people entails that they should believe in him and accept what he brought.
(﴿have taken this Qur'an as abandoned﴾, mahjur, left aside), derived from hajr, and hajr is leaving a thing out of aversion to it. So they took it ﴿as abandoned﴾.
(...) abandoned, meaning they do not pay attention to it. This is more eloquent than saying: My people abandoned the Qur'an. The reason: "hajarū" is a verb, and a verbal sentence does not indicate permanence and continuity, but "ittakhadhūhu mahjūran" is a nominal sentence, since the pronoun and ﴿mahjūran﴾ originally are subject and predicate. So it is as if they made this Qur'an, which deserves care and turning toward it, into a matter ﴿abandoned﴾, an object of aversion, as if it did not deserve turning toward at all. They made it one of the abandoned matters that it is not its nature to be approached. This is more eloquent than their having abandoned it, because they might abandon it while it deserves to be accepted; but when they take it as abandoned, their taking it as abandoned means they abandoned it while it deserved to be abandoned. Is that clear?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Good. What is the difference between (they abandoned it) and (they took it as abandoned)?
* The student: (They abandoned it) means (...).
* The Shaykh: That is: it may be that they abandoned it while it did not deserve to be abandoned.
* The student: But "they took it as abandoned" because they abandoned it while it was (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, and because a nominal sentence indicates permanence and continuity.
The abandonment of the Qur'an is divided into two types: verbal abandonment, which is leaving off its recitation out of aversion to it, and this is what the Prophet ﷺ warned against in his saying: «How wretched is it for one of you to say: I forgot such-and-such a verse; rather he says: I was made to forget»[[Related by al-Bukhari (5032), and Muslim, with the wording his (790/230), from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: «How wretched it is for a man to say: I forgot such-and-such a surah, or such-and-such a verse; rather he has been made to forget.»]]; because "nasiya" indicates desire and abandonment, while "nussītu" indicates that it is not by your choice, but a matter decreed upon you. This is abandonment of recitation.
The second type: abandonment of acting upon it; that is, a person recites it, does not neglect its recitation, but does not act upon it.
A third type may arise: the third type is verbal and practical abandonment, meaning he neither recites it nor acts upon it.
So the types are three: verbal abandonment, which is abandoning its recitation; practical abandonment, which is abandoning acting upon it; and verbal-practical abandonment. Which is the most severe?
* A student: The last.
* The Shaykh: The verbal-practical; after it, the practical; and the third, the verbal. Each of them is forbidden. Even verbal abandonment: if a person leaves its recitation out of aversion to it, it is not permissible. But if he leaves its recitation due to preoccupation with necessary matters, there is no harm in that. Yet a person cannot leave its recitation entirely, because he has the prayer, in which it is obligatory to recite Surat al-Fatihah. So absolute abandonment is impossible, since reciting al-Fatihah in prayer is among the most important things.

﴿Indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as abandoned﴾. This is a complaint from the Messenger, peace be upon him, about his people, because he was distressed by them, so Allah revealed to him consolation and a response to his complaint: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾. The kāf is a noun meaning "like" (mithl), and it comes in the Qur'an frequently; whenever it comes, we parse it this way: as a noun meaning "like." As for its grammatical function, it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), and its governing verb is the verb after it; i.e., "and like that which We have made, We made for every prophet."
So these polytheists who made the Qur'an abandoned, cast it behind their backs, called to its abandonment, and mocked it, are not unprecedented among others; it has already been so for every prophet.
(﴿And thus﴾, as We have made for you an enemy among the polytheists of your people, ﴿We have made for every prophet﴾ before you ﴿an enemy from among the criminals﴾, the polytheists; so be patient as they were patient.) In this there is clear consolation for the Prophet ﷺ; a person is consoled when another has suffered a calamity like his. Al-Khansa' says while lamenting her brother Sakhr:
Were it not for the multitude of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself.
And they do not weep like my brother, but I console myself regarding him with consolation.
So when the Prophet, peace be upon him, knows that this is the custom of the people of the prophets before him, he is consoled and the matter becomes easier for him.
Allah, the Exalted, said: (﴿And sufficient is your Lord as a guide﴾ for you ﴿and a helper﴾, a helper for you against your enemies).
As for His saying: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord﴾, the bā' is said to be grammatically extra, and "Rabbika" is the subject of "kafā"; i.e., "and your Lord suffices." And ﴿hādiyan﴾ is a specification (tamyīz), meaning: His guidance and His help suffice; it is a tamyīz transferred from the subject, because tamyīz may be transferred from the subject and may be transferred from the object; ﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾ [al-Qamar 12] is transferred from the object, because the original is: and We caused springs to burst forth from the earth.
Here, ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as guide and helper﴾, the original is: and the guidance and help of your Lord sufficed, so it is a tamyīz transferred from the subject.

Likewise, they oppose the messengers with war, fighting and other things; so Allah, blessed and exalted, made clear that they cannot prevent Allah's guidance and help: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as guide and helper﴾.
