His saying ﴿a gradual drawing﴾: is the meaning of "gradual" here a description of the act, meaning that Our drawing of it is easy for Us, like His saying: ﴿That is a gathering easy for Us﴾ [Qaf 44]; or is the meaning ﴿gradual﴾, meaning that the drawing was little by little?
* Student: The latter.
* Shaykh: The latter is more apparent. The latter is what comes to mind: that Allah drew in this shade in a ﴿gradual﴾ drawing, little by little. This fits all the previous interpretations: if we say the shade is what lies between the dawn's rising, or between the time of first light and the time of sunrise, then He draws in this shade little by little. Does the light not keep shining until the sun rises? This is one case. If we say the intended meaning is the night, then He also draws it in little by little; meaning that the night is not twelve hours one day and nine hours the next day, but it is drawn in little by little.

Likewise, if we say the intended meaning is the shadow of an object, it is the same thing: it only decreases little by little.

There is no difficulty in the verse except His saying: ﴿Then We drew it in to Us, a gradual drawing﴾ [al-Furqan 46]; ﴿to Us﴾. This ultimate phrase is problematic, for it would have been possible to suffice with "Then We drew it in, a gradual drawing." So what is the wisdom in this ending: ﴿We drew it in to Us, a gradual drawing﴾? Yes?
* Student: To indicate (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. Does anyone see (...)?
* Student: The meaning is that when We drew it in, i.e. (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿We drew it in to Us﴾: He drew it in to Himself. Yes?
* Student: We say the shade is affected in its movement and gradualness by the sun, (...) the sun or the movement of the sun, and the sun moves towards Allah, Exalted is He, prostrating at the Throne. So the meaning is: He drew in this thing which results from (...).
* Shaykh: Meaning the pronoun in His saying ﴿We drew it in﴾ refers to the sun?
* Student: No, to the influence on this thing, which is the sun.
* Shaykh: Because, yes, some hold that the pronoun in His saying ﴿We drew it in﴾ refers to the sun, in its capacity as a guide: ﴿We made the sun over it a guide (45) Then We drew it in﴾ [al-Furqan 45–46], meaning: We drew in this guide ﴿to Us, a gradual drawing﴾.

He is, in any case, subject to the possibility mentioned by the brother: that the intended meaning is that the end point is to Allah, the Exalted, indicating that He alone directs it, and that no one can direct it otherwise.

There is also the possibility that ﴿قَبَضْنَاهُ إِلَيْنَا﴾ ("then We take it back to Us") refers to the evidence, i.e., the sun. The "taking back to Him" would then be what the Prophet ﷺ indicated in his saying in the hadith of Abu Dhar: "It goes off and prostrates beneath the Throne."[[Al-Bukhari (3199), whose wording this is, and Muslim (159 / 250), both with their chains from a hadith of Abu Dhar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said to Abu Dhar when the sun had set: "Do you know where it goes?" I said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "It goes until it prostrates beneath the Throne. It asks permission and is granted permission, and it is about to prostrate, but its prostration is not accepted. It asks permission and is not granted permission. It is said to it: 'Return from where you came,' so it rises from its west. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾ [Yasin: 38]."]]

There is a third possibility, which al-Zamakhshari (al-Zamakhshari, a classical exegete) adopted. He said that the "taking" here refers to what Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿When the sun is folded up, and when the stars fall away﴾ [al-Takwir: 1–2]. The meaning would be the taking of these luminous bodies, the sun and others, on the Day of Resurrection. He held that the phrase ﴿يَسِيرًا﴾ ("with ease") is not a description of the taking, that it happens gradually, but rather a description of the act, meaning that it is easy for Allah, as in His saying: ﴿That is an easy gathering for Us﴾ [Qaf: 44].

However, the last view is far-fetched, because Allah only bestows a favour through something whose benefit people perceive in this world and whose display of Allah's complete power is evident in it. Accordingly, there are two options: either it is said that the end point which Allah mentioned indicates that this is from His direction alone, that the matter belongs to Him alone and not to anyone else, and that this is a proof of the greatness of Allah, the Exalted; or the meaning of the "taking to Him" is that the sun is taken to Allah, in the sense that it goes off and prostrates beneath the Throne, as the hadith from the Prophet ﷺ reports.

* Among the lessons in the verse:
First: Reminding a person of the blessings he sees, by His saying: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord...﴾ [al-Furqan: 45].
Second: Affirming the lordship (rububiyyah) of Allah, the Exalted, by His saying: ﴿how your Lord﴾. The "Lord" (Rabb) is the Creator who directs.
Third: Showing the perfection of Allah's power and His mercy in extending the shade, making the sun its evidence, and taking it back with ease, through these three matters.
Fourth: Affirming that one thing may be used as evidence for another.
Fifth: Using a thing as evidence for its opposite, since a thing is known by its opposite. Someone has said:
"..................... ∗∗∗ and by their opposites things become clear"
This is based on His saying: ﴿Then We made the sun its evidence﴾ [al-Furqan: 45].
* Sixth: Affirming the will of Allah, by His saying: ﴿And if He willed, He would have made it still﴾ [al-Furqan: 45].
* The seventh lesson: a person should not treat blessings as ordinary matters that are inevitable, but should estimate them by their opposite, based on His saying: ﴿And if He willed, He would have made it still.﴾ So if a person says, for example, that the sun's rising over this earth and its setting from it is a routine matter, we say: Yes, it is a routine matter, and because it is routine a person does not feel that it is a blessing. But estimate this thing by its opposite: ﴿And if He willed, He would have made it still.﴾ The leaving of the soul from a person's body is a routine matter, and for this reason a person does not feel the extent of this blessing. But estimate it: if Allah willed, He would have withheld it, and then the magnitude of the blessing becomes clear. So His saying ﴿And if He willed, He would have made it still﴾ should be made a rule for us regarding all the routine blessings we have lived with and become accustomed to, for we do not feel that they are blessings. Instead, we must estimate their opposite, ﴿And if He willed, He would have made it still﴾, so that through it we come to know the value of Allah's blessing in these routine things.
* Student: Is a lesson not drawn from (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. It is the affirmation of Allah's mercy through the existence of these blessings. But alerting a person to gratitude happens only by mentioning the opposite of these blessings, by His saying: ﴿And if He willed, He would have made it still.﴾
Also in it is the lesson of iltifat (a shift of style, changing the mode of address to alert the listener), which is changing the manner of speech to draw the addressee's attention, by His saying: ﴿Then We made the sun its evidence﴾ [al-Furqan: 45].
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, this is affirming blessings through their opposite, knowing the value of blessings by knowing their opposite.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Indeed, yes. Inferring a thing from its opposite. What we mean by blessings is that a person infers, from their opposite, the basis for this blessing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 47–49 (part 1 of 2):

Then he said: (﴿And it is He who made the night a garment for you﴾, covering like a garment, ﴿and sleep a rest﴾, a rest for the bodies by cutting off works, ﴿and made the day a resurrection﴾ [al-Furqan 47], spread out, in which one seeks sustenance and other things).

This too is among the blessings that no one can bring about except Allah.

﴿And it is He who made for you﴾: the lam here indicates purpose, meaning: for your sake, ﴿He made the night a garment﴾. The meaning of ﴿a garment﴾ is (covering like a garment), because of its darkness.

For this reason a person may go out at night in clothes he cannot wear in the daytime; he may go out at night to attend to his needs, which he cannot do in the daytime, because the night conceals, so it is a garment.

Is it a garment for the earth or a garment for us? For all of it, because it clothes the earth and clothes the human being in reality: it covers the earth and it also covers the human being.

As for His saying ﴿and sleep a rest﴾ [al-Furqan 47]: sabat means cutting off. The author explained it as rest, and this is explaining a thing by its consequence. Otherwise, it is a cutting off of fatigue; it cuts off tiredness. In this is the great benefit that it cuts off the fatigue that came before. It is not as the author said, (by cutting off works), because a person may cut off his works while awake, but sleep cuts off fatigue, as is observed. A person becomes tired and then sleeps; when he sleeps his tiredness is undone. So in reality it is a cutting off of past fatigue and a renewal of energy for the future.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, his intention is that when a person sleeps he does not work.
* Student: You mean he does not work for Allah, the Exalted, or for anything else?
* Shaykh: For anything else. When he sleeps he does not work; this is the aspect of its being sabat. But we say: it is not so; it is not a cutting off of work, rather it is a cutting off of the fatigue of the body; therefore the body gains rest. As for the mere cutting off of works, this may occur together with wakefulness and alertness.

﴿And made the day a resurrection﴾ [al-Furqan 47]: meaning, a place of resurrection. For this the author said, (spread out in it); meaning that the day is the place of resurrection for seeking sustenance and other works, and this is from the blessing of Allah, the Exalted.

What we have today, namely that the night is not a garment, does not counter this, because that is an incidental matter caused by the artificial lights that man has made. If these lights were gone, darkness would return to the earth. Moreover, this light and illumination that prevents the night from being a garment is not general in reality; rather it is a relative matter. Furthermore, it is weak and does not include shadow; the shadow that blocks the light of this candle, for example, is black, ﴿a garment﴾.

Likewise, ﴿and made the day a resurrection﴾ is not countered by some incidental cases such as guards, for example: guards sleep in the day and work at night. But these are rare matters, and the rare does not overturn the rules; the rules cannot be (...) by rare matters. The discussion is about the general.

This too is from the blessing of Allah, the Exalted. Could anyone, if Allah had not made the night, bring the night? No one can; even if all creation, from first to last, with all their crafts, gathered together, they could not bring half a night or an hour of night.

Likewise sleep: can anyone make another person sleep? Never, no one can. And these sleeping pills do not refute us, because a person who gives sleeping pills is like one who says: "I can make a person sleep by giving him doses of sleep." We say: this is like the one who said to Abraham: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ [al-Baqarah 258]. Indeed, the one who gives doses of sleep is not the one who makes sleep; he only does the cause by which sleep occurs. Consider: if Allah had made this body unable to sleep, would these doses be able to make it sleep? No. So sleep is something no one can ever bring to the human body. Even if it were brought, for example, a person may take it and it is not a complete cutting off, and does not cut off fatigue. Therefore Allah, the Exalted, bestowed it upon His servants as a favor, and it is a matter no one can do.

Likewise He made the day a resurrection. Who can remove this garment, the garment of the night, until the dawn comes and people spread out to their affairs? The answer: no one can except Allah, mighty and majestic. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, bestowed His favor upon His servants in these three matters: sleep, night, and day.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: May Allah protect us from this, I seek refuge in Allah.
* Student: This means it is evidence that (...), whatever he does with it.
* Shaykh: Known, there is no doubt; this is a known matter.

If someone says: Allah, the Exalted, made the night a garment, made the day a resurrection, and made sleep a sabat; when does sleep occur, at night or in the day?
* Student: At night.
* Shaykh: Originally at night, but it may also be in the day. A person may become tired during the day and sleep and then rest, like the midday rest for example. Therefore no one should say that Allah, the Exalted, mentioned two blessings for the night and one blessing for the day. Rather we say: Allah mentioned in the night one blessing, which is that it is a ﴿garment﴾, and in the day one blessing, which is that it is a ﴿resurrection﴾, and He made sleep in general a blessing, which is that it is a sabat, meaning it cuts off fatigue. And Allah knows best.
* Student: Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Does sleep of every kind cut off fatigue, or only some kinds?
* Shaykh: Natural sleep, which is part of the human constitution. As for sleep that occurs because of illness, since a person may fall ill and sleep much with it, the apparent meaning is that it does not fall under the verse.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: The main point is the apparent; the apparent is that it is a relative matter, and some people find great relief in it.
* Student: Or, for example, after the afternoon (...).
* Shaykh: If I did not sleep a little now before (...), I might not be able to work; I would become sleepy again. We have not tested this previously.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: You say it actually tires a person more when his stomach is full. If he sleeps with a full stomach, it may be so; but the discussion is about generality (...), yes?
* Student: O Shaykh, is sleeping at certain times disliked?
* Shaykh: I do not know anything about this.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is not disliked. "Indeed the Messenger of Allah disliked sleeping before the night prayer" [Footnote: Recorded by al-Bukhari (599) and Muslim (647/236), and the wording is his, from Abu Barzah al-Aslami, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not mind delaying the night prayer until midnight, and he disliked sleeping before it and talking after it.], this is disliked, before the night prayer for a legal reason, not for a bodily reason. As for afternoon sleep, they say the words of the poet:
Indeed, sleeping in the forenoon brings the youth ∗∗∗ corruption, and sleeping in the afternoon brings madness.
This is not correct. Many people now sleep in the afternoon constantly, and they were not afflicted with madness, nor were they called madmen.
* Student: The scholars said that it (...).
* Shaykh: It distracts from thought. A person may make up for it; sometimes he cannot sleep in the middle of the day, but he cannot remain until night; he must sleep (...).
* Student: O Shaykh, (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, perhaps (...).
Yes?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: I do not think this; this is an understanding of the hadith (...), and the common people say: ..
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Not (...), and the common people then say: "less," for the devils do not say less; they delete the yā' (...). Yes?
(...)
(nashūr like rasūl, and the last bashīr): this has several readings. First, the wind has two readings: are both canonical (sab'iyyah), or is one of them irregular (shādhdh)?
* Student: Both canonical.
* Shaykh: What is the proof?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, the proof is that if one says "and in a reading," it is canonical; if one says "and it was read," it is irregular. Yes.
﴿al-riyāḥ﴾ and ﴿al-rīḥ﴾ [al-Furqan 48] have two readings: ﴿al-riyāḥ﴾ and ﴿al-rīḥ﴾. From this we know that what is well known in their saying, that "rīḥ" is only in punishment and "riyāḥ" is in mercy, is not absolute, and that the singular "rīḥ" may be used for a wind of mercy, but it has a context. Here He said: ﴿before His mercy﴾ [al-Furqan 48], so it is known that it is a wind of mercy. Likewise His Exalted saying: ﴿until when you are in the ship and they sail with them by a wind﴾ and what follows? ﴿good﴾ [Yunus 22]. This is a wind of mercy, but it was described. But when unqualified, the wind is usually for punishment.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, like this hadith.

And His saying: ﴿bushran﴾ [al-Furqan 48] has several readings. First: ﴿nushuran﴾ with a damma on the nūn and the shīn, and the meaning of ﴿nushuran﴾, the author says: (scattered); meaning that they sometimes blow from the south, sometimes from the north, sometimes from the west, and sometimes from the east, and by this scattering the clouds form, then the rain.

And His saying: (and in a reading with the shīn sukūn for lightness). How?
* Student: ﴿nushran﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿nushran﴾. His saying "for lightness" means that the meaning is not changed by it; it is only made sukūn for lightness.
(And in another with its sukūn and a fatha on the nūn as a verbal noun).
* Student: ﴿nashran﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿nashran﴾; then the meaning changes. ﴿nushuran﴾ and ﴿nushran﴾ have the same meaning, without difference, because the sukūn is for lightness. But ﴿nashran﴾ means He spreads them out spreading, this is different, being a verbal noun.
(And in another with its sukūn and a ḍamma on the bā' instead of the nūn), that is, the sukūn of the shīn and a ḍamma on the unpointed bā' in place of the nūn, and it is: ﴿bushran﴾, and this is the well-known reading. The meaning of ﴿bushran﴾ on this reading is: i.e., bearers of good news; meaning: they give good news, and they are not a verbal noun, and Allah gives good news by them; they themselves are ﴿bushran﴾. Yes?
* Student: (...) (and in another with its sukūn and a ḍamma on the unpointed bā' in place of the nūn) did he not mention (...)?
* Shaykh: (with its sukūn) I think it is one.
* Student: And the unpointed bā' (...).
* Shaykh: The unpointed bā', yes, ﴿bushran﴾, this is it.
The singular says: (the singular of the first is nushūr). And what is the first? ﴿nushuran﴾.
(like rasūl and rusul), rasūl and rusul, rasūl and rusul (with sukūn), this is the singular of the first when it is not a verbal noun, which is ﴿nashran﴾; if it is a verbal noun, then it is a singular, not a plural.
And the last, ﴿bushran﴾, he says: (the last's singular is bashīr).
The readings have become, I think, four: ﴿nushuran﴾, ﴿nushran﴾, ﴿nashran﴾, and ﴿bushran﴾: four readings for this word.

The benefit of the differences in readings, that is, this is from the inimitability of the Qur'an: that from each reading a meaning is derived, and on this basis it encompasses both being good news and being scattered spreading before the rain.

And His saying: ﴿before His mercy﴾ [al-Furqan 48]: the meant mercy here is the rain or its effects, and this is created mercy, because mercy attributed to Allah, the Exalted, is divided into two kinds: mercy that is His attribute, which is uncreated, and mercy that is an effect of the attribute, which is created. So His saying to Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whomever I will" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850) and Muslim (2846/34) from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him], this is created, is it not? Created. And His saying: ﴿My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [al-A'raf 156] is the attribute, which is not created. So the mercy attributed to Allah is divided into two kinds: created, and called mercy because it is an effect of mercy; and uncreated, which is His attribute.

And what is with us now: ﴿bushran before His mercy﴾ [al-Furqan 48], is it the created or the uncreated?
* Student: Both.
* Shaykh: How both?
* Student: The generality of Allah's mercy.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, it is possible that the meaning of ﴿before His mercy﴾ is: when He wishes to show mercy; if He wishes to show mercy, then it is of the uncreated. And it is possible that ﴿before His mercy﴾ means before the rain itself, and then mercy here is created, because its application to rain requires that.

The author explained it as the created mercy, because he said: (in front of the rain).

﴿And We sent down﴾ [al-Furqan 48].
It is well known that what brings the rain by Allah's permission is the southern winds; therefore our forefathers and grandfathers used to say: when the southern wind blows (...), they said: now the rain comes and there is no need to water the crops, because it seemed to them a customary thing.

﴿And We sent down from the sky water, pure﴾ [al-Furqan 48]: ﴿from the sky﴾ means from the clouds, because every thing above you is sky, and there is no doubt that rain descends only from clouds, so the meaning of ﴿the sky﴾ here is height.

And His saying: ﴿water, pure﴾ means the rain. And "ṭahūr" with a fatḥa on the ṭā' is what one purifies with, or what purification is achieved by; as for "ṭuhūr" by its action, it is the act of purifying, i.e., purification.

Here He says: ﴿And We sent down﴾, and before it: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds﴾ [al-Furqan 48]. In this there is what is called in rhetoric al-iltifāt (shift of address), and its benefit, as we have often seen, is alerting the addressee, because a change of style necessitates attention. And in it also is the concern with what the shift is directed to, because it needed to be emphasized by this shift.

There is no doubt that sending down rain is the purpose of sending the winds, is it not? Therefore the shift to it came in the form of the speaker: ﴿And We sent down from the sky﴾.

And His saying, Exalted: ﴿And We sent down from the sky﴾: is the word ﴿mā'an﴾ for the singular or the plural?
* Student: For the singular.
* Student: It may be for the singular and it may be for the plural.
* Shaykh: But it is suitable for the singular venerated one, and here it is so.

(﴿And We sent down from the sky water, pure (48), that We may give life thereby to a dead land﴾ [al-Furqan 48, 49], with the lightening (taḫfīf), in which masculine and feminine are equal; He said it in masculine by consideration of place, ﴿and We give drink of it﴾, that is, the water, ﴿to what We have created: cattle﴾, camels, cows, and sheep, ﴿and many people﴾ [al-Furqan 49], plural of insān, originally anāsīn, then the nūn was changed to yā' and the yā' was assimilated into it, or plural of insī).

Allah, the Exalted, mentioned two benefits of this rain:
First: the giving of life to the dead land, ﴿a dead land﴾. He did not say "dead" (feminine), because (it is equal for masculine and feminine), so I have this here; what do you have, you (students): (or he made it masculine by consideration of place)?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but the correct formulation is: (or he made it masculine by consideration of place). Because if he says "he made it masculine by consideration of place," then his statement "masculine and feminine are equal in it" is not correct, since if masculine and feminine are equal in it, there is no need to explain that it was made masculine by consideration of place. So we say, for example: the correct formulation is: (or he made it masculine by consideration of place).

So the word (mayt-an) if masculine and feminine are equal in it, then your saying (mayt-an) or (mayta) is on the same footing.
Or (mayta), on the same footing. But if we say it is for the masculine, then we need to answer why it was described with ﴿a land﴾ [al-Furqan 49], which is feminine; he says: he made it masculine by consideration of place.

His saying, ﴿that We may give life thereby﴾ [al-Furqan 49]: the ba' here indicates causation, and the one who gives life is Allah, mighty and majestic, but the rain is the cause.

And His saying: ﴿dead﴾ [al-Furqan 49]: the land is described here as dead; is the meaning the earth itself being dead, or what is on it?
* Student: All the vegetation on it.
* Shaykh: Not what is on it in reality, because the benefit is from the land and what is on it, and what the camels, cows, and sheep graze is what is on the earth, not that they eat dirt and pebbles. So its giving life is in terms of what is in it: that it comes alive, grows, and becomes big.
* Student: (...)?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 47–49 (part 2 of 2):

* The Shaykh: No, but the earth itself is not entered by life and death. The earth itself, meaning the stones and the clay, is not entered by life and death. What enters the earth with life and death is what is on it. Therefore He said in another verse: ﴿It stirs and swells﴾ [al-Hajj 5], and stirring and swelling only happen to what is upon it; as for the earth itself, it does not stir.

His saying: ﴿And that We may give drink to many of the cattle and people that We have created﴾ [al-Furqan 49].

This is another benefit of the rain: that cattle and people are given drink by it. But how does this happen? Is it through the pools that remain on the surface of the earth, or does this water get stored in the earth, or both?

Both together, because the watering by rain happens in these two ways: either through pools that form in hollows (qay'an, sing. qä'), from which people benefit, or the earth absorbs it and it is stored within it, as Allah said: ﴿So We sent down water from the sky and caused you to drink it, and you are not its storers﴾ [al-Hijr 22]. Rather, it is Allah, glorified and exalted, who stores it.

In this verse there is evidence for affirming causes (asbab), because of His saying: ﴿That We may give life thereby to a dead land﴾ [al-Furqan 49].

It also contains evidence for the sending of heralds and precursors before things, as a sign of the strength of hope, because of His saying: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-Furqan 48].

It also contains evidence for the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through the sending of the winds, because if all creation gathered, determined to produce even one of these winds, they would not be able to do so. Yet these winds at times uproot trees and destroy houses. This great power: if all the generators of the world came together to create such air, this would not be achieved.

It also contains evidence of wisdom, of the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in the rain being sent down from the sky. If this rain, by which the earth is revived, came flowing over the surface of the earth, this benefit would not exist, because it would not reach the mountain peaks except after drowning what is beneath them. But when it descends from above, it reaches the mountain peaks and reaches what is lower than them. This is from the wisdom of Allah, glorified and exalted, in that.

It also contains evidence that the basic state of water is purity, because of His saying: ﴿Pure water﴾ [al-Furqan 48]. We know now, as we have recited to you, that the water present on the earth comes from the sky.

* A student: All of it?

* The Shaykh: Yes, all of it. ﴿So We sent down water from the sky and caused you to drink it﴾ [al-Hijr 22]. So if it comes from the sky, then the basic state of what gushes forth from the earth, or what descends from the sky, is that it is pure.

It also contains evidence for affirming wisdom in the acts of Allah, because of His saying: ﴿That We may give life thereby﴾ [al-Furqan 49], the particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil). This is one of hundreds of pieces of evidence for affirming wisdom, and it thus constitutes a refutation of a group of the innovating sects. Who are they?

* A student: The Jahmiyyah and the Mu'tazilah.

* The Shaykh: No, they are not the Mu'tazilah. The Jahmiyyah, because they hold that the acts of Allah are merely by will, not for a reason. The Jahmiyyah do not prefer one thing over another for a wisdom; rather, it is merely by will, and He does nothing except by mere will! There is no doubt that this view is rejected by both transmitted and rational evidence, because one who acts with wisdom is more perfect than one who acts without wisdom, is that not so? They deny wisdom and say: because wisdom is a purpose (gharad), and Allah, glorified and exalted, is free of parts (ab'ad), accidents (a'rad) and purposes (aghrad). Look at the fine expression! Whoever hears this phrasing would say: this is like the phrasing of the Qur'an: free of parts, purposes and accidents. By parts they mean things like the hand, face, eye and the like; by accidents they mean the actions of choice, such as descending, establishing and the like; and by purposes they mean wisdom, because they say: if He acted for a wisdom, He would be deficient without it. This is an inversion of realities. If He acts with wisdom, that is evidence of His perfection, and that He does not do anything merely by will, foolishly.

It also contains evidence for the permissibility of mentioning only some of the benefits, meaning that limiting oneself to some does not count as a deficiency. Here Allah mentioned only two benefits of the rain: the revival of the earth and the watering of cattle and people, although the rain has other benefits, such as purification with it, for example. Purification with it is neither watering nor reviving the earth, and there are other benefits besides. But since the most necessary aspect of the rain is reviving the earth with vegetation so that people and cattle may eat, and likewise watering, and food and drink are among the necessities of life for cattle and for people, Allah, blessed and exalted, limited Himself to mentioning only these two benefits, because they are the two necessary benefits resulting from the descent of rain: the revival of the earth for plants and food, and watering for drink.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿cattle and people﴾ [al-Furqan 49]. Here, "cattle" is not described as many, but "people" is described: ﴿and many people﴾ [al-Furqan 49]. In this expression there are two difficulties:

The first difficulty: why are people described as many while cattle are not described as many?

The second: we know that Allah gives drink with this water to all people, every person drinks from it. So why does He say: ﴿and many people﴾? It seems to imply that some people are not watered by rainwater. So what is the answer to the first difficulty: describing people with multiplicity but not describing cattle?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Does this mean that ﴿many﴾ is an attribute of both together?

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: That is not the apparent meaning, because it would then agree.

* A student: Cattle relative to people are fewer.

* A student: (...).

* A student: Cattle are more numerous than people.

* The Shaykh: Yes. What do you mean?

* The student: I say: cattle are more numerous than people.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: I have, by Allah knows best, that some cattle do not need water, as we hear that some of them do not need water, and some need very little?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: There are many things they count against us, saying: it does not need water, or if it drinks it drinks only very little, perhaps once a year. If this is correct, then it is from wisdom; perhaps this is from wisdom, by not describing it with multiplicity.

But the second difficulty remains, which is more serious than this: ﴿and many people﴾ [al-Furqan 49].

* A student: It is not said regarding the first difficulty.

* The Shaykh: Yes?

* The student: Like cattle, no (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: Unlike the human being (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, but I did not mention only drinking: "that We may give drink to cattle and people."

The second difficulty: that His saying ﴿and many people﴾, although all people drink?

* A student: (...).

* Another student: According to what you said, cattle must be many (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* A student: Describing them with multiplicity is not a restriction of the condition (...). The reality is that people are many.

* The Shaykh: Meaning relative to cattle, meaning?

* The student: No, (...) and you said: the second difficulty is that there are some cattle that do not drink.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: Or they do not benefit from (...). So we say: ﴿many﴾ is not a restriction on drinking for those people who drink, but only a statement of the reality that these people who drink are many, and they all drink, so it is for multiplicity.

* The Shaykh: If I say, for example: "I have many men," would it be understood from that that there are other men who did not attend (...)?

* A student: Yes.

* A student: Allah, glorified and exalted, (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, and for this reason He says: plural of "insan" (human), and its origin...

* A student: (...) that ﴿many﴾ be an attribute of the cattle and the people?

* The Shaykh: Yes?

* The student: Is there anything preventing the attribute from being (...)?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, we said: agreement. But our brother raised an objection, saying: even cattle has a plural, and ﴿many﴾ applies equally to the singular and the plural.

* A student: Perhaps it indicates (...).

* The Shaykh: No, if we say that ﴿many﴾ is an attribute of people and of cattle, the difficulty disappears.

The second difficulty: it is possible to say, as Muhammad said, that Allah, glorified and exalted, is showing that they are many people, and it does not follow from this that some of them do not drink, and that this multiplicity is an encompassing multiplicity, just as you say: "The troops are many," or "The emir has a great army," the phrase "a great army" includes all the soldiers and describes them as many. ("People" [unasi] includes all humans and describes them as many.)

* A student: If he said "most" (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, saying "most" is correct, it is clear.

In any case, then, what comes to mind first as the difficulty, how can it be dispensed with? By making ﴿many﴾ an attribute of both: "many cattle" and "many people." It is not like Allah's saying: ﴿And from both of them He spread forth many men and women﴾ [al-Nisa 1], because ﴿many men﴾ cannot be an attribute of both, since it precedes "women"; but here it can be said that it is an attribute of both the conjoined and the conjoined-to.

As for ﴿many﴾, it is to state the reality and not to exclude the rest. Its parallel in an example is that you say, for instance: "The emir has many troops," or "A large army went out against the enemy," so it is an attribute describing it with multiplicity. That is: ﴿people﴾ are not few, this is the meaning; ﴿cattle﴾ are not few, ﴿people﴾ are not few, rather they are many, and this serves as an explanation of the comprehensiveness of the benefit to creation, both speaking and beast, from this water: ﴿many cattle﴾ and ﴿many people﴾.

Now, we have all arrived at the conclusion that ﴿many﴾ is an attribute of both cattle and people. Regarding the multiplicity of cattle, do we say it is multiplicity of kinds and types, or multiplicity of individuals, or both?

* A student: Both.

* The Shaykh: And regarding people, multiplicity of individuals, because people are one kind.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: how many of the benefits we have passed over from these verses? Seven benefits.

* A student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: Apparently, and Allah knows best, for multiplicity, because it is more: more in kinds and in individuals.

* The student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: Allah knows best. It is not because of the... the discussion on its benefit from the rain. Yes, this is regarding cattle, because it is more. It may be said: the reviving of the earth is for the benefit of human beings, and the watering of cattle is for the benefit of human beings, and the watering of human beings is for their own benefit; so it mentions first what is indirect benefit to the human being, then delays the direct benefit, by way of proceeding from the farther to the farther in benefits, the farther then the farther; because cattle are for the benefit of human beings, and the earth's revival is for the benefit of human beings, and the reviving of cattle is more directly and closely connected to human beings than the reviving of the earth; because how many lands drink the rain and the human being does not reach them and benefit from them, unlike cattle.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 47–49 (part 1 of 2):

Then he said: (﴿And it is He who made the night a garment for you﴾, covering like a garment, ﴿and sleep a rest﴾, a rest for the bodies by cutting off works, ﴿and made the day a resurrection﴾ [al-Furqan 47], spread out, in which one seeks sustenance and other things).

This too is among the blessings that no one can bring about except Allah.

﴿And it is He who made for you﴾: the lam here indicates purpose, meaning: for your sake, ﴿He made the night a garment﴾. The meaning of ﴿a garment﴾ is (covering like a garment), because of its darkness.

For this reason a person may go out at night in clothes he cannot wear in the daytime; he may go out at night to attend to his needs, which he cannot do in the daytime, because the night conceals, so it is a garment.

Is it a garment for the earth or a garment for us? For all of it, because it clothes the earth and clothes the human being in reality: it covers the earth and it also covers the human being.

As for His saying ﴿and sleep a rest﴾ [al-Furqan 47]: sabat means cutting off. The author explained it as rest, and this is explaining a thing by its consequence. Otherwise, it is a cutting off of fatigue; it cuts off tiredness. In this is the great benefit that it cuts off the fatigue that came before. It is not as the author said, (by cutting off works), because a person may cut off his works while awake, but sleep cuts off fatigue, as is observed. A person becomes tired and then sleeps; when he sleeps his tiredness is undone. So in reality it is a cutting off of past fatigue and a renewal of energy for the future.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, his intention is that when a person sleeps he does not work.
* Student: You mean he does not work for Allah, the Exalted, or for anything else?
* Shaykh: For anything else. When he sleeps he does not work; this is the aspect of its being sabat. But we say: it is not so; it is not a cutting off of work, rather it is a cutting off of the fatigue of the body; therefore the body gains rest. As for the mere cutting off of works, this may occur together with wakefulness and alertness.

﴿And made the day a resurrection﴾ [al-Furqan 47]: meaning, a place of resurrection. For this the author said, (spread out in it); meaning that the day is the place of resurrection for seeking sustenance and other works, and this is from the blessing of Allah, the Exalted.

What we have today, namely that the night is not a garment, does not counter this, because that is an incidental matter caused by the artificial lights that man has made. If these lights were gone, darkness would return to the earth. Moreover, this light and illumination that prevents the night from being a garment is not general in reality; rather it is a relative matter. Furthermore, it is weak and does not include shadow; the shadow that blocks the light of this candle, for example, is black, ﴿a garment﴾.

Likewise, ﴿and made the day a resurrection﴾ is not countered by some incidental cases such as guards, for example: guards sleep in the day and work at night. But these are rare matters, and the rare does not overturn the rules; the rules cannot be (...) by rare matters. The discussion is about the general.

This too is from the blessing of Allah, the Exalted. Could anyone, if Allah had not made the night, bring the night? No one can; even if all creation, from first to last, with all their crafts, gathered together, they could not bring half a night or an hour of night.

Likewise sleep: can anyone make another person sleep? Never, no one can. And these sleeping pills do not refute us, because a person who gives sleeping pills is like one who says: "I can make a person sleep by giving him doses of sleep." We say: this is like the one who said to Abraham: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ [al-Baqarah 258]. Indeed, the one who gives doses of sleep is not the one who makes sleep; he only does the cause by which sleep occurs. Consider: if Allah had made this body unable to sleep, would these doses be able to make it sleep? No. So sleep is something no one can ever bring to the human body. Even if it were brought, for example, a person may take it and it is not a complete cutting off, and does not cut off fatigue. Therefore Allah, the Exalted, bestowed it upon His servants as a favor, and it is a matter no one can do.

Likewise He made the day a resurrection. Who can remove this garment, the garment of the night, until the dawn comes and people spread out to their affairs? The answer: no one can except Allah, mighty and majestic. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, bestowed His favor upon His servants in these three matters: sleep, night, and day.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: May Allah protect us from this, I seek refuge in Allah.
* Student: This means it is evidence that (...), whatever he does with it.
* Shaykh: Known, there is no doubt; this is a known matter.

If someone says: Allah, the Exalted, made the night a garment, made the day a resurrection, and made sleep a sabat; when does sleep occur, at night or in the day?
* Student: At night.
* Shaykh: Originally at night, but it may also be in the day. A person may become tired during the day and sleep and then rest, like the midday rest for example. Therefore no one should say that Allah, the Exalted, mentioned two blessings for the night and one blessing for the day. Rather we say: Allah mentioned in the night one blessing, which is that it is a ﴿garment﴾, and in the day one blessing, which is that it is a ﴿resurrection﴾, and He made sleep in general a blessing, which is that it is a sabat, meaning it cuts off fatigue. And Allah knows best.
* Student: Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Does sleep of every kind cut off fatigue, or only some kinds?
* Shaykh: Natural sleep, which is part of the human constitution. As for sleep that occurs because of illness, since a person may fall ill and sleep much with it, the apparent meaning is that it does not fall under the verse.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: The main point is the apparent; the apparent is that it is a relative matter, and some people find great relief in it.
* Student: Or, for example, after the afternoon (...).
* Shaykh: If I did not sleep a little now before (...), I might not be able to work; I would become sleepy again. We have not tested this previously.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: You say it actually tires a person more when his stomach is full. If he sleeps with a full stomach, it may be so; but the discussion is about generality (...), yes?
* Student: O Shaykh, is sleeping at certain times disliked?
* Shaykh: I do not know anything about this.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is not disliked. "Indeed the Messenger of Allah disliked sleeping before the night prayer" [Footnote: Recorded by al-Bukhari (599) and Muslim (647/236), and the wording is his, from Abu Barzah al-Aslami, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not mind delaying the night prayer until midnight, and he disliked sleeping before it and talking after it.], this is disliked, before the night prayer for a legal reason, not for a bodily reason. As for afternoon sleep, they say the words of the poet:
Indeed, sleeping in the forenoon brings the youth ∗∗∗ corruption, and sleeping in the afternoon brings madness.
This is not correct. Many people now sleep in the afternoon constantly, and they were not afflicted with madness, nor were they called madmen.
* Student: The scholars said that it (...).
* Shaykh: It distracts from thought. A person may make up for it; sometimes he cannot sleep in the middle of the day, but he cannot remain until night; he must sleep (...).
* Student: O Shaykh, (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, perhaps (...).
Yes?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: I do not think this; this is an understanding of the hadith (...), and the common people say: ..
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Not (...), and the common people then say: "less," for the devils do not say less; they delete the yā' (...). Yes?
(...)
(nashūr like rasūl, and the last bashīr): this has several readings. First, the wind has two readings: are both canonical (sab'iyyah), or is one of them irregular (shādhdh)?
* Student: Both canonical.
* Shaykh: What is the proof?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, the proof is that if one says "and in a reading," it is canonical; if one says "and it was read," it is irregular. Yes.
﴿al-riyāḥ﴾ and ﴿al-rīḥ﴾ [al-Furqan 48] have two readings: ﴿al-riyāḥ﴾ and ﴿al-rīḥ﴾. From this we know that what is well known in their saying, that "rīḥ" is only in punishment and "riyāḥ" is in mercy, is not absolute, and that the singular "rīḥ" may be used for a wind of mercy, but it has a context. Here He said: ﴿before His mercy﴾ [al-Furqan 48], so it is known that it is a wind of mercy. Likewise His Exalted saying: ﴿until when you are in the ship and they sail with them by a wind﴾ and what follows? ﴿good﴾ [Yunus 22]. This is a wind of mercy, but it was described. But when unqualified, the wind is usually for punishment.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, like this hadith.

And His saying: ﴿bushran﴾ [al-Furqan 48] has several readings. First: ﴿nushuran﴾ with a damma on the nūn and the shīn, and the meaning of ﴿nushuran﴾, the author says: (scattered); meaning that they sometimes blow from the south, sometimes from the north, sometimes from the west, and sometimes from the east, and by this scattering the clouds form, then the rain.

And His saying: (and in a reading with the shīn sukūn for lightness). How?
* Student: ﴿nushran﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿nushran﴾. His saying "for lightness" means that the meaning is not changed by it; it is only made sukūn for lightness.
(And in another with its sukūn and a fatha on the nūn as a verbal noun).
* Student: ﴿nashran﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿nashran﴾; then the meaning changes. ﴿nushuran﴾ and ﴿nushran﴾ have the same meaning, without difference, because the sukūn is for lightness. But ﴿nashran﴾ means He spreads them out spreading, this is different, being a verbal noun.
(And in another with its sukūn and a ḍamma on the bā' instead of the nūn), that is, the sukūn of the shīn and a ḍamma on the unpointed bā' in place of the nūn, and it is: ﴿bushran﴾, and this is the well-known reading. The meaning of ﴿bushran﴾ on this reading is: i.e., bearers of good news; meaning: they give good news, and they are not a verbal noun, and Allah gives good news by them; they themselves are ﴿bushran﴾. Yes?
* Student: (...) (and in another with its sukūn and a ḍamma on the unpointed bā' in place of the nūn) did he not mention (...)?
* Shaykh: (with its sukūn) I think it is one.
* Student: And the unpointed bā' (...).
* Shaykh: The unpointed bā', yes, ﴿bushran﴾, this is it.
The singular says: (the singular of the first is nushūr). And what is the first? ﴿nushuran﴾.
(like rasūl and rusul), rasūl and rusul, rasūl and rusul (with sukūn), this is the singular of the first when it is not a verbal noun, which is ﴿nashran﴾; if it is a verbal noun, then it is a singular, not a plural.
And the last, ﴿bushran﴾, he says: (the last's singular is bashīr).
The readings have become, I think, four: ﴿nushuran﴾, ﴿nushran﴾, ﴿nashran﴾, and ﴿bushran﴾: four readings for this word.

The benefit of the differences in readings, that is, this is from the inimitability of the Qur'an: that from each reading a meaning is derived, and on this basis it encompasses both being good news and being scattered spreading before the rain.

And His saying: ﴿before His mercy﴾ [al-Furqan 48]: the meant mercy here is the rain or its effects, and this is created mercy, because mercy attributed to Allah, the Exalted, is divided into two kinds: mercy that is His attribute, which is uncreated, and mercy that is an effect of the attribute, which is created. So His saying to Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whomever I will" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850) and Muslim (2846/34) from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him], this is created, is it not? Created. And His saying: ﴿My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [al-A'raf 156] is the attribute, which is not created. So the mercy attributed to Allah is divided into two kinds: created, and called mercy because it is an effect of mercy; and uncreated, which is His attribute.

And what is with us now: ﴿bushran before His mercy﴾ [al-Furqan 48], is it the created or the uncreated?
* Student: Both.
* Shaykh: How both?
* Student: The generality of Allah's mercy.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, it is possible that the meaning of ﴿before His mercy﴾ is: when He wishes to show mercy; if He wishes to show mercy, then it is of the uncreated. And it is possible that ﴿before His mercy﴾ means before the rain itself, and then mercy here is created, because its application to rain requires that.

The author explained it as the created mercy, because he said: (in front of the rain).

﴿And We sent down﴾ [al-Furqan 48].
It is well known that what brings the rain by Allah's permission is the southern winds; therefore our forefathers and grandfathers used to say: when the southern wind blows (...), they said: now the rain comes and there is no need to water the crops, because it seemed to them a customary thing.

﴿And We sent down from the sky water, pure﴾ [al-Furqan 48]: ﴿from the sky﴾ means from the clouds, because every thing above you is sky, and there is no doubt that rain descends only from clouds, so the meaning of ﴿the sky﴾ here is height.

And His saying: ﴿water, pure﴾ means the rain. And "ṭahūr" with a fatḥa on the ṭā' is what one purifies with, or what purification is achieved by; as for "ṭuhūr" by its action, it is the act of purifying, i.e., purification.

Here He says: ﴿And We sent down﴾, and before it: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds﴾ [al-Furqan 48]. In this there is what is called in rhetoric al-iltifāt (shift of address), and its benefit, as we have often seen, is alerting the addressee, because a change of style necessitates attention. And in it also is the concern with what the shift is directed to, because it needed to be emphasized by this shift.

There is no doubt that sending down rain is the purpose of sending the winds, is it not? Therefore the shift to it came in the form of the speaker: ﴿And We sent down from the sky﴾.

And His saying, Exalted: ﴿And We sent down from the sky﴾: is the word ﴿mā'an﴾ for the singular or the plural?
* Student: For the singular.
* Student: It may be for the singular and it may be for the plural.
* Shaykh: But it is suitable for the singular venerated one, and here it is so.

(﴿And We sent down from the sky water, pure (48), that We may give life thereby to a dead land﴾ [al-Furqan 48, 49], with the lightening (taḫfīf), in which masculine and feminine are equal; He said it in masculine by consideration of place, ﴿and We give drink of it﴾, that is, the water, ﴿to what We have created: cattle﴾, camels, cows, and sheep, ﴿and many people﴾ [al-Furqan 49], plural of insān, originally anāsīn, then the nūn was changed to yā' and the yā' was assimilated into it, or plural of insī).

Allah, the Exalted, mentioned two benefits of this rain:
First: the giving of life to the dead land, ﴿a dead land﴾. He did not say "dead" (feminine), because (it is equal for masculine and feminine), so I have this here; what do you have, you (students): (or he made it masculine by consideration of place)?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but the correct formulation is: (or he made it masculine by consideration of place). Because if he says "he made it masculine by consideration of place," then his statement "masculine and feminine are equal in it" is not correct, since if masculine and feminine are equal in it, there is no need to explain that it was made masculine by consideration of place. So we say, for example: the correct formulation is: (or he made it masculine by consideration of place).

So the word (mayt-an) if masculine and feminine are equal in it, then your saying (mayt-an) or (mayta) is on the same footing.
Or (mayta), on the same footing. But if we say it is for the masculine, then we need to answer why it was described with ﴿a land﴾ [al-Furqan 49], which is feminine; he says: he made it masculine by consideration of place.

His saying, ﴿that We may give life thereby﴾ [al-Furqan 49]: the ba' here indicates causation, and the one who gives life is Allah, mighty and majestic, but the rain is the cause.

And His saying: ﴿dead﴾ [al-Furqan 49]: the land is described here as dead; is the meaning the earth itself being dead, or what is on it?
* Student: All the vegetation on it.
* Shaykh: Not what is on it in reality, because the benefit is from the land and what is on it, and what the camels, cows, and sheep graze is what is on the earth, not that they eat dirt and pebbles. So its giving life is in terms of what is in it: that it comes alive, grows, and becomes big.
* Student: (...)?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 47–49 (part 2 of 2):

* The Shaykh: No, but the earth itself is not entered by life and death. The earth itself, meaning the stones and the clay, is not entered by life and death. What enters the earth with life and death is what is on it. Therefore He said in another verse: ﴿It stirs and swells﴾ [al-Hajj 5], and stirring and swelling only happen to what is upon it; as for the earth itself, it does not stir.

His saying: ﴿And that We may give drink to many of the cattle and people that We have created﴾ [al-Furqan 49].

This is another benefit of the rain: that cattle and people are given drink by it. But how does this happen? Is it through the pools that remain on the surface of the earth, or does this water get stored in the earth, or both?

Both together, because the watering by rain happens in these two ways: either through pools that form in hollows (qay'an, sing. qä'), from which people benefit, or the earth absorbs it and it is stored within it, as Allah said: ﴿So We sent down water from the sky and caused you to drink it, and you are not its storers﴾ [al-Hijr 22]. Rather, it is Allah, glorified and exalted, who stores it.

In this verse there is evidence for affirming causes (asbab), because of His saying: ﴿That We may give life thereby to a dead land﴾ [al-Furqan 49].

It also contains evidence for the sending of heralds and precursors before things, as a sign of the strength of hope, because of His saying: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-Furqan 48].

It also contains evidence for the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through the sending of the winds, because if all creation gathered, determined to produce even one of these winds, they would not be able to do so. Yet these winds at times uproot trees and destroy houses. This great power: if all the generators of the world came together to create such air, this would not be achieved.

It also contains evidence of wisdom, of the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in the rain being sent down from the sky. If this rain, by which the earth is revived, came flowing over the surface of the earth, this benefit would not exist, because it would not reach the mountain peaks except after drowning what is beneath them. But when it descends from above, it reaches the mountain peaks and reaches what is lower than them. This is from the wisdom of Allah, glorified and exalted, in that.

It also contains evidence that the basic state of water is purity, because of His saying: ﴿Pure water﴾ [al-Furqan 48]. We know now, as we have recited to you, that the water present on the earth comes from the sky.

* A student: All of it?

* The Shaykh: Yes, all of it. ﴿So We sent down water from the sky and caused you to drink it﴾ [al-Hijr 22]. So if it comes from the sky, then the basic state of what gushes forth from the earth, or what descends from the sky, is that it is pure.

It also contains evidence for affirming wisdom in the acts of Allah, because of His saying: ﴿That We may give life thereby﴾ [al-Furqan 49], the particle of causation (lam al-ta'lil). This is one of hundreds of pieces of evidence for affirming wisdom, and it thus constitutes a refutation of a group of the innovating sects. Who are they?

* A student: The Jahmiyyah and the Mu'tazilah.

* The Shaykh: No, they are not the Mu'tazilah. The Jahmiyyah, because they hold that the acts of Allah are merely by will, not for a reason. The Jahmiyyah do not prefer one thing over another for a wisdom; rather, it is merely by will, and He does nothing except by mere will! There is no doubt that this view is rejected by both transmitted and rational evidence, because one who acts with wisdom is more perfect than one who acts without wisdom, is that not so? They deny wisdom and say: because wisdom is a purpose (gharad), and Allah, glorified and exalted, is free of parts (ab'ad), accidents (a'rad) and purposes (aghrad). Look at the fine expression! Whoever hears this phrasing would say: this is like the phrasing of the Qur'an: free of parts, purposes and accidents. By parts they mean things like the hand, face, eye and the like; by accidents they mean the actions of choice, such as descending, establishing and the like; and by purposes they mean wisdom, because they say: if He acted for a wisdom, He would be deficient without it. This is an inversion of realities. If He acts with wisdom, that is evidence of His perfection, and that He does not do anything merely by will, foolishly.

It also contains evidence for the permissibility of mentioning only some of the benefits, meaning that limiting oneself to some does not count as a deficiency. Here Allah mentioned only two benefits of the rain: the revival of the earth and the watering of cattle and people, although the rain has other benefits, such as purification with it, for example. Purification with it is neither watering nor reviving the earth, and there are other benefits besides. But since the most necessary aspect of the rain is reviving the earth with vegetation so that people and cattle may eat, and likewise watering, and food and drink are among the necessities of life for cattle and for people, Allah, blessed and exalted, limited Himself to mentioning only these two benefits, because they are the two necessary benefits resulting from the descent of rain: the revival of the earth for plants and food, and watering for drink.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿cattle and people﴾ [al-Furqan 49]. Here, "cattle" is not described as many, but "people" is described: ﴿and many people﴾ [al-Furqan 49]. In this expression there are two difficulties:

The first difficulty: why are people described as many while cattle are not described as many?

The second: we know that Allah gives drink with this water to all people, every person drinks from it. So why does He say: ﴿and many people﴾? It seems to imply that some people are not watered by rainwater. So what is the answer to the first difficulty: describing people with multiplicity but not describing cattle?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Does this mean that ﴿many﴾ is an attribute of both together?

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: That is not the apparent meaning, because it would then agree.

* A student: Cattle relative to people are fewer.

* A student: (...).

* A student: Cattle are more numerous than people.

* The Shaykh: Yes. What do you mean?

* The student: I say: cattle are more numerous than people.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: I have, by Allah knows best, that some cattle do not need water, as we hear that some of them do not need water, and some need very little?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: There are many things they count against us, saying: it does not need water, or if it drinks it drinks only very little, perhaps once a year. If this is correct, then it is from wisdom; perhaps this is from wisdom, by not describing it with multiplicity.

But the second difficulty remains, which is more serious than this: ﴿and many people﴾ [al-Furqan 49].

* A student: It is not said regarding the first difficulty.

* The Shaykh: Yes?

* The student: Like cattle, no (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: Unlike the human being (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, but I did not mention only drinking: "that We may give drink to cattle and people."

The second difficulty: that His saying ﴿and many people﴾, although all people drink?

* A student: (...).

* Another student: According to what you said, cattle must be many (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* A student: Describing them with multiplicity is not a restriction of the condition (...). The reality is that people are many.

* The Shaykh: Meaning relative to cattle, meaning?

* The student: No, (...) and you said: the second difficulty is that there are some cattle that do not drink.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: Or they do not benefit from (...). So we say: ﴿many﴾ is not a restriction on drinking for those people who drink, but only a statement of the reality that these people who drink are many, and they all drink, so it is for multiplicity.

* The Shaykh: If I say, for example: "I have many men," would it be understood from that that there are other men who did not attend (...)?

* A student: Yes.

* A student: Allah, glorified and exalted, (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, and for this reason He says: plural of "insan" (human), and its origin...

* A student: (...) that ﴿many﴾ be an attribute of the cattle and the people?

* The Shaykh: Yes?

* The student: Is there anything preventing the attribute from being (...)?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, we said: agreement. But our brother raised an objection, saying: even cattle has a plural, and ﴿many﴾ applies equally to the singular and the plural.

* A student: Perhaps it indicates (...).

* The Shaykh: No, if we say that ﴿many﴾ is an attribute of people and of cattle, the difficulty disappears.

The second difficulty: it is possible to say, as Muhammad said, that Allah, glorified and exalted, is showing that they are many people, and it does not follow from this that some of them do not drink, and that this multiplicity is an encompassing multiplicity, just as you say: "The troops are many," or "The emir has a great army," the phrase "a great army" includes all the soldiers and describes them as many. ("People" [unasi] includes all humans and describes them as many.)

* A student: If he said "most" (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, saying "most" is correct, it is clear.

In any case, then, what comes to mind first as the difficulty, how can it be dispensed with? By making ﴿many﴾ an attribute of both: "many cattle" and "many people." It is not like Allah's saying: ﴿And from both of them He spread forth many men and women﴾ [al-Nisa 1], because ﴿many men﴾ cannot be an attribute of both, since it precedes "women"; but here it can be said that it is an attribute of both the conjoined and the conjoined-to.

As for ﴿many﴾, it is to state the reality and not to exclude the rest. Its parallel in an example is that you say, for instance: "The emir has many troops," or "A large army went out against the enemy," so it is an attribute describing it with multiplicity. That is: ﴿people﴾ are not few, this is the meaning; ﴿cattle﴾ are not few, ﴿people﴾ are not few, rather they are many, and this serves as an explanation of the comprehensiveness of the benefit to creation, both speaking and beast, from this water: ﴿many cattle﴾ and ﴿many people﴾.

Now, we have all arrived at the conclusion that ﴿many﴾ is an attribute of both cattle and people. Regarding the multiplicity of cattle, do we say it is multiplicity of kinds and types, or multiplicity of individuals, or both?

* A student: Both.

* The Shaykh: And regarding people, multiplicity of individuals, because people are one kind.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: how many of the benefits we have passed over from these verses? Seven benefits.

* A student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: Apparently, and Allah knows best, for multiplicity, because it is more: more in kinds and in individuals.

* The student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: Allah knows best. It is not because of the... the discussion on its benefit from the rain. Yes, this is regarding cattle, because it is more. It may be said: the reviving of the earth is for the benefit of human beings, and the watering of cattle is for the benefit of human beings, and the watering of human beings is for their own benefit; so it mentions first what is indirect benefit to the human being, then delays the direct benefit, by way of proceeding from the farther to the farther in benefits, the farther then the farther; because cattle are for the benefit of human beings, and the earth's revival is for the benefit of human beings, and the reviving of cattle is more directly and closely connected to human beings than the reviving of the earth; because how many lands drink the rain and the human being does not reach them and benefit from them, unlike cattle.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 47–49 (part 1 of 2):

Then he said: (﴿And it is He who made the night a garment for you﴾, covering like a garment, ﴿and sleep a rest﴾, a rest for the bodies by cutting off works, ﴿and made the day a resurrection﴾ [al-Furqan 47], spread out, in which one seeks sustenance and other things).

This too is among the blessings that no one can bring about except Allah.

﴿And it is He who made for you﴾: the lam here indicates purpose, meaning: for your sake, ﴿He made the night a garment﴾. The meaning of ﴿a garment﴾ is (covering like a garment), because of its darkness.

For this reason a person may go out at night in clothes he cannot wear in the daytime; he may go out at night to attend to his needs, which he cannot do in the daytime, because the night conceals, so it is a garment.

Is it a garment for the earth or a garment for us? For all of it, because it clothes the earth and clothes the human being in reality: it covers the earth and it also covers the human being.

As for His saying ﴿and sleep a rest﴾ [al-Furqan 47]: sabat means cutting off. The author explained it as rest, and this is explaining a thing by its consequence. Otherwise, it is a cutting off of fatigue; it cuts off tiredness. In this is the great benefit that it cuts off the fatigue that came before. It is not as the author said, (by cutting off works), because a person may cut off his works while awake, but sleep cuts off fatigue, as is observed. A person becomes tired and then sleeps; when he sleeps his tiredness is undone. So in reality it is a cutting off of past fatigue and a renewal of energy for the future.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, his intention is that when a person sleeps he does not work.
* Student: You mean he does not work for Allah, the Exalted, or for anything else?
* Shaykh: For anything else. When he sleeps he does not work; this is the aspect of its being sabat. But we say: it is not so; it is not a cutting off of work, rather it is a cutting off of the fatigue of the body; therefore the body gains rest. As for the mere cutting off of works, this may occur together with wakefulness and alertness.

﴿And made the day a resurrection﴾ [al-Furqan 47]: meaning, a place of resurrection. For this the author said, (spread out in it); meaning that the day is the place of resurrection for seeking sustenance and other works, and this is from the blessing of Allah, the Exalted.

What we have today, namely that the night is not a garment, does not counter this, because that is an incidental matter caused by the artificial lights that man has made. If these lights were gone, darkness would return to the earth. Moreover, this light and illumination that prevents the night from being a garment is not general in reality; rather it is a relative matter. Furthermore, it is weak and does not include shadow; the shadow that blocks the light of this candle, for example, is black, ﴿a garment﴾.

Likewise, ﴿and made the day a resurrection﴾ is not countered by some incidental cases such as guards, for example: guards sleep in the day and work at night. But these are rare matters, and the rare does not overturn the rules; the rules cannot be (...) by rare matters. The discussion is about the general.

This too is from the blessing of Allah, the Exalted. Could anyone, if Allah had not made the night, bring the night? No one can; even if all creation, from first to last, with all their crafts, gathered together, they could not bring half a night or an hour of night.

Likewise sleep: can anyone make another person sleep? Never, no one can. And these sleeping pills do not refute us, because a person who gives sleeping pills is like one who says: "I can make a person sleep by giving him doses of sleep." We say: this is like the one who said to Abraham: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ [al-Baqarah 258]. Indeed, the one who gives doses of sleep is not the one who makes sleep; he only does the cause by which sleep occurs. Consider: if Allah had made this body unable to sleep, would these doses be able to make it sleep? No. So sleep is something no one can ever bring to the human body. Even if it were brought, for example, a person may take it and it is not a complete cutting off, and does not cut off fatigue. Therefore Allah, the Exalted, bestowed it upon His servants as a favor, and it is a matter no one can do.

Likewise He made the day a resurrection. Who can remove this garment, the garment of the night, until the dawn comes and people spread out to their affairs? The answer: no one can except Allah, mighty and majestic. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, bestowed His favor upon His servants in these three matters: sleep, night, and day.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: May Allah protect us from this, I seek refuge in Allah.
* Student: This means it is evidence that (...), whatever he does with it.
* Shaykh: Known, there is no doubt; this is a known matter.

If someone says: Allah, the Exalted, made the night a garment, made the day a resurrection, and made sleep a sabat; when does sleep occur, at night or in the day?
* Student: At night.
* Shaykh: Originally at night, but it may also be in the day. A person may become tired during the day and sleep and then rest, like the midday rest for example. Therefore no one should say that Allah, the Exalted, mentioned two blessings for the night and one blessing for the day. Rather we say: Allah mentioned in the night one blessing, which is that it is a ﴿garment﴾, and in the day one blessing, which is that it is a ﴿resurrection﴾, and He made sleep in general a blessing, which is that it is a sabat, meaning it cuts off fatigue. And Allah knows best.
* Student: Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Does sleep of every kind cut off fatigue, or only some kinds?
* Shaykh: Natural sleep, which is part of the human constitution. As for sleep that occurs because of illness, since a person may fall ill and sleep much with it, the apparent meaning is that it does not fall under the verse.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: The main point is the apparent; the apparent is that it is a relative matter, and some people find great relief in it.
* Student: Or, for example, after the afternoon (...).
* Shaykh: If I did not sleep a little now before (...), I might not be able to work; I would become sleepy again. We have not tested this previously.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: You say it actually tires a person more when his stomach is full. If he sleeps with a full stomach, it may be so; but the discussion is about generality (...), yes?
* Student: O Shaykh, is sleeping at certain times disliked?
* Shaykh: I do not know anything about this.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is not disliked. "Indeed the Messenger of Allah disliked sleeping before the night prayer" [Footnote: Recorded by al-Bukhari (599) and Muslim (647/236), and the wording is his, from Abu Barzah al-Aslami, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not mind delaying the night prayer until midnight, and he disliked sleeping before it and talking after it.], this is disliked, before the night prayer for a legal reason, not for a bodily reason. As for afternoon sleep, they say the words of the poet:
Indeed, sleeping in the forenoon brings the youth ∗∗∗ corruption, and sleeping in the afternoon brings madness.
This is not correct. Many people now sleep in the afternoon constantly, and they were not afflicted with madness, nor were they called madmen.
* Student: The scholars said that it (...).
* Shaykh: It distracts from thought. A person may make up for it; sometimes he cannot sleep in the middle of the day, but he cannot remain until night; he must sleep (...).
* Student: O Shaykh, (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, perhaps (...).
Yes?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: I do not think this; this is an understanding of the hadith (...), and the common people say: ..
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Not (...), and the common people then say: "less," for the devils do not say less; they delete the yā' (...). Yes?
(...)
(nashūr like rasūl, and the last bashīr): this has several readings. First, the wind has two readings: are both canonical (sab'iyyah), or is one of them irregular (shādhdh)?
* Student: Both canonical.
* Shaykh: What is the proof?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, the proof is that if one says "and in a reading," it is canonical; if one says "and it was read," it is irregular. Yes.
﴿al-riyāḥ﴾ and ﴿al-rīḥ﴾ [al-Furqan 48] have two readings: ﴿al-riyāḥ﴾ and ﴿al-rīḥ﴾. From this we know that what is well known in their saying, that "rīḥ" is only in punishment and "riyāḥ" is in mercy, is not absolute, and that the singular "rīḥ" may be used for a wind of mercy, but it has a context. Here He said: ﴿before His mercy﴾ [al-Furqan 48], so it is known that it is a wind of mercy. Likewise His Exalted saying: ﴿until when you are in the ship and they sail with them by a wind﴾ and what follows? ﴿good﴾ [Yunus 22]. This is a wind of mercy, but it was described. But when unqualified, the wind is usually for punishment.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, like this hadith.

And His saying: ﴿bushran﴾ [al-Furqan 48] has several readings. First: ﴿nushuran﴾ with a damma on the nūn and the shīn, and the meaning of ﴿nushuran﴾, the author says: (scattered); meaning that they sometimes blow from the south, sometimes from the north, sometimes from the west, and sometimes from the east, and by this scattering the clouds form, then the rain.

And His saying: (and in a reading with the shīn sukūn for lightness). How?
* Student: ﴿nushran﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿nushran﴾. His saying "for lightness" means that the meaning is not changed by it; it is only made sukūn for lightness.
(And in another with its sukūn and a fatha on the nūn as a verbal noun).
* Student: ﴿nashran﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿nashran﴾; then the meaning changes. ﴿nushuran﴾ and ﴿nushran﴾ have the same meaning, without difference, because the sukūn is for lightness. But ﴿nashran﴾ means He spreads them out spreading, this is different, being a verbal noun.
(And in another with its sukūn and a ḍamma on the bā' instead of the nūn), that is, the sukūn of the shīn and a ḍamma on the unpointed bā' in place of the nūn, and it is: ﴿bushran﴾, and this is the well-known reading. The meaning of ﴿bushran﴾ on this reading is: i.e., bearers of good news; meaning: they give good news, and they are not a verbal noun, and Allah gives good news by them; they themselves are ﴿bushran﴾. Yes?
* Student: (...) (and in another with its sukūn and a ḍamma on the unpointed bā' in place of the nūn) did he not mention (...)?
* Shaykh: (with its sukūn) I think it is one.
* Student: And the unpointed bā' (...).
* Shaykh: The unpointed bā', yes, ﴿bushran﴾, this is it.
The singular says: (the singular of the first is nushūr). And what is the first? ﴿nushuran﴾.
(like rasūl and rusul), rasūl and rusul, rasūl and rusul (with sukūn), this is the singular of the first when it is not a verbal noun, which is ﴿nashran﴾; if it is a verbal noun, then it is a singular, not a plural.
And the last, ﴿bushran﴾, he says: (the last's singular is bashīr).
The readings have become, I think, four: ﴿nushuran﴾, ﴿nushran﴾, ﴿nashran﴾, and ﴿bushran﴾: four readings for this word.

The benefit of the differences in readings, that is, this is from the inimitability of the Qur'an: that from each reading a meaning is derived, and on this basis it encompasses both being good news and being scattered spreading before the rain.

And His saying: ﴿before His mercy﴾ [al-Furqan 48]: the meant mercy here is the rain or its effects, and this is created mercy, because mercy attributed to Allah, the Exalted, is divided into two kinds: mercy that is His attribute, which is uncreated, and mercy that is an effect of the attribute, which is created. So His saying to Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whomever I will" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850) and Muslim (2846/34) from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him], this is created, is it not? Created. And His saying: ﴿My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [al-A'raf 156] is the attribute, which is not created. So the mercy attributed to Allah is divided into two kinds: created, and called mercy because it is an effect of mercy; and uncreated, which is His attribute.

And what is with us now: ﴿bushran before His mercy﴾ [al-Furqan 48], is it the created or the uncreated?
* Student: Both.
* Shaykh: How both?
* Student: The generality of Allah's mercy.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, it is possible that the meaning of ﴿before His mercy﴾ is: when He wishes to show mercy; if He wishes to show mercy, then it is of the uncreated. And it is possible that ﴿before His mercy﴾ means before the rain itself, and then mercy here is created, because its application to rain requires that.

The author explained it as the created mercy, because he said: (in front of the rain).

﴿And We sent down﴾ [al-Furqan 48].
It is well known that what brings the rain by Allah's permission is the southern winds; therefore our forefathers and grandfathers used to say: when the southern wind blows (...), they said: now the rain comes and there is no need to water the crops, because it seemed to them a customary thing.

﴿And We sent down from the sky water, pure﴾ [al-Furqan 48]: ﴿from the sky﴾ means from the clouds, because every thing above you is sky, and there is no doubt that rain descends only from clouds, so the meaning of ﴿the sky﴾ here is height.

And His saying: ﴿water, pure﴾ means the rain. And "ṭahūr" with a fatḥa on the ṭā' is what one purifies with, or what purification is achieved by; as for "ṭuhūr" by its action, it is the act of purifying, i.e., purification.

Here He says: ﴿And We sent down﴾, and before it: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds﴾ [al-Furqan 48]. In this there is what is called in rhetoric al-iltifāt (shift of address), and its benefit, as we have often seen, is alerting the addressee, because a change of style necessitates attention.
