Good. As for His saying: ﴿And your Lord is ever Powerful﴾ [al-Furqan 54], the author says: (capable of whatever He wills).

We discuss with the author, may God have mercy on him, his interpretation of ﴿qadiran﴾ as (qadir, capable), and his restricting the unrestricted with (whatever He wills).

As for interpreting ﴿qadiran﴾ as (qadir), this is considered a deficiency in the interpretation, because ﴿qadiran﴾ is either a resembling adjective (sifah mushabbahah) or an intensive form (sigha mubalaghah). As for (qadir), it is a bare active participle, which does not express what the resembling adjective expresses, nor what the intensive form expresses. This is a kind of shortcoming in the interpretation of the Qur'an.

Second: The Qur'an states ﴿And your Lord is ever Powerful﴾ without restriction, and here he restricted it with his saying (whatever He wills). We know that for some people this restriction indicates an innovation they committed, because the Qadariyyah say that God, Glorified and Exalted, is only capable of what He wills, and that He does not will the actions of the servants, and on this basis He would not be capable of them. There is no doubt that this view is refuted by the texts and by reason. God is the One who guides and misguides, and the meaning of guidance and misguidance is only that He, Glorified and Exalted, does what He wills, even regarding the actions of the servant. Therefore we see that restricting power by will is not fitting and not appropriate, for the following reasons:

First: God, Glorified and Exalted, applied this attribute to Himself without restriction, and it is not appropriate for us to restrict what God has applied, because the attributes of God are tawqifiyyah (based on revelation), in which one stops at what has been transmitted.

The second thing: It contradicts the method of the Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, and his Companions, indeed the method of all the messengers, because they say: ﴿Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us. Indeed You are over all things competent﴾ [al-Tahrim 8]. They do not say: "Indeed You are competent over what You will." ﴿Indeed You are over all things competent.﴾

The third thing: It gives the impression that power relates only to what He wills, and on this basis what He does not will would not be within God's ability. This meaning is false. He is capable of what He wills and of what He does not will, but what He wills comes to be and what He does not will does not come to be. So He is capable of both, not only of what He wills.

For these three reasons we see that using this expression is not appropriate, and that it is something the servant should be guided away from and told: do not say this, do not restrict what God has applied to Himself.

A student: Is it "guided" or "not appropriate" (...)?

The Shaykh: No, its origin is on the basis that the one who says it does not intend this meaning. We say: it is guided away from, and it is said: this is not appropriate.

And if it is asked: what is the reconciliation, or what is the answer to the saying of God, blessed and exalted: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and what He has dispersed therein of creatures; and He, over their gathering when He wills, is competent﴾ [al-Shura 29]. Here He says: ﴿over their gathering when He wills, is competent﴾, and we prohibit linking power to will?

A student: ("idha" meaning "whenever"): whenever God, Glorified and Exalted, wills, it is a matter of time, meaning.

The Shaykh: There is no contradiction: whenever He wills He is competent. And whenever He does not will?

The student: He is competent too, but the intended meaning is time, meaning that God is competent over gathering them when He wills, meaning that when the time comes at which God has willed to gather them, He gathers them (...).

The Shaykh: Yes, not (...).

The answer is that this restricts the will to the gathering. That is, the gathering is an act, and this act is denied by the disbelievers who deny the Resurrection. So God, Mighty and Majestic, says: the thing preventing that is not inability, but the absence of will. So when He wills to gather them, He gathers them, contrary to whom? To those who deny that, who say that it is impossible for Him to gather them. So here the restriction is on the act, the restriction of the will returns to the act, not to the power. He is capable of gathering them at all times, but since He, Glorified and Exalted, does not wish to gather them except at a specific time: ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the latter (49) will surely be gathered for the appointed time of a known Day﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 49–50], appointed, ﴿and We do not delay it except for a term﴾, look, ﴿counted﴾ [Hud 104]. All the worldly life is a counted term, which is evidence of its brevity however long it lasts.

So we say: this returns to the gathering, which is an act. It is as if God says: it is... 
...what does not benefit them if they worship Him, nor harm them if they disobey Him. God, the Exalted, said in Surat al-Ahqaf: ﴿And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah those who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Ahqaf 5]. That is, if he keeps calling this idol until the Day of Resurrection, it will not respond to him. Is there anyone more astray than this? There is no one more astray than this at all: a person tries to have this idol benefit or harm him, and even if he keeps calling it until the Day of Resurrection, it does not respond to him. This is among the most extreme forms of misguidance. Yes indeed.

(﴿And the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord﴾ [al-Furqan 55]: assisting Satan by his obedience), meaning: by obedience to Satan.

The disbeliever is a helper against his Lord, an assistant against God, Glorified and Exalted, not for Him, an assistant against Him, not for Him. That is, a warrior against God. Whenever the disbeliever finds an enemy of God, he helps him against his Lord. This is just as the author said, that he assists Satan in disobeying God, because the human being (...) an assistant to Satan in his rebellion against God, Glorified and Exalted.

It also includes whoever has this description from among non-disbelievers: everyone who assists in falsehood is an assistant against God, is he not? Every person who assists someone in falsehood is a helper against his Lord, because God, Exalted, is the Truth and He wills the truth. So if you help the owner of falsehood against the owner of truth, you are an assistant against God. Is that so or not?

The Shaykh: Because what is the meaning of "ẓahīr"? So the disbeliever always helps against God, and whoever assists falsehood against truth is an assistant against God, meaning he is an assistant of falsehood against truth, because God is the Truth and He loves the truth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verses 50–55 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, exalted is He, said: (﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them﴾, i.e., the water, ﴿that they may remember﴾. The original is "yatadhakkaru" (they may remember), and the "ta'" was assimilated into the "dhal", so it became "liyadhdhakkaru".) ﴿That they may remember﴾. (And in another reading: ﴿liyadhkuru﴾ with the "dhal" unvocalized and the "kaf" vocalized, meaning: the blessing of Allah in it.) ﴿But most of the people refused except denial﴾ [al-Furqan 50], denying the blessing, as they said: "We were given rain by such-and-such a star-rising (nawʾ)."

﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them﴾. What does this mean? "Sarraftu al-shay'" means I changed the thing and turned it in its direction. That is, Allah, exalted is He, changed this rain in relation to the people and distributed it among them, between the one who has little and the one who has much. Some of them have abundant rain and some have little. This is in regard to "bayniyya" (among them).

Likewise, Allah, exalted is He, distributes it among them in relation to each individual: sometimes the rain is abundant in one year and scant in another.

As for the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿that they may remember﴾, the author (Ibn Kathir / the author of the text) made the remembrance here only the remembrance of the blessing, but the more correct view is that it is more general. ﴿That they may remember﴾ the blessing of Allah when it descends upon them, and ﴿that they may remember﴾, i.e., may take admonition, when it does not descend.

Likewise, ﴿that they may remember﴾ in it the power of Allah, since He turns it from one place to another.

The main point is that the distribution of this rain in one place and not another, or in one year and not another, is undoubtedly a cause for a person's remembrance: either remembrance of the blessing when it falls, or remembrance of the affliction and of one's sins when it is withheld, or remembrance of the power of Allah when he knows that it is abundant in one place and scarce in another.

As for His saying: ﴿But most of the people refused except denial﴾ [al-Furqan 50], it means that most people refused to remember, and it only increased them in disbelief.

* Student: The second reading (...)?
* Shaykh: Like ﴿liyadhdhakkaru﴾: they remember the blessing of Allah when it descends, and they remember what they are upon of sins and wrongdoings when it is withheld.

As for His saying: ﴿But most of the people refused﴾, "most of the people" means: the minority were grateful, remembered, and took admonition, but most people refused except to disbelieve.

The author mentioned only one example of disbelief, which is his saying: "We were given rain by such-and-such a star-rising." What the author gave as an example can be supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani (may Allah be pleased with him), when he led them in prayer after a rainfall that had occurred during the night at al-Hudaybiyyah. He (ﷺ) said: "Do you know what your Lord said?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "He said: 'In the morning, some of My servants became believers in Me and some disbelievers. As for the one who said: "We were given rain by the grace of Allah and His mercy," he is a believer in Me and a disbeliever in the star. As for the one who said: "We were given rain by such-and-such a star-rising," he is a disbeliever in Me and a believer in the star.'"[1] This is disbelief. And how is it disbelief? Because he attributed the rain to something that is not a cause, and made this from the bounty of that star-rising, whereas the bounty belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is forbidden and is disbelief, as the hadith states.

But if a person says: "We were given rain during such-and-such a star-rising (fi nawʾ kadha)," is that permissible or not?
* Student: Yes, it is permissible.
* Shaykh: It is permissible with "fi" because it indicates time (zarfiyya); but with "bi" (by) it is not permissible because it indicates causation (sababiyya). However, among the common people, among our people here in Najd, they use "ba'" (bi) to mean "fi" (in). They say: "We were given rain (...)" and similar things. Would this be disbelief?
* Student: No.
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Or do we say that "ba'" often comes to indicate time, and they intend it that way, so there is no harm in it?
* Student: According to what is intended.
* Shaykh: According to the intention, yes.

Among the forms of disbelief regarding this rain, which the author did not mention, is that a person makes it a cause of insolence and exultation, as happens with some people when the rains fall and abundance (...) becomes a cause of their insolence, exultation, and transgression. This is one of its causes.

Also among the causes of disbelief is that when the rain is withheld, its withholding becomes a cause for a person's despair of Allah's mercy. Despair of Allah's mercy is one of the major sins; it is no small matter. It is not permissible for a person to despair of Allah's mercy, nor to feel secure from Allah's plan, neither this nor that.

As for the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿But most of the people refused﴾ [al-Furqan 50]: this is evidence that people are divided into two categories: disbeliever and believer. And so it is, not only regarding this blessing but regarding all blessings. Some people believe in them, and some people disbelieve in Allah, exalted is He, and in this blessing.

From this verse, there are the following benefits:
First: It is evidence of the perfection of Allah's power, from His saying: ﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them﴾ [al-Furqan 50].
Second: It is evidence of the affirmation of Allah's wisdom, from His saying: ﴿that they may remember﴾ [al-Furqan 50], the "lam" of causation (lam al-ta'lil).
Third: It is evidence that some people reach the extreme of disbelief, since if Allah shows them a sign so that they may remember by it, and they only increase in disbelief, this is, may Allah protect us, the utmost degree of disbelief. For when signs do not come to a person he may be excused for his disbelief, but when signs come and he does not benefit, it becomes more severe.

In this verse there is also evidence for the use of emphatic particles where emphasis is appropriate. From where do we derive it?
* Student: From the oath.
* Shaykh: Yes, from the oath, from His saying: ﴿And We have certainly﴾ [al-Furqan 50]; because this expression, as we have passed over many times, is considered emphasized by three emphatics: the "lam", "qad", and the oath. And Allah knows best.

* Shaykh: Yes indeed, clear, well done. Yes, there is in it evidence refuting the doctrine of the Jabriyya (determinists); from His saying: ﴿But most of the people refused except denial﴾ [al-Furqan 50], making this a matter of their choice: they refused except to disbelieve.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Good. First, the saying of some of the early generations (al-salaf) is not itself evidence; the saying of some of the salaf is not evidence unless evidence for it is found. Is there in the verse we just read anything that supports his saying?
* Student: I do not know.
* Shaykh: No, read.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, correct. Allah mentioned that He sent it down to give life thereby to a dead land (﴿that We may give life thereby to a dead land﴾ [al-Furqan 49]). This causal statement implies that no drop falls from the sky without life coming to the earth through it; otherwise the cause would be defeated. But it is said: this is a cause, and causes may be unfulfilled due to the presence of obstacles; they may not take effect because of obstacles. The sins of the children of Adam are among the obstacles to the earth's revival even when rain falls. And this will be more severe, more painful, and more effective in remembrance when rain falls and the earth does not grow. Sometimes abundant rains come and you find no life in the earth, and sometimes little rain comes and the earth comes alive with good life. The third view is what the Ustadh mentioned: if the verse can bear it, when we take it that there is a barrier between them, meaning there is a separating thing that we do not know. Also among the perfection of God's power, Glorified and Exalted, is that He created a human being from water and divided him into two kinds. What are they?

A student: Lineage (nasab) and marriage by alliance (sihr).

The Shaykh: Lineage and marriage by alliance (sihr).

The student: Lineage (...).

The Shaykh: In marriage, yes. We said that these are the causes of connection between people: either a connection by birth, which is lineage, or by marriage, which is affinity (musahara).

Good. As for His saying: ﴿And your Lord is ever Powerful﴾ [al-Furqan 54], the author says: (capable of whatever He wills).

We discuss with the author, may God have mercy on him, his interpretation of ﴿qadiran﴾ as (qadir, capable), and his restricting the unrestricted with (whatever He wills).

As for interpreting ﴿qadiran﴾ as (qadir), this is considered a deficiency in the interpretation, because ﴿qadiran﴾ is either a resembling adjective (sifah mushabbahah) or an intensive form (sigha mubalaghah). As for (qadir), it is a bare active participle, which does not express what the resembling adjective expresses, nor what the intensive form expresses. This is a kind of shortcoming in the interpretation of the Qur'an.

Second: The Qur'an states ﴿And your Lord is ever Powerful﴾ without restriction, and here he restricted it with his saying (whatever He wills). We know that for some people this restriction indicates an innovation they committed, because the Qadariyyah say that God, Glorified and Exalted, is only capable of what He wills, and that He does not will the actions of the servants, and on this basis He would not be capable of them. There is no doubt that this view is refuted by the texts and by reason. God is the One who guides and misguides, and the meaning of guidance and misguidance is only that He, Glorified and Exalted, does what He wills, even regarding the actions of the servant. Therefore we see that restricting power by will is not fitting and not appropriate, for the following reasons:

First: God, Glorified and Exalted, applied this attribute to Himself without restriction, and it is not appropriate for us to restrict what God has applied, because the attributes of God are tawqifiyyah (based on revelation), in which one stops at what has been transmitted.

The second thing: It contradicts the method of the Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, and his Companions, indeed the method of all the messengers, because they say: ﴿Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us. Indeed You are over all things competent﴾ [al-Tahrim 8]. They do not say: "Indeed You are competent over what You will." ﴿Indeed You are over all things competent.﴾

The third thing: It gives the impression that power relates only to what He wills, and on this basis what He does not will would not be within God's ability. This meaning is false. He is capable of what He wills and of what He does not will, but what He wills comes to be and what He does not will does not come to be. So He is capable of both, not only of what He wills.

For these three reasons we see that using this expression is not appropriate, and that it is something the servant should be guided away from and told: do not say this, do not restrict what God has applied to Himself.

A student: Is it "guided" or "not appropriate" (...)?

The Shaykh: No, its origin is on the basis that the one who says it does not intend this meaning. We say: it is guided away from, and it is said: this is not appropriate.

And if it is asked: what is the reconciliation, or what is the answer to the saying of God, blessed and exalted: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and what He has dispersed therein of creatures; and He, over their gathering when He wills, is competent﴾ [al-Shura 29]. Here He says: ﴿over their gathering when He wills, is competent﴾, and we prohibit linking power to will?

A student: ("idha" meaning "whenever"): whenever God, Glorified and Exalted, wills, it is a matter of time, meaning.

The Shaykh: There is no contradiction: whenever He wills He is competent. And whenever He does not will?

The student: He is competent too, but the intended meaning is time, meaning that God is competent over gathering them when He wills, meaning that when the time comes at which God has willed to gather them, He gathers them (...).

The Shaykh: Yes, not (...).

The answer is that this restricts the will to the gathering. That is, the gathering is an act, and this act is denied by the disbelievers who deny the Resurrection. So God, Mighty and Majestic, says: the thing preventing that is not inability, but the absence of will. So when He wills to gather them, He gathers them, contrary to whom? To those who deny that, who say that it is impossible for Him to gather them. So here the restriction is on the act, the restriction of the will returns to the act, not to the power. He is capable of gathering them at all times, but since He, Glorified and Exalted, does not wish to gather them except at a specific time: ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the latter (49) will surely be gathered for the appointed time of a known Day﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 49–50], appointed, ﴿and We do not delay it except for a term﴾, look, ﴿counted﴾ [Hud 104]. All the worldly life is a counted term, which is evidence of its brevity however long it lasts.

So we say: this returns to the gathering, which is an act. It is as if God says: it is... 
...what does not benefit them if they worship Him, nor harm them if they disobey Him. God, the Exalted, said in Surat al-Ahqaf: ﴿And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah those who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Ahqaf 5]. That is, if he keeps calling this idol until the Day of Resurrection, it will not respond to him. Is there anyone more astray than this? There is no one more astray than this at all: a person tries to have this idol benefit or harm him, and even if he keeps calling it until the Day of Resurrection, it does not respond to him. This is among the most extreme forms of misguidance. Yes indeed.

(﴿And the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord﴾ [al-Furqan 55]: assisting Satan by his obedience), meaning: by obedience to Satan.

The disbeliever is a helper against his Lord, an assistant against God, Glorified and Exalted, not for Him, an assistant against Him, not for Him. That is, a warrior against God. Whenever the disbeliever finds an enemy of God, he helps him against his Lord. This is just as the author said, that he assists Satan in disobeying God, because the human being (...) an assistant to Satan in his rebellion against God, Glorified and Exalted.

It also includes whoever has this description from among non-disbelievers: everyone who assists in falsehood is an assistant against God, is he not? Every person who assists someone in falsehood is a helper against his Lord, because God, Exalted, is the Truth and He wills the truth. So if you help the owner of falsehood against the owner of truth, you are an assistant against God. Is that so or not?

A student: Yes.

The Shaykh: Because what is the meaning of "ẓahīr"? The ẓahīr is the helper, as God, Exalted, said: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if they were to each other assistants﴾ [al-Isra' 88]. So the disbeliever always helps against God, and whoever assists falsehood against truth is an assistant against God, meaning he is an assistant of falsehood against truth, because God is the Truth and He loves the truth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verses 50–55 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, exalted is He, said: (﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them﴾, i.e., the water, ﴿that they may remember﴾. The original is "yatadhakkaru" (they may remember), and the "ta'" was assimilated into the "dhal", so it became "liyadhdhakkaru".) ﴿That they may remember﴾. (And in another reading: ﴿liyadhkuru﴾ with the "dhal" unvocalized and the "kaf" vocalized, meaning: the blessing of Allah in it.) ﴿But most of the people refused except denial﴾ [al-Furqan 50], denying the blessing, as they said: "We were given rain by such-and-such a star-rising (nawʾ)."

﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them﴾. What does this mean? "Sarraftu al-shay'" means I changed the thing and turned it in its direction. That is, Allah, exalted is He, changed this rain in relation to the people and distributed it among them, between the one who has little and the one who has much. Some of them have abundant rain and some have little. This is in regard to "bayniyya" (among them).

Likewise, Allah, exalted is He, distributes it among them in relation to each individual: sometimes the rain is abundant in one year and scant in another.

As for the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿that they may remember﴾, the author (Ibn Kathir / the author of the text) made the remembrance here only the remembrance of the blessing, but the more correct view is that it is more general. ﴿That they may remember﴾ the blessing of Allah when it descends upon them, and ﴿that they may remember﴾, i.e., may take admonition, when it does not descend.

Likewise, ﴿that they may remember﴾ in it the power of Allah, since He turns it from one place to another.

The main point is that the distribution of this rain in one place and not another, or in one year and not another, is undoubtedly a cause for a person's remembrance: either remembrance of the blessing when it falls, or remembrance of the affliction and of one's sins when it is withheld, or remembrance of the power of Allah when he knows that it is abundant in one place and scarce in another.

As for His saying: ﴿But most of the people refused except denial﴾ [al-Furqan 50], it means that most people refused to remember, and it only increased them in disbelief.

* Student: The second reading (...)?
* Shaykh: Like ﴿liyadhdhakkaru﴾: they remember the blessing of Allah when it descends, and they remember what they are upon of sins and wrongdoings when it is withheld.

As for His saying: ﴿But most of the people refused﴾, "most of the people" means: the minority were grateful, remembered, and took admonition, but most people refused except to disbelieve.

The author mentioned only one example of disbelief, which is his saying: "We were given rain by such-and-such a star-rising." What the author gave as an example can be supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani (may Allah be pleased with him), when he led them in prayer after a rainfall that had occurred during the night at al-Hudaybiyyah. He (ﷺ) said: "Do you know what your Lord said?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "He said: 'In the morning, some of My servants became believers in Me and some disbelievers. As for the one who said: "We were given rain by the grace of Allah and His mercy," he is a believer in Me and a disbeliever in the star. As for the one who said: "We were given rain by such-and-such a star-rising," he is a disbeliever in Me and a believer in the star.'"[1] This is disbelief. And how is it disbelief? Because he attributed the rain to something that is not a cause, and made this from the bounty of that star-rising, whereas the bounty belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is forbidden and is disbelief, as the hadith states.

But if a person says: "We were given rain during such-and-such a star-rising (fi nawʾ kadha)," is that permissible or not?
* Student: Yes, it is permissible.
* Shaykh: It is permissible with "fi" because it indicates time (zarfiyya); but with "bi" (by) it is not permissible because it indicates causation (sababiyya). However, among the common people, among our people here in Najd, they use "ba'" (bi) to mean "fi" (in). They say: "We were given rain (...)" and similar things. Would this be disbelief?
* Student: No.
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Or do we say that "ba'" often comes to indicate time, and they intend it that way, so there is no harm in it?
* Student: According to what is intended.
* Shaykh: According to the intention, yes.

Among the forms of disbelief regarding this rain, which the author did not mention, is that a person makes it a cause of insolence and exultation, as happens with some people when the rains fall and abundance (...) becomes a cause of their insolence, exultation, and transgression. This is one of its causes.

Also among the causes of disbelief is that when the rain is withheld, its withholding becomes a cause for a person's despair of Allah's mercy. Despair of Allah's mercy is one of the major sins; it is no small matter. It is not permissible for a person to despair of Allah's mercy, nor to feel secure from Allah's plan, neither this nor that.

As for the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿But most of the people refused﴾ [al-Furqan 50]: this is evidence that people are divided into two categories: disbeliever and believer. And so it is, not only regarding this blessing but regarding all blessings. Some people believe in them, and some people disbelieve in Allah, exalted is He, and in this blessing.

From this verse, there are the following benefits:
First: It is evidence of the perfection of Allah's power, from His saying: ﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them﴾ [al-Furqan 50].
Second: It is evidence of the affirmation of Allah's wisdom, from His saying: ﴿that they may remember﴾ [al-Furqan 50], the "lam" of causation (lam al-ta'lil).
Third: It is evidence that some people reach the extreme of disbelief, since if Allah shows them a sign so that they may remember by it, and they only increase in disbelief, this is, may Allah protect us, the utmost degree of disbelief. For when signs do not come to a person he may be excused for his disbelief, but when signs come and he does not benefit, it becomes more severe.

In this verse there is also evidence for the use of emphatic particles where emphasis is appropriate. From where do we derive it?
* Student: From the oath.
* Shaykh: Yes, from the oath, from His saying: ﴿And We have certainly﴾ [al-Furqan 50]; because this expression, as we have passed over many times, is considered emphasized by three emphatics: the "lam", "qad", and the oath. And Allah knows best.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, clear, well done. Yes, there is in it evidence refuting the doctrine of the Jabriyya (determinists); from His saying: ﴿But most of the people refused except denial﴾ [al-Furqan 50], making this a matter of their choice: they refused except to disbelieve.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Good. First, the saying of some of the early generations (al-salaf) is not itself evidence; the saying of some of the salaf is not evidence unless evidence for it is found. Is there in the verse we just read anything that supports his saying?
* Student: I do not know.
* Shaykh: No, read.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, correct. Allah mentioned that He sent it down to give life thereby to a dead land (﴿that We may give life thereby to a dead land﴾ [al-Furqan 49]). This causal statement implies that no drop falls from the sky without life coming to the earth through it; otherwise the cause would be defeated. But it is said: this is a cause, and causes may be unfulfilled due to the presence of obstacles; they may not take effect because of obstacles. The sins of the children of Adam are among the obstacles to the earth's revival even when rain falls. And this will be more severe, more painful, and more effective in remembrance when rain falls and the earth does not grow. For this reason the hadith says: "Drought is not that you are not rained upon; rather, drought is that you are rained upon and the earth does not produce anything."[2] This is the correct view. Sometimes abundant rains come and you find no life in the earth, and sometimes little rain comes and the earth comes alive with good life. This indicates that this rain is a cause of the earth's life, but causes may have their effects unfulfilled because of obstacles.
* Student: The saying of Allah ﴿But most of the people refused except denial﴾ [al-Furqan 50] (...) or that ﴿denial﴾ is by denying Allah's power to revive the dead?
* Shaykh: It is general; this includes every type of disbelief that can be imagined (...), such as if it became a cause of insolence and exultation: people go out, frolic, and transgress, and do not perform what Allah has made obligatory upon them, such as congregational prayer and other things. * Shaykh: That this barrier (barzakh) is this dry land.

The third view is what the Ustadh mentioned: if the verse can bear it, when we take it that there is a barrier between them, meaning there is a separating thing that we do not know. Because here the separation between the salt and the sweet is in their very essence. That is, it is not a matter (...) of this from that; rather the separation is by the very sweetness and the very bitterness. So there is nothing between them. Rather, the nature of this and the nature of that requires that each separate from the other. If the Qur'an can bear this, then it is without doubt one of the greatest signs: for example, a river flowing a long distance in the midst of salt water without mixing with it.

So if the Qur'an can bear it, and it is possible for us to take "baynahuma" to mean in their very reality and constitution, because what we understood now is that the cause of non-transgression is not something separating them; rather, it is the very constitution of this and that.

* Student: Good, did they not consider "bayn"?
* Shaykh: That is why we weakened this view.

* Shaykh: Good. If you say: "Between you and your companion is a stone."
* Student: That is a place.
* Shaykh: Yes, and the sea is also a place; so it remains a space (ḥayyiz).
* Student: "Between me and so-and-so is knowledge," meaning (...), so this depends on the meaning.
* Shaykh: Correct, because knowledge is in essence a meaning; but water and water are bodies that remain a space.
* Student: But between me and so-and-so?
* Shaykh: In any case, I cannot be certain. O brothers, now we are explaining the words of Allah. If the Qur'an bears the meaning that Ustadh Nabil mentioned, and those who mentioned this, then there is no doubt it is among the miracles of the Qur'an, if it can bear it. If the word ﴿between them is a barrier﴾ prevents this possibility, and we say that the barrier here in reality requires a third thing other than the two seas, then we say: praise be to Allah, this which we have come to know through knowledge is among the signs of Allah, exalted is He, even if the Qur'an does not indicate it.
* Student: Could one not say, for example, that this barrier is a part of this and that, and if they were to merge, (...)?
* Shaykh: Indeed, it is possible: if it is established, we may say that the proportion between them is not pure water.
* Student: Neither from this nor from that.
* Shaykh: It is not pure sweetness nor pure bitterness; like this barrier.
* Student: So it would be like the barrier, and the word ﴿barzakh﴾ (...) this world and the Hereafter.
* Shaykh: Possibly; Allah knows best.
* Student: In light of a scientific discovery, sometimes it is permissible to give a specific meaning, because sometimes in the absence of this scientific reality, a (...) is formed. I recall that the interpretation of a verse in Surah al-Nur: ﴿in a deep sea, covered by waves, above which are waves﴾ [al-Nur 40]. Most exegetes said: since there are not two waves one above the other, "above" (fawq) here is understood to mean "after it, a wave". This is an interpretation that the Arabic language often allows.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: I read a research paper some five years ago by a scientist in America, originally Egyptian, who took American citizenship and is famous for research in space, who descended in the first submersible to explore the depths of the oceans. He said: the prevailing opinion among scholars before this experiment was that the bottom of the oceans and seas is completely still. He said: then we were surprised to find that at the bottom of the oceans there are waves, and the waves on the surface are nothing compared with those waves in their intensity and greatness. So now the word ﴿above it﴾ has no justification for being interpreted; rather, ﴿above it﴾ means there is a wave below and a wave above it. This means the existence of a cosmic phenomenon that helps direct the meaning in a specific direction without forcing the meaning.
* Shaykh: Yes. In truth, even the apparent waves on the surface of the sea: a wave may be low, then a larger wave comes and rises above it.
* Student: (...) for the sake of demonstrating the miraculousness of the Qur'an (...) from us.
* Shaykh: In any case, we should not waste time.
Now we say: the verse can bear three meanings: the meaning that many exegetes mentioned, the meaning we mentioned, and the meaning you also mentioned, which was mentioned by an Iraqi man in a book called Haqa'iq Jughrafiyya (Geographical Facts), who mentioned the meaning we pointed to. The third meaning, if the verse can bear it, is what Ustadh Nabil told us about these rivers that exist in the midst of the oceans.

We have heard the discussion now on the word ﴿between them﴾ [al-Furqan 53] and what it can bear. If there is a layer, when the two are taken as absolutes, that lies between the sweet and the salt, then it may be said: this is a barrier, though with some strain, because its apparent meaning is that the barrier is what prevents mixing. This may be said: it prevents their mixing because of their closeness.
* Student: Does a person encounter (...), because the Qur'an mentioned the barrier as (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, the rivers that are in the midst of the sea.

* Shaykh: Good. In any case, we have nothing but the word ﴿between them﴾; this "betweenness" requires that there be a third thing that is neither of this nor of that.

* Shaykh: Yes, we have heard this.

* Shaykh: Yes, but the spring requires (that it come) from the bottom of the sea.

Also among the perfection of God's power, Glorified and Exalted, is that He created a human being from water and divided him into two kinds. What are they?

A student: Lineage (nasab) and marriage by alliance (sihr).

The Shaykh: Lineage and marriage by alliance (sihr).

The student: Lineage (...).

The Shaykh: In marriage, yes. We said that these are the causes of connection between people: either a connection by birth, which is lineage, or by marriage, which is affinity (musahara).

Good. As for His saying: ﴿And your Lord is ever Powerful﴾ [al-Furqan 54], the author says: (capable of whatever He wills).

We discuss with the author, may God have mercy on him, his interpretation of ﴿qadiran﴾ as (qadir, capable), and his restricting the unrestricted with (whatever He wills).

As for interpreting ﴿qadiran﴾ as (qadir), this is considered a deficiency in the interpretation, because ﴿qadiran﴾ is either a resembling adjective (sifah mushabbahah) or an intensive form (sigha mubalaghah). As for (qadir), it is a bare active participle, which does not express what the resembling adjective expresses, nor what the intensive form expresses. This is a kind of shortcoming in the interpretation of the Qur'an.

Second: The Qur'an states ﴿And your Lord is ever Powerful﴾ without restriction, and here he restricted it with his saying (whatever He wills). We know that for some people this restriction indicates an innovation they committed, because the Qadariyyah say that God, Glorified and Exalted, is only capable of what He wills, and that He does not will the actions of the servants, and on this basis He would not be capable of them. There is no doubt that this view is refuted by the texts and by reason. God is the One who guides and misguides, and the meaning of guidance and misguidance is only that He, Glorified and Exalted, does what He wills, even regarding the actions of the servant. Therefore we see that restricting power by will is not fitting and not appropriate, for the following reasons:

First: God, Glorified and Exalted, applied this attribute to Himself without restriction, and it is not appropriate for us to restrict what God has applied, because the attributes of God are tawqifiyyah (based on revelation), in which one stops at what has been transmitted.

The second thing: It contradicts the method of the Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, and his Companions, indeed the method of all the messengers, because they say: ﴿Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us. Indeed You are over all things competent﴾ [al-Tahrim 8]. They do not say: "Indeed You are competent over what You will." ﴿Indeed You are over all things competent.﴾

The third thing: It gives the impression that power relates only to what He wills, and on this basis what He does not will would not be within God's ability. This meaning is false. He is capable of what He wills and of what He does not will, but what He wills comes to be and what He does not will does not come to be. So He is capable of both, not only of what He wills.

For these three reasons we see that using this expression is not appropriate, and that it is something the servant should be guided away from and told: do not say this, do not restrict what God has applied to Himself.

A student: Is it "guided" or "not appropriate" (...)?

The Shaykh: No, its origin is on the basis that the one who says it does not intend this meaning. We say: it is guided away from, and it is said: this is not appropriate.

And if it is asked: what is the reconciliation, or what is the answer to the saying of God, blessed and exalted: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and what He has dispersed therein of creatures; and He, over their gathering when He wills, is competent﴾ [al-Shura 29]. Here He says: ﴿over their gathering when He wills, is competent﴾, and we prohibit linking power to will?

A student: ("idha" meaning "whenever"): whenever God, Glorified and Exalted, wills, it is a matter of time, meaning.

The Shaykh: There is no contradiction: whenever He wills He is competent. And whenever He does not will?

The student: He is competent too, but the intended meaning is time, meaning that God is competent over gathering them when He wills, meaning that when the time comes at which God has willed to gather them, He gathers them (...).

The Shaykh: Yes, not (...).

The answer is that this restricts the will to the gathering. That is, the gathering is an act, and this act is denied by the disbelievers who deny the Resurrection. So God, Mighty and Majestic, says: the thing preventing that is not inability, but the absence of will. So when He wills to gather them, He gathers them, contrary to whom? To those who deny that, who say that it is impossible for Him to gather them. So here the restriction is on the act, the restriction of the will returns to the act, not to the power. He is capable of gathering them at all times, but since He, Glorified and Exalted, does not wish to gather them except at a specific time: ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the latter (49) will surely be gathered for the appointed time of a known Day﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 49–50], appointed, ﴿and We do not delay it except for a term﴾, look, ﴿counted﴾ [Hud 104]. All the worldly life is a counted term, which is evidence of its brevity however long it lasts.

So we say: this returns to the gathering, which is an act. It is as if God says: it is... 
...what does not benefit them if they worship Him, nor harm them if they disobey Him. God, the Exalted, said in Surat al-Ahqaf: ﴿And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah those who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Ahqaf 5]. That is, if he keeps calling this idol until the Day of Resurrection, it will not respond to him. Is there anyone more astray than this? There is no one more astray than this at all: a person tries to have this idol benefit or harm him, and even if he keeps calling it until the Day of Resurrection, it does not respond to him. This is among the most extreme forms of misguidance. Yes indeed.

(﴿And the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord﴾ [al-Furqan 55]: assisting Satan by his obedience), meaning: by obedience to Satan.

The disbeliever is a helper against his Lord, an assistant against God, Glorified and Exalted, not for Him, an assistant against Him, not for Him. That is, a warrior against God. Whenever the disbeliever finds an enemy of God, he helps him against his Lord. This is just as the author said, that he assists Satan in disobeying God, because the human being (...) an assistant to Satan in his rebellion against God, Glorified and Exalted.

It also includes whoever has this description from among non-disbelievers: everyone who assists in falsehood is an assistant against God, is he not? Every person who assists someone in falsehood is a helper against his Lord, because God, Exalted, is the Truth and He wills the truth. So if you help the owner of falsehood against the owner of truth, you are an assistant against God. Is that so or not?

A student: Yes.

The Shaykh: Because what is the meaning of "ẓahīr"? The ẓahīr is the helper, as God, Exalted, said: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if they were to each other assistants﴾ [al-Isra' 88]. So the disbeliever always helps against God, and whoever assists falsehood against truth is an assistant against God, meaning he is an assistant of falsehood against truth, because God is the Truth and He loves the truth.

﴿And the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord﴾ [al-Furqan 55]. What is the connection of this sentence to the one before it: ﴿And they worship besides Allah that which neither benefits them nor harms them, and the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord﴾ [al-Furqan 55]?

A student: Meaning that they (...) are assistants against God through Satan.

The Shaykh: Meaning that this is one of Satan's commands?

The student: Yes?

The Shaykh: Meaning that their worship is one of Satan's commands?

The student: Yes.

The Shaykh: Good, and also?

A student: The denunciation of them.

Another student: (...).

The Shaykh: Meaning, it is as if he made this a rival to God, made this idol a rival to God, worshipping it as one worships God. And it is known that the idol is the opposite of what the messengers brought, so supporting this idol is an aid against God.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 56–58:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [al-Furqan 56].

When He had reproached these people for what relates to establishing monotheism, namely worshipping other than Allah, He moved on after that to establishing the message (risalah), because Islam is the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. So establishing worship came with rebuking them for worshipping other than Allah, and then establishing the message came with His saying: (﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good tidings﴾ of Paradise, ﴿and a warner﴾ [al-Furqan 56]: one who warns of the Fire).

In this verse, ﴿And We have not sent you except﴾ is an exception covering the most general of states. That is, your condition in the message is nothing but these two matters: good tidings and warning. Good tidings to whom? To the believers, of Paradise. And what is the evidence for this?

* Student: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that for them is from Allah a great bounty﴾ [al-Ahzab 47].

* The Shaykh: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that for them is from Allah a great bounty﴾. And Allah the Exalted said in Surah al-Kahf: ﴿to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that for them is a good reward, staying therein forever, and to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son." They have no knowledge of it﴾ [al-Kahf 2–5]. It has already passed that the nadhir (warner) means one who warns with what frightens.

So this is the description of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, with respect to what relates to the message: these two matters only.

If someone says: Is the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, not a teacher? Does he not teach people the rulings?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes. How then is this exception from the most general of states? We say: this is an exception from the most general of states, meaning: his condition is nothing but this?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Do we say that this teaching is among the means of warning and good tidings, or do we say that this restriction is relative (idafi)?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The speech of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, sometimes informs people and teaches them without urging them, encouraging them, or frightening them, as is well known; and sometimes he frightens and warns in general terms; and sometimes he frightens and warns against violating this specific matter. So we answer this by saying: the Messenger's teaching, peace and blessings be upon him, is among the means or the ways by which what is promised with good tidings or what is warned of is attained. When he commands us to something, what does that mean? It means that if we do it, we reach what he mentioned; and when he forbids us from something, it means that if we fall into it, we fall into what he warned of, peace and blessings be upon him.

This is better than saying the restriction is relative, because if you say the restriction is relative, you take the statement away from its literal reality; whereas if you say this is a necessary implication, the statement remains in its reality, but it indicates this matter (...).

(﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it﴾, i.e., for conveying what I have been sent with, ﴿except﴾, but ﴿whoever wills to take a way to his Lord﴾ [al-Furqan 57]: a path, by spending his wealth in seeking the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted. So I do not prevent him from that).

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it﴾ [al-Furqan 57].

We all know that ﴿mā﴾ is a negation particle, and that ﴿min﴾ in His saying ﴿min ajr﴾ is extra (za'idah). Is it extra in its grammatical function (i'rab) or in meaning?

* Student: In i'rab.

* The Shaykh: It is extra in i'rab. For this reason some scholars refer to it as ṣilah, out of scruple about calling it extra. In reality, once the meaning is understood the problem disappears. As long as we say it is extra in i'rab, there is no harm in that. As for meaning, it is not extra. What is its benefit? Its benefit is to make explicit the generality, because ﴿ajr﴾ is an indefinite noun in a negative context, and this is one of the forms of generality. But when ﴿min﴾ is added to it, it becomes more explicit (...) in generality.

(I do not ask you for a reward for it), it is true that there is no reward at all, but ﴿min ajr﴾ makes you feel that it is not any reward, not even a little, neither small nor large. So its benefit is making the generality explicit.

As for His saying ﴿min ajr﴾: if we say ﴿min﴾ is extra in i'rab, how do we parse ﴿ajr﴾?

We say: ﴿min﴾ is an extra preposition in i'rab, and ﴿ajr﴾ is a second object of (as'alu, "I ask") in the accusative case, marked by a presumed fatha at its end, prevented from being manifest by the occupation of the position by the vowel of the extra preposition. This is its parsing according to them.

* Student: Some say: it is accusative in position and genitive in form?

* The Shaykh: Yes, there is a possibility in this. What you said: that it is accusative in position. But this only applies (...). There is a possibility that you say ﴿ajr﴾ is an accusative direct object, and it was given a kasra to match the preposition. The whole matter is a matter of consideration.

The main point is that we know the verb now bears directly on ﴿ajr﴾, not through a preposition, because this particle is extra in terms of i'rab; but in terms of meaning it has a great benefit. And Allah is the Granter of success.

* Student: Here He said: ﴿And the disbeliever is ever a supporter against his Lord﴾ [al-Furqan 55]. Does this mean: any sinner, for example, while committing his sin, is a helper in sin?
* The Shaykh: Yes?

* Student: Does any sinner while committing his sin become a helper in sin?

* The Shaykh: Yes, that is correct.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...). But here He said ﴿And the disbeliever﴾, because He is speaking about those who worship alongside Allah. Therefore a person may be mentioned in many matters. ﴿And the disbeliever﴾ here is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun; ﴿and they worship besides Allah that which neither benefits them nor harms them﴾ [al-Furqan 55]. The context would require saying "and they were against their Lord," but He said ﴿the disbeliever﴾, as an indication that this worship led them to disbelief. Also, it is for the purpose of generalization, meaning (...) even if it is other than worship, other than shirk. For example, a person who is a materialist and worships nothing at all is also a supporter against his Lord. (...)

I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed (...). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾ [al-Furqan 59].

It has already been said that among the benefits of the verses we recited yesterday is the obligation of relying upon Allah, the Exalted, and we explained that its rank in religion is half of religion, because Allah commands both worship and reliance.

It has also passed that the verse indicates the perfection of Allah, the Exalted, and the negation of any deficiency from Him, through His saying ﴿And glorify Him with His praise﴾ [al-Furqan 58], because tasbih is declaring Him free from imperfection, and hamd is affirming perfection.

And that it contains the affirmation of Allah's knowledge, the Exalted: ﴿And sufficient is He as Knower of the sins of His servants﴾ [al-Furqan 58], and there are other benefits that have already been mentioned.

* Student: Does any sinner while committing his sin become a helper in sin?

* The Shaykh: Yes, that is correct.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...). But here He said ﴿And the disbeliever﴾, because He is speaking about those who worship alongside Allah. Therefore a person may be mentioned in many matters. ﴿And the disbeliever﴾ here is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun; ﴿and they worship besides Allah that which neither benefits them nor harms them﴾ [al-Furqan 55]. For example, a person who is a materialist and worships nothing at all is also a supporter against his Lord. (...)

I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed (...). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾ [al-Furqan 59].

It has already been said that among the benefits of the verses we recited yesterday is the obligation of relying upon Allah, the Exalted, and we explained that its rank in religion is half of religion, because Allah commands both worship and reliance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 56–58:

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [al-Furqan 56].

When He had reproached these people for what relates to establishing monotheism, namely worshipping other than Allah, He moved on after that to establishing the message (risalah), because Islam is the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. So establishing worship came with rebuking them for worshipping other than Allah, and then establishing the message came with His saying: (﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good tidings﴾ of Paradise, ﴿and a warner﴾ [al-Furqan 56]: one who warns of the Fire).

In this verse, ﴿And We have not sent you except﴾ is an exception covering the most general of states. That is, your condition in the message is nothing but these two matters: good tidings and warning. Good tidings to whom? To the believers, of Paradise. And what is the evidence for this?

* Student: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that for them is from Allah a great bounty﴾ [al-Ahzab 47].

* The Shaykh: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that for them is from Allah a great bounty﴾. And Allah the Exalted said in Surah al-Kahf: ﴿to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that for them is a good reward, staying therein forever, and to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son." They have no knowledge of it﴾ [al-Kahf 2–5]. It has already passed that the nadhir (warner) means one who warns with what frightens.

So this is the description of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, with respect to what relates to the message: these two matters only.

If someone says: Is the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, not a teacher? Does he not teach people the rulings?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes. How then is this exception from the most general of states? We say: this is an exception from the most general of states, meaning: his condition is nothing but this?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Do we say that this teaching is among the means of warning and good tidings, or do we say that this restriction is relative (idafi)?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The speech of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, sometimes informs people and teaches them without urging them, encouraging them, or frightening them, as is well known; and sometimes he frightens and warns in general terms; and sometimes he frightens and warns against violating this specific matter. So we answer this by saying: the Messenger's teaching, peace and blessings be upon him, is among the means or the ways by which what is promised with good tidings or what is warned of is attained. When he commands us to something, what does that mean? It means that if we do it, we reach what he mentioned; and when he forbids us from something, it means that if we fall into it, we fall into what he warned of, peace and blessings be upon him.

This is better than saying the restriction is relative, because if you say the restriction is relative, you take the statement away from its literal reality; whereas if you say this is a necessary implication, the statement remains in its reality, but it indicates this matter (...).

(﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it﴾, i.e., for conveying what I have been sent with, ﴿except﴾, but ﴿whoever wills to take a way to his Lord﴾ [al-Furqan 57]: a path, by spending his wealth in seeking the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted. So I do not prevent him from that).

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it﴾ [al-Furqan 57].

We all know that ﴿mā﴾ is a negation particle, and that ﴿min﴾ in His saying ﴿min ajr﴾ is extra (za'idah). Is it extra in its grammatical function (i'rab) or in meaning?

* Student: In i'rab.

* The Shaykh: It is extra in i'rab. For this reason some scholars refer to it as ṣilah, out of scruple about calling it extra. In reality, once the meaning is understood the problem disappears. As long as we say it is extra in i'rab, there is no harm in that. As for meaning, it is not extra. What is its benefit? Its benefit is to make explicit the generality, because ﴿ajr﴾ is an indefinite noun in a negative context, and this is one of the forms of generality. But when ﴿min﴾ is added to it, it becomes more explicit (...) in generality.

(I do not ask you for a reward for it), it is true that there is no reward at all, but ﴿min ajr﴾ makes you feel that it is not any reward, not even a little, neither small nor large. So its benefit is making the generality explicit.

As for His saying ﴿min ajr﴾: if we say ﴿min﴾ is extra in i'rab, how do we parse ﴿ajr﴾?

We say: ﴿min﴾ is an extra preposition in i'rab, and ﴿ajr﴾ is a second object of (as'alu, "I ask") in the accusative case, marked by a presumed fatha at its end, prevented from being manifest by the occupation of the position by the vowel of the extra preposition. This is its parsing according to them.

* Student: Some say: it is accusative in position and genitive in form?

* The Shaykh: Yes, there is a possibility in this. What you said: that it is accusative in position. But this only applies (...). There is a possibility that you say ﴿ajr﴾ is an accusative direct object, and it was given a kasra to match the preposition. The whole matter is a matter of consideration.

The main point is that we know the verb now bears directly on ﴿ajr﴾, not through a preposition, because this particle is extra in terms of i'rab; but in terms of meaning it has a great benefit. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 59 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Who created the heavens and the earth﴾. Written before ﴿Who created﴾ in my copy is: (He is ﴿Who created﴾ [al-Furqan 59]), and it is written as if it were part of the original text, and this is not correct; it is not from the Qur'an (He).
* A student: It is marked as omitted (mukhrajah).
* The Shaykh: Omitted?
* The student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: No, I have its place beside the bracket, and it is also vocalized as if it were Qur'an.
His words: (He is ﴿Who created﴾), the author estimated this subject (mubtada') so that the sentence would be a new, separate sentence (mustanaf) in terms of grammatical analysis (i'rab) from what precedes it, although there is another possibility in it: that it be an attribute (sifah) of His words ﴿the Ever-Living, who does not die﴾ [al-Furqan 58], meaning: ﴿And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die﴾ [al-Furqan 58], ﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Furqan 59]. Thus in His words ﴿the Ever-Living who does not die﴾ there is a clarification of His essential attribute, and in His words ﴿who created﴾ a clarification of His active attribute. By this it is established that He, glory be to Him and exalted, is worthy of reliance and trust, because whoever has this description and this action is deserving of being singled out for trust.
As for what the author adopted, he makes the sentence a resumptive sentence (isti'nafiyyah), a new sentence; and although it is a new sentence in terms of grammatical analysis, it is connected in meaning to what precedes it, indicating the perfection of His power, and that He is deserving of being singled out for trust, blessed and exalted.
﴿Created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Furqan 59]: He brought them into existence. Bringing into existence is called khalq (creation) only when it is preceded by a measuring (taqdir), because the original meaning of khalq is taqdir. But it is applied both to that and to the act itself. When khalq is applied to the act, its meaning becomes that it is an act based on measure, so the precise planning (ihkam) is prior, then the act follows the course of that precise planning. Thus He created them perfectly, and whoever reflects upon them, considers them and contemplates them, finds in them the utmost precision.
And His words: ﴿in six days﴾ [al-Furqan 59]. He says: (of the days of this world, meaning in their measure; because there was then no sun, and had He willed, He would have created them in a blink, but the deviation from that was to teach His creation steadiness).
* A student: In my copy it is (wal-'adl) (and justice).
* The Shaykh: In my copy it is (al-'uduwl) (deviation); 'adala, ya'dilu, 'adlan and 'udulan, it is correct.
He says: (﴿in six days﴾ [al-Furqan 59] of the days of this world), this is the well-known opinion, and it is the preferred one.
As for whoever said: ﴿in six days﴾ means days of the Hereafter, and that a day is like a thousand years, or whoever said that what is meant by ﴿days﴾ is time in general, meaning in moments, this too is a weaker opinion, because the Qur'an addresses people only in what they know, and what they know (...). So the correct view is that what is meant by (﴿in six days﴾ of the days of this world), as the author said, the first of them being Sunday and the last being Friday, for with it the creation of the heavens and the earth was completed, and Adam was created at its end.
And his words: (meaning in their measure, because there was no sun), the measuring of days is by the sun, and the sun did not exist at the time of creation; so on this basis what is meant by ﴿in six days﴾ is: in the measure of these six days.
Then the author addressed an answer to a question that the mind may suppose: that someone might say: why did Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, not create them with the word ﴿His command is only when He intends a thing that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82], so that it happens according to the will of Allah, glory be to Him and exalted?
He answered that He did so (to teach His creation steadiness). This is what the scholars have followed: that Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, created them in six days in order to show the servants that the aim is precision, not haste, so that people act with deliberation, even in what they are able to do, as they should observe precision in it rather than hastening its execution.
I have seen a fine statement from some of them, who said: the creation of the heavens and the earth has causes, and it is an expression of formation (takwin), and this formation needs a period, like the way a fetus develops in its mother's womb gradually over a period; likewise this creation has causes that formed it, and these causes were during this period ﴿in six days﴾. But those who hold this view prefer the opinion that the days meant are the long days of the Hereafter, so that the developments leading to perfection are appropriate.
In my view this is not necessary, because Allah the Exalted is able to make these causes, which by their nature require extension due to the greatness of the created thing, occur at this speed. And Allah knows best. This last rationale would mean the reason for its delay, that it was not completed except in six, because it needs developments, these developments gradually until they reach perfection, as is known in what we observe of what Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, creates other than the heavens and the earth: we find that these creatures do not come all at once, but have causes and states through which they develop until they reach the degree of perfection.
* A student: The author said: (there was no sun).
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: Is this Muslim (narrated)?
* The Shaykh: Yes; because the sun was created after that, as His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He inspired in each heaven its command﴾ [Fussilat 12], after He created it, He inspired in it its command, and this includes everything related to the heaven.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, but it was created at the end of Friday, or on a Friday after a long time.
* The student: (...) before the creation of water?
* The Shaykh: We do not know; Allah knows best.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿Then He istawa over the Throne﴾ [al-Furqan 59]. Is ﴿then﴾ here for sequence in mention (tartib dhikri) or sequence in meaning (tartib ma'nawi)?
* A student: Meaning.
* Another student: From the meaning of the verse.
* The Shaykh: Sequence in meaning, because that is the basic usage. The basic principle is that it denotes sequence in meaning, not sequence in the mind. The difference between them is that sequence in mention does not require that what follows be later than what precedes; rather, what follows may be before it but was mentioned after it. The scholars call this sequence in mention, but they only resort to it when necessary: when sequence in meaning is not possible, they say it is sequence in mention, and they cite the well-known verse whose composer I do not know:
Whoever became master, then his father became master,
then after that his grandfather became master.
They said: this is of the type of sequence in mention, since the grandfather's mastery precedes the father's, and the father's mastery precedes the son's. This is the known and familiar pattern, although the matter may be reversed: a noble man may become master, and through his mastery his father becomes master, then his grandfather, but the known pattern is the reverse.
In any case, the sequence in this verse is sequence in meaning, because that is the basic sense, and one does not resort to the first except when necessary.
His words: ﴿istawa﴾ means: he rose high (ala) over the Throne, and this height is a specific height, not like the height over the rest of creation, because Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is high over all creation with absolute height; but this height over the Throne is a specific height, and it indicates the perfection of the one who is high, because this root (istawa) indicates perfection in itself. You say: the fruit istawa, meaning its ripeness was perfected; and you say: the man istawa, meaning he was perfected in intellect: ﴿And when he reached his full strength and became mature﴾ [al-Qasas 14].
Here, when it is followed by (ala), it denotes height but includes perfection; so on this basis ﴿istawa﴾ means: rose high in a specific manner, in the form of perfection.
The author's words: (﴿over the Throne﴾ is in language the king's couch).
This Throne: not every seat is called a throne; a teacher's chair is not called a throne, but the seat specific to a king is called a throne. This is the original meaning in language. Allah, blessed and exalted, said of the Queen of Sheba: ﴿And she has a great throne﴾ [al-Naml 23], and He said: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾ [Yusuf 100] in the story of Yusuf. But what is meant by the Throne here is greater than that: it is that great creation which encompasses the heavens, the earth and the Kursi. For a hadith says that the seven heavens and the seven earths, compared to the Kursi, are like a ring thrown into a desert, a ring, meaning the ring of a coat of mail or armor, what is it compared to the desert? Nothing. And the excellence of the Throne over the Kursi is like the excellence of the desert over that ring.[[Al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat (861) from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I entered upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was in the mosque, and he mentioned the hadith, in which he said: I said: Which verse did Allah reveal to you that is greatest? He said: "The verse of the Kursi." Then he ﷺ said: "O Abu Dharr, the seven heavens compared to the Kursi are only like a ring thrown in a desert land, and the excellence of the Throne over the Kursi is like the excellence of the desert over that ring."]] So none knows its measure except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
And it is excessive profundity and overstepping the bounds to search and ask about the reality of this Throne: what is it made of? Gold? Silver? Emerald? Something else? Reports have been narrated about this, but they are not authentic, nor are they transmitted from an infallible source, and one should not delve into it, because what concern is it of ours what its material is? The important thing is to know the greatness of this Throne, and that it is the one upon which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, istawa.
The author says: (﴿the Most Merciful﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in ﴿istawa﴾, meaning: an istiwa' befitting Him).
﴿Istawa over the Throne, the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan 59]. That is, you do not say that ﴿the Most Merciful﴾ is the subject (fa'il) of ﴿istawa﴾, because it came before it, nothing indicates that the pronoun in ﴿istawa﴾ refers back to it: ﴿Who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then istawa over the Throne, the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan 59]. The author's statement means that it is not parsed as the subject of ﴿istawa﴾ because it precedes it, and the pronoun in ﴿istawa﴾ does not refer to it. But there is no objection to making it the subject, as an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (idhar fi maqam al-idmar); there is no objection to it. Indeed, the apparent context requires that ﴿created the heavens﴾ and ﴿then istawa﴾ have a hidden pronoun as subject, meaning He. The author's view that it is a substitute (badal) is one possibility, but we say it is not decisive, since it may be that ﴿the Most Merciful﴾ is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun.
They also mentioned a third possibility: that it is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is ﴿ask about Him of one who is aware﴾ [al-Furqan 59], and that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: He is the Most Merciful.
But what we have adopted is preferable, and the benefit of the explicit noun here is to show that this istiwa' and specific height is not like the height of the arrogant tyrants, but is the height of the All-Merciful, vast in mercy. For it is customary among people or kings that when they sit upon their thrones, there is usually a great deal of arrogance and grandeur that they imagine when they are seated on their thrones. But Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, despite His height and great throne, is the Most Merciful, vast in mercy, blessed and exalted: ﴿Then istawa over the Throne, the Most Merciful﴾.
The author's words: (istawa befitting Him). The first question on this sentence: does this sentence indicate that the author did not distort?
* A student: It does not indicate that he did not distort.
* The Shaykh: It does not indicate?
* The student: That is, it indicates the opposite.
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah.
* The student: That is, he distorts.
* The Shaykh: Correct.
* A student: Yes, true.
* Another student: If it had not come, meaning if all the verses other than istawa said such-and-such, there would be evidence.
* The Shaykh: By Allah, I have considered what precedes it, he says such-and-such; I reviewed several passages, he says such-and-such, (...).
* A student: This is a contradiction.
* The Shaykh: Yes. Well, it is not contradictory; you say that it indicates that he did not distort.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Huh?
* A student: That is, perhaps what is befitting for Him, ﴿the Most Merciful﴾, is that it be taken to mean the...
* The Shaykh: The height.
* The student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Why do you say it indicates the opposite?
* The student: It indicates the opposite, because he did not say that the linguistic meaning of (ala) became (...). He gives you this sentence to convince you that he holds the view of the Sunnah, as is the belief of some, but it is the opposite.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: That is, if he had meant the true height that the scholars explained (...).
* The Shaykh: On (...).
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: In reality he neither affirms nor denies; in my view, because he mentioned only the attribute of istiwa', merely stating that the attribute of istiwa' is befitting for Him, but he did not speak about the meaning of istiwa'. However, in truth I see that this points to the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah and the Congregation; because if he held that ﴿istawa﴾ means istawla (seized power), he would not have said "istiwa' befitting Him," since it is not possible for the meaning to be "he seized power in a manner befitting Him." Such an expression is used only when istiwa' is made an attribute, not... an attribute of action, so it would be "istiwa' befitting Him." But even so, this interpretation is not complete, and he should have said: "He rose high in a manner befitting Him." Is it clear?
* A student: (...) he feared it would fall into (...) ta'wil, so he departed from ta'wil?
* The Shaykh: No, that is not what is intended. If he had meant it, he would have said: ﴿istawa﴾ means istawla, just as he said: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾ [al-Fajr 22], he explained it by saying: "the command of your Lord came."
* A student: Then he interprets all the verses of height.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. In any case, his words here do not indicate affirmation or negation. But in my belief they indicate interpretation as height, as evidenced by the fact that one does not say "it is an istawla befitting Him"; this cannot be conceived. Yet even so he did not explain it as he should have, and what should have been said is: ﴿istawa over the Throne﴾: rose high over it in a manner befitting Him.
* A student: So the explanation of the verses is not in accordance with his own doctrine?
* The Shaykh: We have nothing before us except this.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: These verses here. I traced what precedes them in several places and found that he says this, and I was truly surprised. Notice that this book we have is not by al-Suyuti; this is al-Mahalli, because al-Suyuti explained the beginning of the Qur'an, and al-Mahalli explained the end of the Qur'an. So I say I was surprised by this, even though he does not affirm the essential height, and this is among the strange things; it is considered a contradictory method for the author.

So the correct view in any case is: "istiwa' befitting Him" has a correct meaning, but it needs completion, namely that he explain, that is clarify and make clear, the meaning of istiwa'.

﴿Istawa over the Throne﴾: rose high over it in a manner befitting Him.

If someone says: Is not Allah high above all creation?

The answer: Yes, but this height is a specific height in relation to the intellect. This was already discussed in the creed, and there is no need to repeat it, that the people of ta'til (negation) distorted the meaning of istiwa' to mean istila' (seizing power), and we explained there that this distortion is false for several linguistic, legal and rational reasons, and that this interpretation entails false implications that are not befitting Allah, glory be to Him and exalted.

His words: ﴿the Most Merciful﴾, meaning: the one characterized by mercy. When it is mentioned separately from al-Rahim, it indicates both attribute and action. Al-Rahim too, when mentioned separately from it, indicates both attribute and action. When the two are combined, al-Rahman is explained with reference to what relates to the attribute, and al-Rahim with reference to what relates to the action. Is this understood?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: So here al-Rahman is mentioned alone, so it includes both attribute and action. What is your question?
* A student: The statement of the Exalted in the verse of the Kursi: ﴿His Kursi encompasses the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 255], and here He says: ﴿Then istawa over the Throne﴾. How, if someone comes, for example, and says (...), ﴿His Kursi encompasses the heavens and the earth﴾, and here He says: ﴿Then istawa over the Throne﴾?
* The Shaykh: (...) there is no disagreement between them.
* The student: Not at all?
* The Shaykh: Not at all. What is the disagreement, (...)?

**Student:** ﴿وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ﴾ (...)?

**Shaykh:** Good. What does it mean?

**Student:** The meaning is that the Throne is above the Kursi.

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** And here the Kursi "encompassed the heavens and the earth."

**Shaykh:** It encompasses the heavens and the earth entirely. That is, because of its greatness and vastness, it is wide enough for both of them together, for all the heavens and the earth.

**Student:** The Kursi?

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** And the Throne is above it?

**Shaykh:** And the Throne is above it.

(﴿ثُمَّ اسْتَوَى عَلَى الْعَرْشِ الرَّحْمَنُ فَاسْأَلْ﴾ O human, ﴿بِهِ﴾ about the Most Merciful, ﴿خَبِيرًا﴾ one who is aware, who will inform you of His attributes.)

**Student:** Shaykh?

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** How does "ar-Rahim" indicate the act when it is linked (to a verb)?

**Shaykh:** Yes. Indeed, the pattern *fa'il* indicates the occurrence of the act. *Sami'* means "one who hears the sound," *Rahim* means "one who shows mercy to creation." *Ar-Rahman* is similar to the word *ghadban*, meaning "filled with anger." Likewise, *ar-Rahman* means "vast in mercy." For this reason, some of the early scholars (al-salaf) explained it by saying: "Ar-Rahman is the One of general mercy, and ar-Rahim is the One who is merciful to the believers." Yes.
