Shaykh: In addition to what has been mentioned, there is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord, do not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾ [al-Furqan 73].

﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord﴾: the one who reminds is not specified, so that it encompasses every reminder. This is also to show that their acceptance of reminder is not because of a particular person who reminds. For among people there are those who accept the truth only from a specific individual; if it comes from someone else, they do not accept it, as the People of the Book did with the Prophet ﷺ, and others too, who accept the truth only from a particular group or a particular person: ﴿And even if you brought those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qiblah﴾ [al-Baqarah 145].

So here He said ﴿when they are reminded﴾ without specifying who reminds, as an indication that they accept the truth because it is the truth, not because of the one who speaks it. Yes, they do not accept reminder out of regard for a particular person who reminds, nor do they reject it on account of a particular person who reminds; rather they accept it because it is a reminder. This is the benefit of omitting the agent.

(﴿And those who, when they are reminded﴾ are admonished ﴿of the signs of their Lord, do not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾ [al-Furqan 73]).

Here: ﴿they are reminded of the signs of their Lord﴾. Is the meaning that they are reminded by them, i.e., that they are made a means of remembrance or admonition, or that they are reminded with them, i.e., with what they judge, so that they act upon it?

* Student: It encompasses all.

* Shaykh: It encompasses all?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: That is, whether they are reminded by means of the signs, by having them recited to them so that they may take heed, or they are reminded with them, i.e., it is said to them: remember the rulings of Allah and act upon them. It encompasses both matters.

As for his statement: (﴿of the signs of their Lord﴾ [al-Furqan 73], i.e., the Qur'an), the correct view is generality: the Qur'an and other than the Qur'an, and also that it is more general in terms of whether the signs are cosmic or legislative. So we say: the Qur'an and other earlier books; and we also say: the Qur'an and the Books, or the cosmic signs. The cosmic signs are indeed reminders, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ regarding the eclipse: «Allah makes them a means of frightening His servants»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1059) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and Muslim, and the wording is his (911/21) from the hadith of Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari.]]. So the cosmic signs are frightening and reminding of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; for this reason Allah, glorified and exalted, constantly urges reflection upon these cosmic signs, because of what they contain of indication of the Creator and of His attributes: of wisdom, mercy and other than that.

We now have two generalities regarding reminder by the signs: the first generality is that they include both cosmic and legislative signs; the second is that they include the Qur'an and other than the Qur'an of the earlier Books. This is because the intended meaning of His words ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth﴾ [al-Furqan 63] is not restricted to the servants of the Most Merciful from this nation, but is general to all servants of the Most Merciful from every nation.

(﴿When they are reminded of the signs of their Lord, do not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾ [al-Furqan 73]: they do not fall upon them ﴿deaf and blind﴾, but rather they come to them hearing, seeing, and benefiting).

﴿do not fall upon them deaf﴾: plural of aṣamm, the one who does not hear; ﴿and blind﴾: plural of aʿmā, the one who does not see. He restricted it to these two faculties only because they are the means by which things reach the heart: things are either visible, whose means is sight, or audible, whose means is hearing. So He negated that they be deaf, and negated that they be blind.

As for His words ﴿do not fall﴾, the author says: (do not collapse), rather they approach them with the approach of one who hears and sees; not that they collapse upon them in this manner.

If someone says: this attribute is negative, and positive attributes are more eloquent in praise, so why did He not say: when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord, they approach them seeing and hearing?

* Student: Because first, the believers are described by the opposite of these attributes from among the positive attributes, so ﴿do not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾ indicates that they benefit from them (...) upon them.

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: Second: it contains an implicit allusion to those who fall upon them deaf and blind, who are the disbelievers.

* Shaykh: Excellent, yes. The first works out as a state under the first aspect; for we say: even if we say that this negation contains an affirmation, and negation is not praise unless it contains an affirmation, we still say: why was it not affirmed in the first place? So the difficulty is not removed. Rather it is said: it is an allusion to those who fall upon them deaf and blind. You know that this sūrah, from its beginning to its end, is a debate with those who deny what the Messenger ﷺ brought, and if they are deniers, they fall upon the signs deaf and blind. So this, and Allah knows best, is the point of relevance in turning from mentioning the positive attribute to mentioning the negative attribute: ﴿do not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: We say: an implicit allusion; for the sake of alluding to those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord, fall upon them deaf and blind.

* Student: (...) more.

* Shaykh: Huh?

* Student: (...) on their opposite.

* Shaykh: Yes, on their opposite. But we say: they are on their opposite; why did He not say: they fall upon them seeing and hearing? For the reason we mentioned.

(﴿do not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾ [al-Furqan 73] rather they come to them hearing, seeing, and benefiting).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verses 74–77 (part 1 of 5):

Then he said: (﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and our offspring"﴾ [al-Furqan 74], with the plural and singular readings).
﴿وَذُرِّيَّاتِنَا﴾ is plural, and ﴿وَذُرِّيَّتِنَا﴾ is singular.
﴿Grant us﴾ from them ﴿comfort of eyes, and make us leaders for the righteous﴾ (﴿comfort of eyes﴾ for us, by our seeing them obedient to You; ﴿and make us leaders for the righteous﴾ [al-Furqan 74] in goodness).

After Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the righteousness of these people themselves, He mentioned that they also strive to reform others connected to them, from spouses and offspring, so He said: ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, grant us"﴾ [al-Furqan 74]. In this there is clear evidence that the practice of the believers is to supplicate to Allah. As for the one who says, "His knowledge of my condition suffices instead of my asking," this is a false statement and is not correct, because we say: Allah, the Exalted, described the Messengers and their followers as those who supplicate to Allah, while they know with certainty that Allah knows their condition. Whoever says such a thing shows his arrogance toward supplicating to Allah, the Glorified and Exalted. Is that right?

* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: And what did we say?
* Student: We said that those who say that Allah's knowledge of the believer's condition is sufficient (...) about it.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: So the believers supplicated with the supplication of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and likewise the Messengers.
* Shaykh: Anything more?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. We said that this statement indicates the arrogance of the one who says it and his non-submission to his Lord. Otherwise, it is well known that Allah knows every person. So why do you not say, "O my Lord"? Why did you not say it? But this, and we seek refuge in Allah, is one of the satanic methods that Satan has sent upon those who follow them, from the Sufis and others.

﴿They say, "Our Lord, grant us"﴾: ﴿grant﴾ (hibah) means a gift. ﴿Grant us from our spouses and our offspring﴾ [al-Furqan 74].

Is ﴿مِنْ﴾ partitive, or is it explanatory of the kind?

* Student: It is explanatory of the kind.
* Shaykh: Eh?
* Student: For all of them: the righteousness of the offspring, all of them.
* Another student: For righteousness.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, it is explanatory of the kind. They do not mean: "Grant us some of our spouses, comfort of eyes from them," but rather all of them. No, but it is for clarification. ﴿مِنْ﴾ is explanatory, not partitive.

And His saying ﴿مِنْ أَزْوَاجِنَا﴾ is the plural of "zawj." Is it referring to the male or the female?

* Student: No (...).
* Shaykh: A man says it: ﴿And those who say﴾, because (alladhina) is for the masculine. A woman also says it, because address or speech in the masculine plural form includes the feminine as well. So a woman says it and a man says it too.

He says: ﴿Grant us from our spouses and our offspring﴾. There are two readings: ﴿وَذُرِّيَّتِنَا﴾ and ﴿وَذُرِّيَّاتِنَا﴾. As for the reading ﴿وَذُرِّيَّاتِنَا﴾, its meaning is apparent both in wording and in meaning. In wording, because of its agreement with the plural before it: ﴿from our spouses and our offspring﴾. In meaning, because it is more comprehensive, and its comprehensiveness is clear: it is for all of them.

As for ﴿وَذُرِّيَّتِنَا﴾, it does not match what comes before it in form, because it is singular, but it matches it in meaning, because it is a singular noun in the construct state (mufrad mudaf), and the singular construct noun denotes generality. Is that right?

* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Is there an example from the Quran showing that the singular construct noun denotes generality?
* Student: From the Quran?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: I do not recall.
* Shaykh: You do not recall?
* Student: Yes.
* Another student: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He has completed upon you His favors, apparent and hidden﴾ [Luqman 20].
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: His saying ﴿His favors﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, it is plural. Is there something similar you do not recall?
* Student: ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [al-Nahl 18].
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it.﴾ Certainly the meaning of ﴿favor﴾ here is the plural, because He said ﴿if you should count﴾. A single favor is not counted in the first place, and the second thing cannot be enumerated, and Allah says ﴿you could not enumerate it﴾. So this is a very clear example that the singular construct noun denotes generality and comprehensiveness.

So ﴿وَذُرِّيَّتِنَا﴾ in the singular reading agrees with what precedes it in meaning, because it includes all the offspring.

Who is meant by "offspring"? The offspring means children, males and females, and the children of sons, but not the children of daughters. The children of daughters are not offspring linguistically or legally according to many jurists. Yes, but it has been said: rather, the children of daughters are offspring, because Allah, the Exalted, said about Abraham: ﴿And among his offspring were David and Solomon and Job and Joseph and Moses and Aaron. Thus do We reward the doers of good. And Zechariah and John and Jesus﴾ [al-An'am 84–85]. Jesus was the son of a daughter and not the son of a son, yet Allah counted him among the offspring. This shows that the children of daughters are offspring.

But we say: there is no evidence in the verse, because Jesus, peace be upon him, had no father; that is, he had no lineage through a father, so it was cut off. For this reason, when a husband denies a child from his wife in a mutual curse (li'an), she becomes both mother and father.

So the correct view is that the children of daughters are not included in "offspring," linguistically and legally. As for endowments (waqf), gifts (hibah), and similar matters in which a person disposes of his property freely, this depends on what he stipulates. If he says, for example: "This is an endowment for my male and female offspring, and whoever of them dies leaving a child, his share goes to his child," what happens then? It belongs to all of them.

Likewise, if he says: "This is an endowment for my offspring and whoever descends from them," and he has only daughters, then the children of daughters are undoubtedly included. Or if he says, for example: "For my offspring and the children of daughters, who descend in the status of their mothers." Likewise: if he stipulates something, or the context indicates it, the children of daughters are included. But this inclusion follows what the wording requires by custom or by explicit statement, not by the Sharia or the Arabic language.

﴿Grant us from our spouses and our offspring comfort of eyes﴾ [al-Furqan 74]. What is the meaning of "comfort of eyes" (qurrat a'yun)? Is the meaning of "comfort of eyes" stability, derived from stability? Or is it derived from "qarr," which is cold, because they say that tears of a sad eye are hot and the eye that is comforted is cool?

Yes, this is the closer view, and it is not from stability, because a person's happiness is not described as his eye being comforted, nor is his sadness... (...). The matter is not like that. Rather, it is from "qarr," which is coolness, because when a person is sad his eye becomes hot. For this reason it is said: the tears of the sorrowful are hot.

So the meaning is joy, tranquility, and similar things. The eye is used figuratively because it is affected.

As for the author's words, "by our seeing them obedient to You," this is in truth one of the things that comfort the eye of the believer: that he sees his spouses and offspring obedient to Allah. Strangely, a Muslim, when he sees his spouses and offspring obedient to Allah, his eye is comforted even if he himself is a sinner. Strangely, a father rejoices that his child becomes obedient to Allah, avoiding sins, while he himself is a sinner! He loves that his child prays in congregation even though he himself does not pray, and likewise he loves that his child does not smoke, even though he himself smokes, because the Muslim is naturally disposed to love obedience to Allah. These are the ones who become a comfort of the eyes; that is, by our seeing them obedient to You. This is one point.

And it is also correct to say: "and for us," because a person's eye is comforted when his child and wife agree to obey him. Is his eye comforted or not? It is comforted, provided that this is combined with obedience to Allah. But if they obey him and disobey Allah, his eye is comforted in one respect: when he mentions their obedience to Allah and their performing acts of obedience to Allah, he is pleased and rejoices. But if he sees them disobeying Allah, he says to the child, "Sit in the café and wait for the men," but he goes out, yes.

And he says to the wife, "Prepare the food," but she does not prepare it. Undoubtedly this distresses him, and his eye is not comforted by it, even though this matter is disobedience to Allah. That is, if we wished, we could say that his saying "by our seeing them obedient to You" includes even their obedience to their father and a wife's obedience to her husband. It includes this and that, and likewise a man's fulfilling what is owed to his wife is included in that. That is, if we wished to say it this way, we could say it, but it goes against the apparent meaning of the words. So the correct view is: "by our seeing them obedient to You, and fulfilling what is obligatory upon them toward us," because by that the eye is settled.

He says: ﴿and make us leaders for the righteous﴾ [al-Furqan 74]. ﴿Leaders﴾ means examples, and an imam is an example who is followed.

His saying ﴿for the righteous﴾: the discussion of taqwa (God-consciousness) has been mentioned several times before, and that the meaning of taqwa is taking a protection from Allah's punishment, by doing what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden.

The meaning of their being ﴿leaders for the righteous﴾ is examples, that is, their being characterized by taqwa and their being characterized by knowledge. A person cannot be an example unless knowledge and taqwa are found in him, because if he is not knowledgeable, people will not trust him in matters of knowledge. The ignorant person is not followed. And if he is knowledgeable but has deviation in statement, action, or belief, he also cannot be an example for the righteous, not because of his lack of knowledge, but because of his lack of sincere counsel.

So this supplication, ﴿and make us leaders for the righteous﴾, includes three matters: knowledge, taqwa, and influence. Whoever is not knowledgeable is not an example, whoever is not God-conscious is not an example, and whoever has no influence is not an example either. Influence, by speech and by action, has a great role. You may find, for example, two men close in knowledge, but Allah turns hearts toward one of them so that they take him as an example, while the other does not attain this. So we say: add influence to knowledge and taqwa. And influence, as you know, has as its cause the strength of expression and eloquence if the influence is by speech, and it also has as its cause uprightness and good conduct if the influence is by action.

In any case, leadership is not complete except by these three matters: knowledge, taqwa, and influence by speech or by action.

In the verse there is a verbal difficulty, which is His saying: ﴿and make us leaders for the righteous﴾ [al-Furqan 74]. Because "make" (aj'al) is a verb that takes two objects, the first of which is a subject (mubtada') and the second a predicate (khabar). One of the conditions of the subject and predicate is that they agree in singularity, duality, and plurality.

Here, is the subject plural or not? ﴿and make us﴾: "us" (na) is plural. And ﴿for the righteous﴾, ﴿leaders﴾: this is the predicate, and it is the second object. Is it singular or plural?

* Student: Singular.
* Shaykh: Singular. It is singular, so a difficulty remains: the predicate does not agree with the subject. Agreement would require saying: "and make us leaders (a'immah) for the righteous." So what is the answer to this?

* Student: Can the predicate not be a clause?
* Shaykh: Where is the clause?
* Student: There is an implied element in it: ﴿leaders﴾ (...)?
* Shaykh: It does not become a clause, because this ﴿imaman﴾ is in the accusative case, so the verb governs it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. If he said, "for the righteous, a leader (imamun)," it would become a clause, although that is not appropriate, because it lacks a connecting pronoun. Yes?

* Student: We say that this is one of the descriptive words that suit the singular, the dual, and the plural.
* Shaykh: Is that so?
* Student: Perhaps, it is a point of view.
* Shaykh: You mean an argument of this kind?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, some have said this. They said that ﴿imaman﴾ is a word that suits the singular and other than it, like "fulk" (a ship, used for singular and plural) and "junub" (in a state of major impurity, used for singular and plural), and many other words of this type. According to this, there is no difficulty, because ﴿imaman﴾ means "a'immah," which is suitable for the plural.

And some have said: ﴿and make us leaders for the righteous﴾ [al-Furqan 74]: that "us" (na) stands for each one individually, not for the collective group. That is, make each one of us a leader.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is, each one supplicates for himself. That is, make each one of us a leader. Yes?

* Student: Or from their offspring?
* Shaykh: No, it is not from their offspring. ﴿and make us﴾ means we ourselves. So according to this...
* Student: Does it include them, sir?
* Shaykh: According to this there is also no difficulty. If we take the pronoun in ﴿and make us﴾ as not referring to the group, but to each individual from among all of them, then there is no difficulty in the matter. This is closer to the truth, because each believer does not ask Allah, Glorified and Exalted, that He make the whole group leaders. Rather, he wants to make each one of them a leader.

In this is evidence for the virtue of leadership in religion, including leading the prayer in mosques, because the imam in the mosque is a leader for the righteous, those who come to pray are righteous, God willing, so he is their leader. This indicates the virtue of taking on leadership of the prayer in mosques, and I think this is well known. The virtue of leading in mosques is well known. Even if there were nothing in it except that a person becomes an example, and that leadership helps him perform the prayer, the imam is not made to miss the prayer every day, whereas others miss it or miss part of it.

Likewise, when the imam speaks he is listened to more, and how many people have not become prominent except through their leadership, especially if they take on the sermon (khutbah).

The point is that these matters from which people, unfortunately, now shy away: you find that even some students of knowledge cannot take on leadership of a mosque even when there is a need for it. Whereas the obligation, or the strongly recommended duty, is that they themselves take on this leadership, so that they benefit and benefit others, and fill the gap that may be filled by someone whose religion and conduct cannot be trusted.

* Student: O Shaykh, if we could, for example, make awareness or guidance for people about loving leadership, so that (...), because until now, people who are willing to lead are approached by their fathers or relatives who say to them empty words: "You will bear the congregation's sin on the Day of Resurrection, and you may invalidate their prayers"?

* Shaykh: True, yes.
* Student: Yes, by Allah.
* Shaykh: Yes. Some people think that the imam is responsible for his congregation. He is not responsible at all; he is responsible for his own prayer. This responsibility is correct in terms of completing the prayer. For example, if I pray alone, I may limit myself to the obligatory acts only. But if I am an imam for others, I may not limit myself to the obligatory acts; I must perform the prayer completely. This is also a matter that imams must keep in mind, because some people say: "Since I am an imam, I will do the minimum obligatory." We say: Yes, if you were praying alone, there would be no harm in limiting yourself to the minimum obligatory, and no harm in lengthening it as much as you wish, as the Messenger (ﷺ) said. But if you are an imam, then you are now in a position of authority, and what must the one in authority do regarding the matter? Is it not the best? ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ [al-An'am 152]. So as long as you are now in charge, you must perform your prayer in the most complete manner, not limit yourself to the obligatory.

The jurists, may Allah have mercy on them, say: a hastiness that prevents the follower from doing what is sunnah is disliked, and a hastiness that prevents the follower from doing what is obligatory is forbidden. This is correct, but for me, even the first kind, hastiness that prevents the follower from doing what is sunnah, is not merely disliked, but forbidden. Why forbidden? Because you are now in charge, and the one in charge must do what is most beneficial for those under his charge, and there is no doubt that the most beneficial thing is to follow the Sunnah.

Just as we said regarding matters in which a person is given a choice: if it concerns himself, the choice is one of whim, he does what he desires, like the choice among the expiations for an oath, for example: feeding ten needy persons, or clothing them, or freeing a slave.

And if the choice concerns the benefit of others, is the choice one of whim or of benefit? It is a choice of benefit.

* Student: Some imams, O Shaykh, say: "I (...)." Is there responsibility on his part?
* Shaykh: The imam has no responsibility in this beyond what is on anyone else. Every person who sees an evil should change it.
* Student: And his responsibility is not increased in that?
* Shaykh: Not at all, it is not increased.
* Student: But (...)?
* Shaykh: He is like others. Likewise, if there is a person of standing in the mosque whose word is heard, he has more authority than the imam. We say: he is like others, according to his situation. The person who can change by his hand changes by his hand, the one who cannot change by his tongue, and the one who cannot change by his heart.

**Student:** But, Shaykh, for example, he is able to be just, he is able to verify?

**Shaykh:** He is not obligated to be just at all.

**Student:** But (...)?

**Shaykh:** No, cooperation? Everyone wants cooperation in this matter.

**Student:** That the matter is well known (...)?

**Shaykh:** Even if we suppose that the man said: "If I become an imam, I will bind myself to this." Is this from good or from evil?

**Student:** From good.

**Shaykh:** Yes, praise be to God. If it is from good, let it be something that calls to the imamate and encourages it. The truth is that God, glorified and exalted, has made conditions for things: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾ [al-'Ankabut 69]. God does not guide a person to His path except after he strives in it. If you want to reach something that brings joy, delight and happiness, it is not possible on the wings of the wind. There must be thorns, stones and everything else. "Paradise is surrounded by hardships."[[Narrated by Muslim (2822 / 1) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]]

**Student:** Shaykh, now (...)?

**Shaykh:** It is not necessary, brother. There is no doubt that it is a perfection for the imam to be a scholar or a student of knowledge who can speak. But if he is not?

**Student:** He forbids what is right, even if (...).

**Shaykh:** No, I (...) the imam. I say: it is obligatory that we fill the vacancy with someone other than them, because they are numerous and foreigners among us, and all our mosques have become (...). The imam has influence. That is, if it were not that people have adherence and lack of trust in foreigners, and great trust in citizens, all those who pray behind the foreigners would be saying the basmalah aloud, performing the qunut in the dawn prayer, and so on. But, praise be to God, until now they have not gained acceptance in the country, and this is from the blessing of God. Otherwise they would have had a tremendous influence. So the imam undoubtedly influences those behind him. Yes, we say: it is obligatory upon the citizens among us to fill this vacancy, lest it be occupied by someone who is not trustworthy.

**Student:** The one who smokes (...)?

**Shaykh:** (...), and smoking is less serious than creed, because the problem now is creed. The important thing is creed. Yes.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** The matter of closing this mosque is a duty (*wazifa*). Even the jurists call them duties.

**Student:** He is obligated to things other than (...).

**Another student:** True, because I saw (...). It is obligatory on the imam to do such-and-such, and it is obligatory on him to do such-and-such.

**Shaykh:** It does not contradict. It is obligatory on the imam to do such-and-such by virtue of the imamate. And does this also prevent (...)? Because if you do not do it, a foreigner will do it.

**Student:** If he does not believe this thing and he prevents it (...)?

**Shaykh:** How does he not believe? Whatever you believe?

**Student:** The person who guides people (...) until he says a good word.

**Shaykh:** And what makes you know that he will say a good word?

**Student:** Clear, the person (...).

**Shaykh:** Not at all, it is not clear. Before he speaks, and he is unknown to you, it is not clear.

**Student:** Perhaps if good does not happen (...).

**Shaykh:** Difficult.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** No, not at all.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Then also, the imam himself may not have the understanding to say that good word. He may bring you a fabricated hadith: (...) characteristic, yes, all of them are fabricated hadiths. How do you know this? That is, guarding against evil before falling into it is better for a person (...).

**Student:** The better thing, Shaykh, is not to prevent (...) from speaking.

**Shaykh:** First, I do not think anyone speaks while the Messenger is present.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** This is one point. Likewise, we have not known anyone to speak while the imams are present. The second point: we are not saying that the truth must be prevented. But we say: who says that these people want the truth? We find that many speak, and when they achieve their aims they say: "Give us." This is what must be prevented and also struck. That is, they hunt the world with religion? (...).

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes, if we have (...), we hear about this.

**Student:** But perhaps he may be known, Shaykh?

**Shaykh:** And what is it that is known?

**Student:** This person.

**Shaykh:** The one who speaks?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** If he becomes known, he is never prevented. If he becomes known, he is not prevented. But now they say, that is, I have not received anything of this (...), but I firmly affirm that they say: "The one you do not know, no (...)."

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** The important thing is that this does not prevent it, brothers. It is not a barrier to assuming the imamate. Just as, if you were not an imam, and someone who assumes the imamate allowed people to speak, would you do so? Never. My point is that the imamate has many benefits, not only for the person himself, because he can speak what he wishes and guide people when he is not an imam. If he came to speak, the imam would say to him: "Do not speak, on their words." But if he becomes the imam, will anyone prevent him from saying, "Let me speak"? Thus he benefits people with his knowledge.

Furthermore, it also helps one to obedience. I feel this. When I was not an imam, sometimes I would miss some prayers and become lazy, and sometimes we would go to that mosque and sometimes to that mosque. But when I became an imam, praise be to God, I do not miss the congregational prayer.

**Student:** But what about the reward, Shaykh, if the one who regulates the prayer, and he was from the beginning (...), does his reward not decrease because of his earliness?

**Shaykh:** It does not decrease at all. Because things encouraging a person, the fact that a person has motivations toward good, does not nullify his reward. Why did God make the incentives toward good in the Book and the Sunnah, if not for a reward one strives for?

**Student:** But there are people (...)?

**Shaykh:** No, this is not a matter of earliness. It is a matter that you are helped (...) only toward earliness, toward attaining the congregation as well. Perhaps I would not be early.

**Student:** Yes, indeed, attaining it.

**Shaykh:** Yes, this is among what helps. Did God not make for people a share of the spoils of war? Did He not make a provision from the public treasury for the imams and the muezzins? Did the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, not encourage giving to those whose hearts are to be reconciled (*al-mu'allafa qulubuhum*)? And other than that. That is, the fact that a person has motivations toward good does not nullify his reward. The matter rests on the intention, originally. If you do this for the world, this is correct, and this affects you greatly. But if God makes easy for you, from the causes of obedience, what helps you in it, then this is good, and it does not diminish the reward.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** Indeed, the Messenger ﷺ encouraged this matter, what helps: "Take a pre-dawn meal, for in the pre-dawn meal there is blessing."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1923) and Muslim (1095 / 45) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]] "And he would pour water over his head while fasting because of the heat."[[Abu Dawud (2365) narrated from some Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ, on his journey in the year of the Conquest, command the people to break the fast, and he said: 'Strengthen yourselves for your enemy.' The Messenger of God ﷺ fasted." Abu Bakr, one of the narrators, said: "The one who related to me said: 'I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ at al-'Araj pouring water over his head while fasting, from thirst or from heat.'"]] All of this helps one toward obedience. So motivations toward good do not diminish the good. The matter rests only on the intention: if you do this thing for the world, you see it as correct, this (...).

**Student:** But perhaps the person may hasten, Shaykh, his intention (...), that is, for example, it becomes his habit?

**Shaykh:** Yes, if he shows off to people in this, that is another matter. Even the one who is not an imam may see that he is missed in the congregation, and he should not be missed even if he is not an imam. So the matter returns to the intention. If he is ashamed before people, then this undoubtedly diminishes his reward. But if he does not say, "I hasten to fulfill my duty and not to disturb the people," sometimes he goes forward and sometimes he goes back, this is good. He hastens only to perfect his action.

**Student:** Some of the imams now (...)?

**Shaykh:** But the one who (...), we cannot say to him "delay," because our original choice is at the beginning of the imam's appointment. So if an imam is found, we cannot dismiss him except for a legal reason.

**Student:** Voluntary, that is, perhaps the person is a volunteer, he says: (...).

**Shaykh:** But he is not obedient.

**Student:** This is problematic.

**Shaykh:** No, it is not problematic. You have its meaning (...) the imams, the country that is in this description (...).

**Student:** (...) four young men behind a lay imam.

**Shaykh:** We wish they would come to us, these ones.

**Student:** The speech (...).

**Shaykh:** No, (...) in the Tarawih some of them performed some of the duty, but (...).

**Student:** Shaykh.

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** Do we not make an awareness campaign regarding encouraging people to take up the imamate?

**Shaykh:** (...) without an awareness campaign.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** No, by God, I have not done it.

**Student:** Perhaps, Shaykh, if you do it, there will be an enthusiasm among the young men?

**Shaykh:** By God, perhaps, God willing. It will happen, God willing, if there is an occasion.

**Student:** (...) if he agrees?

**Shaykh:** Yes, if he agrees there is no objection, especially if the one who assumes it is better than him. If the one who will assume it is better than him, this is good.

**Student:** But if this imam were present, (...).

**Shaykh:** Then this is a concession from him, because the salary, to whom will it go? It goes to the second, and the second receives it by his concession. It does not matter. And this happened, as I heard, to the muezzin of the Great Mosque in Riyadh, Ibn Majid. He was calling the adhan at a mosque (...). When that new, large mosque was built, they asked him to be its muezzin, but its first imam was not content with that. So they gave him a salary, and the duties of the mosque, and they gave him a new salary.

**Student:** Shaykh.

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** There are some imams, for example, whose path is at home, for example (...), I pray, for example, at the times I can attend the mosque, and he appoints another person from the people of the town, who used to help him at times (...)?

**Shaykh:** I say: there is no objection. If you are absent, then pray.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** No, this is most of what (...), just as the brother said. He says: "By God, this ties one down and occupies one. I wish one day to walk here, one day to walk there, and one day..."

**Student:** Its intention, Shaykh, this (...)?

**Shaykh:** By God, I say: ﴿And whoever fears God, He will make for him a way out of his affair with ease﴾ [at-Talaq 4]. All these obstacles, their original state is non-existence. So be certain, and seek the reward from God, and God will help you. God will make ease for you in your affair.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** Yes, indeed, correct.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** That does not mean, if we say that the adhan is better than the imamate, that the imamate has no (...).

**Student:** Perhaps, Shaykh.

**Shaykh:** We say: be a muezzin (...), may God reward you with good. If you were eager for good, then be a muezzin, and be an imam.

**Student:** And the first hadith, the hadith: "The imam is a guarantor"?[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (517) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]

**Shaykh:** The hadith "The imam is a guarantor," if it is authentic at all. The hadith has some discussion, but if it is authentic, the meaning is that the imam is responsible for those behind him, that is, a guarantor for them. He must perform his prayer in the most perfect manner, as we said a little while ago.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** Yes, if he leads them in prayer, yes, (...). If one prays with them, and the imam is in a state of ritual impurity, and what (...).

**Student:** Shaykh.

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** If an imam, for example, became convinced that (...).

**Shaykh:** It is better that he takes it. We see that it is better that he takes it, neither the salary nor the duties of the mosque.

**Student:** Perhaps he says: this is an addition of good and reward, God willing.

**Shaykh:** Yes, he is upon good. He takes it, as long as his intention was originally only for God. Did the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and his Companions not take from the spoils of war or not?

**Student:** Yes indeed.

**Shaykh:** Is there anyone more sincere than them?

**Student:** No.

**Shaykh:** (...) and if you wish, take it and spend it on something beneficial to you. That is, the reality of the matter, as they said: if you do not take it yourself, the mosque will be disrupted. If a new imam comes after you, he will need a new transaction. Yes indeed. Likewise, the duties: some people say, "By God (...) the imam or the muezzin." We say: this is up to you. That is, whether you take it or do not take it is another matter. But considering that if you leave it and (...), you go to someone else as well, because the imam in reality is not independent, nor the muezzin, in what is given from every aspect.

**Shaykh:** (Among them: ﴿Those, God will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾ [al-Furqan 70].)
This is an exception from His saying: ﴿he will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan 68], and what was substituted from it. That is: ﴿except one who repents﴾ [al-Furqan 70], for he will not meet a penalty, his punishment will not be multiplied, and he will not abide in it.

It has preceded that the conditions of repentance are five: sincerity to God, remorse for what occurred, ceasing from it, resolving not to return to it, and that it be at the time when repentance is accepted, in its time.

It has also preceded that this exception includes all three great sins: polytheism, killing a soul, and fornication. As for what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, "that the murderer has no repentance,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4764) and Muslim (3023 / 19).]] if he means it absolutely, then it is not correct. If he means that the murderer has no repentance regarding the right of the one killed, then this is correct. Yet we say: it is not far-fetched that if he repents a sincere repentance, God, the Mighty and Blessed, will bear on his behalf the right of the one killed and satisfy him.

**Student:** The statement of Ibn al-Qayyim in *I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in* that the legal punishments (*hudud*) fall away with repentance (...), and he cited the hadith of an-Nasa'i: "A man had intercourse with a woman, and she called out for help to a man, and he passed by (...), and they seized the man whom she had called for help, and they took him to the Prophet ﷺ, and she said: 'This is the one who committed fornication with me.' When the Prophet ﷺ wanted to carry out upon him the punishment for slander, a man confessed in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'I am the one who did it to her.' 'Umar said: 'Will you not carry out the punishment on this one who confessed?' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'He has repented.'"[[Ahmad (27240) narrated from the hadith of Wa'il ibn Hujr, who said: A woman went out to the prayer, and a man met her and covered her with his garments, and he fulfilled his need from her and departed. Another man came to her, and she said to him: "The man did such-and-such to me." The man went in pursuit of him. A group of the Ansar came upon her and stood over her, and she said to them: "A man did such-and-such to me." They went in pursuit of him and brought the man who had gone in pursuit of the man who had had intercourse with her, and they took him to the Prophet ﷺ, and she said: "He is the one." When the Prophet ﷺ ordered his stoning, the one who had had intercourse with her said: "O Messenger of God, by God, I am the one." He said to the woman: "Go, for God has forgiven you," and he said to the man a good word. It was said: "O Prophet of God, will you not stone him?" He said: "He has repented a repentance which, if the people of Madinah repented it, would have been accepted from them." Abu Dawud (4379) and at-Tirmidhi (1454) also narrated it from the hadith of Wa'il ibn Hujr in another wording, that the Prophet ﷺ said a good word to the man who was seized. Abu Dawud said: that is, the man who was seized. He said to the man who had had intercourse with her: "Stone him," and he said: "He has repented a repentance which, if the people of Madinah repented it, would have been accepted from them."]] (...)?

**Shaykh:** This is correct by the Qur'an: ﴿Except those who repent before you have power over them; so know that God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 34].

**Student:** But the punishment is not carried out on him?

**Shaykh:** The punishment is not carried out on him if he repents before you have power over him. If this is about highway robbers (*qutta' at-tariq*), and their sin is among the greatest sins, then it is all the more so. Except for the punishment for slander, if we say that it is a right of the human being, then it does not fall away except by the pardon of the one slandered.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Huh?

**Student:** His confession..

**Shaykh:** Regarding the matter of repentance, or that the Messenger knew this from him. The important thing is that if he repents before you have power over him, the punishment is not carried out on him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 25, verse 74–77 (part 3 of 5):

﴿Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Furqan 70]. Repentance (tawbah) has already been discussed. Faith (iman) linguistically means affirmation and acknowledgment, but in the Shari'ah it is the affirmation of the heart that necessarily entails acceptance and submission. It is not mere affirmation; it is an affirmation that necessarily entails this. If it does not entail it, it is not faith.

We say: necessarily entails what? Acceptance and submission: he accepts what the Shari'ah has brought and submits to it, so he affirms it if it is a report, and acts upon it if it is a command.

* Student: And if the murderer does not repent?
* Shaykh: If the murderer does not repent, then he is subject to the threat that Allah the Exalted mentioned.
* Student: Is it not one of the major sins (kaba'ir)?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed.
* Student: And major sins are under the Will of Allah?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is under the Will, but who says that He will forgive him?

His saying: ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾ [al-Furqan 70]. Here he mentioned the deed and described it as righteous, because a deed that is not righteous does not benefit its doer. A righteous deed is that which combines two conditions: sincerity to Allah (ikhlas), and following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (mutaba'ah). If it lacks sincerity, it is not accepted; and if it lacks following, it is not accepted. In the Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah the Exalted said: I am the most independent of partners from association. Whoever does a deed in which he associates others with Me, I leave him and his association." This is evidence that a deed without sincerity is rejected.

As for a deed without following, it is because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected." Agreed upon; al-Bukhari with similar wording (2697), and Muslim (1718/18) with his wording, from the hadith of 'A'ishah.

Both are combined in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf 110].

His saying: (منهم) "from among them" — from whom? That is, from the doers of these three matters: associating partners with Allah, killing a soul, and fornication. He restricted it to these by the context, and so that it does not repeat with what follows.

(﴿then Allah will replace their evil deeds﴾ mentioned ﴿with good deeds﴾ [al-Furqan 70] in the Hereafter.) He replaces them. Tabdil (replacement) is placing one thing in the place of another. Is this replacement a qadari (decreed) replacement or a jaza'i (recompense) replacement?

The people of knowledge differed on this. Some said it is a qadari replacement, and some said it is a jaza'i replacement. How so?

Those who say it is a qadari replacement say: the meaning of the replacement of evil deeds with good deeds is that when he believed and did righteous deeds, his faith and righteous deeds replaced the disbelief, fornication and killing; meaning that this faith and righteous deed he performed are the good deeds with which Allah, Blessed and Exalted, replaced the evil deeds. So this replacement is qadari.

It was also said: rather it is jaza'i, meaning that these sins themselves become good deeds: Allah replaces the previous evil deeds, making them good deeds, in addition to his later good deeds which were decreed for him so that he did them. How so? They say: because when he repented from these evil deeds, he gained for every repentance from these evil deeds a good deed, so the evil deeds became good deeds through repentance from them; and because whenever he remembers what preceded of his evil actions, he renews repentance for them, so these previous deeds became good deeds through repentance from them.

The correct view is that the verse includes both of these, and that the verse encompasses both matters: ﴿whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds﴾ has his previous evil deeds replaced so they become good deeds, but they are not the same first deeds; and likewise, if he repents from them, he is rewarded for this repentance, so the evil deeds become good through repentance from them.

The author's speech leans toward the second view, that this replacement is a jaza'i replacement, due to his saying: (في الآخرة) "in the Hereafter." Because if it were qadari, it would not be in the Hereafter, since qadari replacement occurs only in this world, as it is his deed.

The correct view is that the verse includes both. By faith and righteous deeds his deeds are changed into righteous deeds, and by repentance from evil deeds the previous evil deeds become good deeds, because through this repentance he increases in elevation and rank with Allah, the Exalted.

(﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan 70], meaning He has never ceased to be characterized by that.)

Here "kana" (was/is) is, as we have passed, stripped of time, and what is meant by it is that its subject is characterized by its predicate as a necessary attribute. For this reason he said: (meaning He has never ceased to be characterized by that), that is, by forgiveness and mercy.

Al-Ghafur is either an intensive form (sighah mubalaghah) or an attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah), and both indicate permanence, continuity and abundance.

Forgiveness (maghfirah) is covering the sin together with overlooking it; meaning covering the sin and removing its punishment, not mere covering, because it is derived from al-maghfar (helmet), and by the helmet there is covering and protection.

As for al-Rahim, he is the possessor of mercy that reaches those who are shown mercy, because it indicates the act together with the attribute. Mercy is an attribute of Allah, the Exalted, through which bounty and kindness to creation occur by bringing benefits and warding off harms.

As for those who interpret mercy as kindness or as the will to be kind, their statement is mistaken, because the will to be kind is one of the effects of mercy, and so is kindness; it is not mercy itself.

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan 70]. Yes?

* Student: Shaykh, our saying ﴿And Allah was Forgiving⦆ here is an attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah), perhaps (...), Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Although it is in the accusative and does not govern or take a genitive.
* Shaykh: It is not necessary that it governs or is annexed. Its accusative case is due to the governing element, its accusative is due to the governing element.
* Student: A hadith has been reported with the meaning: the servant continues to see his evil deeds placed in the scale of his good deeds; meaning the one who repents.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Until he wishes that he had committed more evil deeds?
* Shaykh: I do not know this hadith, but considering that they are the replacement of evil deeds with good deeds, it is possible from this aspect.

(﴿And whoever repents﴾ [al-Furqan 71] from his sins, other than those mentioned.) Therefore, regarding those mentioned earlier, he said: (﴿and does righteous deeds﴾ [al-Furqan 70] from among them), from these people.

He said "other than those mentioned" so that repetition does not follow. But there is no objection to saying: there is no need for an exception, and the second verse is general, so it is of the type of mentioning the general after the specific, because excluding those mentioned earlier from the generality of this verse has no basis. The better view is that the second verse is general, including those mentioned earlier and others.

(﴿And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, then indeed he returns to Allah with a return﴾ [al-Furqan 71], meaning he returns to Him with a return, so He recompenses him with good.)

Look: ﴿whoever repents and does righteous deeds﴾. ﴿Repents﴾: he turns back from his sin. ﴿Does righteous deeds﴾: he seeks more of righteous deeds. So this man has sought to make amends for what he did and has increased in goodness.

He says: ﴿then indeed he returns to Allah with a return﴾, meaning: ﴿a return﴾ complete. The verbal noun here is for magnification, to magnify this repentance; that is, a great return due to the perfection of this repentance. Otherwise, someone might say: this is a tautology, whoever repents is certainly a penitent?!

No, the intent is that his repentance is a complete, great repentance. The use of the verbal noun: ﴿then indeed he returns to Allah with a return﴾ indicates that this repentance has occurred in its proper place and is complete. This is true, for when a man repents and increases in righteous deeds, the soundness and perfection of his repentance become evident.

The scholars differed, may Allah have mercy on them: is it a condition of repentance that the deed be reformed or not?

Some said: reforming the deed is a condition for it, and on this view it is a sixth condition in addition to the five conditions, and whoever repents but does not reform his deed is not a penitent.

Some scholars said: rather repentance is valid without reforming the deed. Others said: if the deed is of the same kind as what he repented from, then its reform is necessary, otherwise repentance is not valid.

An example: a man repents from fornication but steals. On the first view, his repentance from fornication is not valid because the deed is not reformed; on the second view, it is valid, because theft is not of the same kind as fornication; on the third view, a fortiori, reforming the deed is not required absolutely, and whoever repents from a sin, his repentance is accepted.

Another man repents from fornication but continues in forbidden gazing, looking at women in a forbidden way. On the view that reforming the deed is not required, his repentance from fornication is valid; on the view that reforming the deed is necessary, his repentance from fornication is not valid; and on the middle view, that if it is of the same kind as what he repented from it is not accepted, it is also not valid, because this is the fornication of the eye, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said.

[Hadith: Ahmad (8356) from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The eye commits fornication, and the heart commits fornication; the fornication of the eye is looking, and the fornication of the heart is desire, and the private part confirms that or denies it."]

But the correct view is to say: if by repentance is meant describing this man as among the penitents who receive praise and to whom the description of "penitent" truly applies, then his repentance cannot be valid, nor can he deserve the description of repentance, except by reforming the deed; because he has not repented with absolute repentance, but has only a general repentance. As for if by repentance is meant repentance from this specific deed, the correct judgment is that his repentance is accepted, because this is the requirement of the justice of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: whoever does good, it is for him, and whoever does evil, it is against him. ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah 7–8]. How then can we say that this man's repentance from a deed he repented from, turned back from and regretted is not valid, because he persists in another sin? That is not correct.

So the correct view in this matter is: as for deserving the description of penitents in an absolute sense, the penitent does not deserve it except by reforming the deed; for how can one be a penitent to Allah while he persists in disobedience, even if it is of a different kind from what he repented from or of the same kind!

As for when the intent is repentance from this specific deed, meaning a general repentance, not absolute repentance, it is certainly valid, because this is the requirement of the justice of Allah, the Exalted.

* Student: Shaykh, in the hadith: "A man committed a sin, then repented, then sinned again, then repented, then sinned again, then repented. Then Allah, the Exalted, said: My servant knows that (...), so let My servant do what he wills," or as he said.

**Shaykh Ibn 'Uthaymin's Commentary (Tafsir al-Qur'an al-Karim) on Surah al-Furqan, verses 74–77 (part 4 of 5)**

(...) after the prayer is ordinary, a habit. The reality is that these are matters..., and this is what in truth corrupts us: that we do not feel the actions of the heart. You find many of us observing the Sunnah of raising the finger during supplication, but raising the heart during supplication, no one investigates it, even though this is more important. We have said that His saying, "then indeed he turns to Allah with a return," is not like the speaker's saying, "The earth is beneath us and the sky above us," meaning a self-evident statement. Rather, the meaning is that this is the true, sincere, complete repentance.
And His saying, "to Allah": meaning he returns to Allah with a complete, thorough return, as the author (al-Mu'allif, i.e., the author of the work being commented upon) said.
"And those who do not bear witness to falsehood" (25:72). Is this conjoined to His saying?
* **Student:** "And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who" (25:63).
* **Another student:** No, it is conjoined to the whole set of attributes.

("And those who do not bear witness to falsehood" (25:72): meaning lies and vanity.)
This is the meaning of *al-zur* (falsehood), from *izdarra*, meaning he inclined and deviated: "And you see the sun, when it rises, inclining away from their cave to the right" (18:17). So the meaning of *al-zur* is every verbal or practical deviation. If it is a statement, it is described as a lie. If it is an action, it is described as vanity. So every statement or action that deviates from the path is *zur*. Is this understood now?
* **Student:** Yes.
* **Shaykh:** Lying is *zur*. Insulting, cursing, and backbiting are also *zur*. Usurpation, theft, fornication, and others are also *zur*.

* **Shaykh:** *Zur*. It is *zur*, but we may call it vanity when it is an action.
So the point is that they "do not bear witness to falsehood." If they do not bear witness to falsehood, do they perform it?
* **Student:** No.
* **Shaykh:** All the more so. For if they do not attend it, they certainly do not do it, since if they did it they would attend it. Every doer is present, but not every present person is a doer in the literal sense. Yet he is a doer in judgment, based on the saying of Allah, the Exalted: "And He has already revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being denied and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in another topic. This indicates that the one who sits, whether sitting, reclining, or standing, the point is that the one who witnesses the sinner's act is like the sinner in judgment before Allah. Yes, except one who was forced to attend. That is a different matter, having no ruling, just as one who was forced to act.

* **Shaykh:** All sins, yes.
("And those who do not bear witness to falsehood, and when they pass by idle talk," meaning ugly speech and other things, "they pass by with dignity" (25:72), meaning turning away from it.)
"And when they pass by idle talk" (*al-laghw*). The correct view is that it is not ugly speech, because ugly speech falls under *zur*. Rather, *al-laghw* means whatever has no benefit. Everything without benefit is *laghw*, because it is not intended. And what is not intended is *laghw*: "Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle (*laghw*) in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have intended in the oaths" (5:89). So *laghw* is what has no benefit.
* **Student:** Even if it is permissible?

His saying here: "And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity" (25:72), is not like the earlier verse: "And when the ignorant address them, they say, 'Peace'" (25:63). Because there, there is a specific, direct address, so they must say something by which they are safe. But here, they pass by something without being addressed by it. What is meant by passing by it is whether they pass by it in a path, or are sitting and something without benefit comes up, which is *laghw*. They pass by with dignity. The meaning of passing by with dignity here is that nothing from it touches them, but rather they try to reform it, because the noble person gives to others. He benefits himself and others.
So when they "pass by idle talk," they pass by "with dignity," trying to benefit from their presence by turning this idle talk into something beneficial. Did you understand or not? For this reason He said "they pass by with dignity," not "they say, 'Peace,'" because there they are addressed with what offends them, so they say something by which they are safe, since the situation only requires that you be safe. So he benefits and is benefited.
